I. Introductory. To reduce the law of evidence to clear, universal rules, to rules which have no exceptions, seems impossible. 

To formulate substantive law into rules is difficult; but the law of evidence which must govern at times the trial of all disputes which may arise in all fields of human activity is so broad in its operation, that to codify it seems almost beyond human power. Yet the aim of jurists has been to establish, as far as possible, in the form of rules, the principles which govern the admission and exclusion of evidence, and their aim has been accomplished, to a considerable extent, by establishing certain principles which apply to a part of the law of evidence, and by establishing likewise certain exceptions to those principles.¹ 

Scarcely a rule of evidence exists which has not an exception; and though courts have established certain rules which are well recognized in all American jurisdictions, such as the exclusion of hearsay and the parol evidence rule, yet the field in which the trial court has absolute or limited discretion in the admission and exclusion of evidence is still large.¹ 

Here then are illustrated the two important and contradictory theories on which the law of evidence rests. On the one hand is the theory that we should live under a government of laws and not of men," that judges should be limited in their discretion, that the substantive and adjective law should be matters of positive rule, and that in passing on the admissibility of evidence the personal element should be reduced to a minimum. The followers of this principle seek positive rules of evidence which will govern and override the trial court's discretion. On the other hand there is a group which adopts the theory that each case and controversy differ in their minute details from every other case and controversy, that an individual judge should not be hampered by complicated and set rules of evidence, and that the best person to determine what evidence, in a particular case, should be admitted is the trial court.6 

Though the latter group of jurists is not small, yet it may be stated with assurance that the tendency is and will be toward the

II. General principles which determine admissibility. It is well to consider the principles which govern, in large, the admission and exclusion of evidence. To be admitted, the subject matter offered must have a logical bearing on the issue on trial or on some collateral issue, such as the credibility of a witness, which renders it of some logical value to the tribunal which is to determine the facts. This seems self evident. The law has passed the stage where it recognized the superstitions that water would reject the guilty, and that the righteous would survive in battle. 

It has yet to face the possible inroads of science. As yet, however, men and cases are not to be tried by the administration of a truth serum," and the theories of Professor Munsterberg are yet but interesting reading. To-day the basis of the rules of evidence is logic.

Though the offered evidence is found to have a logical connection with the issue, it is not always to be received. It must, before its reception, pass the test of the established rules which exclude incompetent evidence. The court on objection will consider whether it is to be shut out by either of three principles. 

Is it inadmissible by the substantive law? Is it inadmissible under the statutory law? Is it admissible under the established rules of evidence? If the evidence is to be excluded under either of the two former of these, though an objection to the evidence will exclude it, yet the question of admission or exclusion is not solely a matter of evidence and no rule of evidence should be

Testimony of this character barring the sufficient fact that it cannot be otherwise classified than a self-serving declaration, is, in the present state of human knowledge, unworthy of serious consideration. If it is, it is to be excluded unless it fails under one of the exceptions. As an illustration let us assume that evidence logically relevant to the issue is offered. No rule of substantive law excludes it, no statute renders it inadmissible. It is objected to as hearsay. If it were admitted without objection it would have probative value. The court must consider before admitting it whether the evidence is hearsay. If it is he must exclude it unless it falls within one of the exceptions to the hearsay rule.10 If it falls within such exception it is to be admitted unless some other rule of law or evidence excludes it. What other rules of law or evidence may exclude it? It may be remote,¹¹ it may tend to prejudice the jury,¹º it may be shown inadmissible by some preliminary finding of the court,18 or it may be excluded by rules of public policy or privilege.14 This is but an illustration. Many principles other than those that are based on the rules against hearsay may render evidence, which logically bears on the issue, inadmissible. 

It is to the consideration of those principles that this chapter is directed.

IV. Suggested general rules. To lay down rules of evidence in all matters, as said above, at present seems impossible. No sooner is a rule suggested than exceptions arise. Even a rule so general as "All evidence relevant to the issue is admissible',26 is subject to so many exceptions that it means almost nothing. 

Evidence that in everyday life we would consider of importance in determining facts, at the trial of a case, frequently is excluded. 

Hearsay, privileged matter,27 the character of the person with whom we deal,28 his acts at other times,29 and many other matters generally considered relevant out of court, meet rules of exclusion at the trial of a case which render them, though relevant, inadmissible. So with a rule that "Nothing which is not relevant to the issue on trial is to be admitted. ''80 It has exceptions.

V. Rules of absolute exclusion distinguished from rules which tend to cause exclusion. The rules of exclusion of evidence are of two classes-those which absolutely exclude an offered proof and those which but tend to. exclude it. If offered evidence falls within the first class, it is to be excluded unless the rule has an exception; if it falls within the second the matter which tends to exclude the evidence is to be considered by the court, with all attendant circumstances, and then the court, within his discretion, will admit or exclude the evidence.84 Illustrations will make this clearer. Let us first note a statutory provision for exclusion,—namely that neither husband nor wife shall testify to a private conversation between them.35 Here is an absolute rule. The court, regardless of the importance of the testimony or of the attendant circumstances except when statutory exception permits a different result, in the face of objection, cannot allow the evidence to be presented.37 It is absolutely barred by a rule of law. So of hearsay evidence. If evidence offered is mere hearsay,38 the court on objection must exclude it unless the offered testimony comes within one of the established exceptions to the rules of exclusion. Of course new questions may arise, and new exceptions to the rules of exclusion may be created, but the general rule is that hearsay evidence, unless it falls within the exceptions later pointed out,40 must be excluded.

Contrast these two illustrations with a case wherein the offered evidence is objected to as remote. On such objection the court will consider remoteness as one of the factors which will tend

Knowledge is the fundamental basis of a witness's ability to testify; and though, at present, experts may express opinions on matters which in the words of the old authority they do not "see and hear," and certain statements by deceased persons 45 and certain book entries are to be received as evidence of the truth of their contents, as will be hereafter set forth, yet these are but exceptions to the ancient rule, and personal knowledge, at least is an important factor in determining the weight of evidence, the qualification of the expert and ultimate admissibility. 1. Application of the rule: Hearsay. In our daily life we frequently make our decisions on facts which come to us as hearsay. In our courts, however, this form of testimony is and always has been objectionable.48 A witness to facts and conversations must testify to what he himself saw and heard; and he must stand up to cross examination on these facts. What others told him, unless the evidence falls within the exceptions to the rules of exclusion, on objection 50 is not to be received as proof of the matter which it embodies. Such evidence if admitted without objection, to be sure, has probative value,51 and a party may sus tain the burden of proof, unless a positive rule of law forbids,52 by hearsay evidence admitted without objection.58 Still the rule stands as the strongest and clearest in the law of evidence. 

Hearsay is not admissible. The rule is absolute. The court has no discretion in admitting or excluding hearsay. If the evidence offered to prove a fact is hearsay, is objected to, and does not lie within the exceptions to the rules of exclusion,54 it is not admissible and must be excluded. 

No sooner is the rule a. Exceptions to the hearsay rule. stated than the exceptions to the rule become apparent. Indeed in these exceptions lies the great bulk of the law of evidence.55 

No other rule of evidence has so many, so important, or so clearly established qualifications. Though the rule declares that hearsay is not admissible, yet certain statements made by partners, co-partners,57 or agents,58 associated with, or employed by an adversary, if within the scope of their association or authority, when material, are admissible against the adversary;59 so of admissions and confessions of a party when offered against him;60 of certain testimony at former trials,61 to a limited extent 56

2. Application of the rule: Requirement of observation and attention: Conjecture: Negative testimony. Mere conjecture or surmise is not proof." Hence testimony based solely on conjecture or surmise is to be excluded. Evidence that a witness did not see an event or did not hear a sound usually is not to be admitted unless it appears not only that he was in a position to see or to hear but also that he was attentive.76 Such evidence, unless the witness is attentive or is in a position to see or to hear, is merely negative." The many illustrations of this rule concern evidence that a locomotive 78 bell was not rung, or that an automobile or street car 80 did not sound a signal of its approach. The rule has been stated as follows:-"The weight to be attached to the testimony of a witness respecting the question whether a bell, horn, or other signal was rung or sounded, depends upon the attendant circumstances. If a witness testifies that a signal was or was not given, or that he did or did not hear it, and it appears that there was no particular reason why he should or should not have heard it had it been given, such testimony is merely negative and of no value as evidence. the rule thus:-"Ordinarily, all that a witness can say, in such a case, when called to prove that a bell was not rung, is that he did not hear it. Such a statement, with no accompanying facts, is merely negative, and of no value as evidence. 

A witness may be in any conceivable attitude of attention or inattention, which will give his evidence value, or leave it with little or no weight; but where his position is such that the sound would have been likely to attract his attention if the bell had been rung, his failure to hear it is some evidence that there was no ringing.''93 

A distinction under this rule lies in the circumstance of the witness's attention and position. The witness need not testify in so many words that he was attentive, listening or observing. 

If the evidence tends to show that the witness probably was attentive, the evidence has probative value. If his mind is occu-

In these circumstances it is a reasonable inference that if the gong had been sounded it is likely that she would have heard it. Her testimony that it was not rung was affirmative evidence to that effect. If the jury believed her testimony, the ordinance was violated, and such violation was evidence of negligence of the defendant.

C. Evidence should not tend to usurp jury's province. Evidence which tends to usurp the province of the jury is not to be admitted.107 This is not an absolute rule which excludes all evidence of that nature; but if evidence is offered solely to show the jury directly what deductions it should draw and directly what finding it should make, it is to be excluded.

Exceptions to the rule which excludes inferences: Opinion and value. The exceptions to this rule lie chiefly in evidence which involves opinion,115 and value.116 In these matters evidence based on inferences is allowable. In the former when the inference is one that may be drawn by the simplest of mental processes by a person in everyday life, or when the inference is one of expert knowledge and drawn by a qualified expert, it is admissible.117 In the latter when the inference is drawn by an owner or by a qualified expert likewise it is received.118 b. 2. Illustrations of the rule: The apprehension of bystanders not admissible to show that they considered an act negligent. 

The effect which an act has on the mind of by-standers is not admissible to show the act negligent.122 Hence that a person was concerned or frightened by the speed of a car furnishes no valuable guide as to the rate of its speed.128 What a disinterested, remote, bystander did on observing a car just before a collision in which he was in no way involved or concerned, even if it tends to indicate the bystander's fright, is not admissible to show the driver of that car negligent.124 Here the judge has no discretion; he must on objection exclude the evidence.

1. Illustrations of rule which requires definiteness: Speed.

When speed of a vehicle is material, evidence that it "was going 'fast' is too indefinite without anything to indicate the rate of speed, to warrant a finding of negligence.''189 Expressions whereby a witness states that a train "came in fast," 140 was "bowling along pretty fast when it went past me," or "going pretty fast," 141 or that an automobile "was going very fast,” 142 are of similar nature. E. Res inter alios. A fundamental principle in the trial of cases is that the proof shall be confined to the issue on trial. To frame the issue, the common law system of pleading was created. 

Acts of others which have no bearing on the issue framed are not to be shown to prove or disprove the allegations of the pleadings. 

Transactions between other persons usually are "res inter alios" and not to be received as evidence. This rule frequently excludes evidence of prior or subsequent acts of those not parties to the cause on trial,161 to establish the non-feasance or misfeasance of a present defendant. Likewise that others were injured, at other times, by the same cause, at the same place where the plaintiff in the case on trial was injured, usually is not to be received.162 The extent of the court's discretion cannot be defined with precision.168 

1. Illustrations. Many cases tend to illustrate this rule. A plaintiff on a highway struck by a baseball knocked in play by the defendant's employees may not show to prove negligence that another person was likewise struck, before the plaintiff's injury; this is so even though such injury has been suffered two or three times within two years.164 Likewise a party cannot prove that certain plumbers made certain holes, and thus caused certain damage by showing a custom of plumbers to make like holes.165 Speed of other automobiles at other times does not tend to show the speed of the defendant's automobile at the time of the accident.166 Many other illustrations are set forth and considered later.167

3. Exceptions: Illegality. One important exception should be specifically pointed out. If the payee of a negotiable note endorses it for an unlawful consideration, in a suit by the endorsee against the maker, the maker may show the illegality of the consideration between the payee 169 and the endorsee. The maker is not a party to the illegality; the unlawfulness is between others and arises in another transaction. Yet the plaintiff is not without fault. Of course if the plaintiff were a subsequent bona fide purchaser for value, a different result might be reached.

5. Other exceptions. Other exceptions to this rule are numerous and can not be classified with precision. They are considered in the chapters on "Value," 175 "Similar Circumstances, Events, Conditions and Acts," 176 and "Writings." 177 In this matter trade customs and habits are frequently admitted to show the trade meaning of words and phrases,178 or to assist the jury in establishing the degree of care which is proper in a particular instance peculiar to the trade.179 So evidence of remarks of others in observing the condition of a tree has been admitted to show that its dangerous condition was such that the town authorities should have observed it.180 If an issue is whether an act was caused wilfully or negligently, the fact that many other similar acts have occurred at the same place under like circumstances may tend to show wilfulness.181

On this subject there are many interesting cases. These with an attempt to codify them will be later considered.182

G. Self serving evidence. A party is not permitted to "create" evidence in his favor. Hence his self serving evidence is frequently excluded.195 This does not mean that evidence of every act performed, and word uttered, by a party which aids his case is to be excluded; yet the rule, with many exceptions, is that self serving evidence is to be excluded.

5. Illustrations: Unanswered letters. Letters which assert a party's claim, if unanswered usually are not admissible in favor of the writer to establish the truth of the statements therein.208 a. Exceptions. The exceptions to this illustration are many. 

If the letter shows an intent to hold the addressee liable for future, or perhaps for present indebtedness, for work done or services performed, it may be admissible.209 Likewise when a husband living apart from his wife in a letter to her offers to furnish her with necessaries and to take her back to his home, these statements, though in a sense self serving and "created" evidence, are admissible to show his willingness to perform his obligations. They tend to show his mental state and constitute a conciliatory offer.210 Elsewhere other illustrations have been collected.211 

6. Illustrations: Assertions of innocence. A criminal de fendant's assertion of innocence after a crime has been committed,212 or his assertion of innocence when he asks the cause of his arrest are self serving and to be excluded.218

8. Possible future rule. The possible rule which may result from the various decisions seems as follows. Any act, omission, or statement, part of the res gestae of the event directly on trial, though self serving, unless forbidden by statute or by some rule of substantive law or of evidence may be presented in evidence; but acts, omissions or statements performed, omitted or made by a party before or after the event in issue, if self serving and not a direct result or cause of the event or otherwise directly connected with it, unless they are admissible by statute, or by some positive rule of law or of evidence, when offered by that party must be excluded. What is a direct result or cause of the event and what is directly connected with it, are matters which lie largely within the sound judicial discretion of the trial court. 

Evidence of words is more likely to be excluded than evidence of acts or omissions. 

H. Matters likely to mislead the jury. The court in attempting to procure a fair trial, looks with suspicion on any evidence which tends to raise false issues, to arouse undue animosity, or to suggest to the jury matter which will lead them from the true issues and into fields of prejudice, undue suspicion, or misunderstanding.219 Any attempt of an attorney to arouse by unfair questions an inference which may create prejudice in the mind of the jury, will be frowned on.220 This does not mean that all evidence that may tend to prejudice a jury or to arouse its disgust is to be excluded.221 If the evidence is relevantly im-

This would tend only to confuse and to mislead the jury. 223 How far the plaintiff shall be permitted to go into particulars in offering such evidence should depend somewhat on the circumstances of the case, and must, within reasonable limits, be left to the discretion of the presiding judge.224 Certain matters, however, though likely to arouse animosity are admissible as a matter of law. If the evidence is a material part of the case it must be received even though it arouses resentment or other improper emotion. The court in several cases has pointed out this fact.225 It has been ruled that though a photograph of the face of a victim of a murder may tend to arouse the jury which is trying the alleged murderer, yet such photograph is admissible; 226 and by a majority decision the court has decided that, though evidence that the father of a plaintiff was killed in the same accident as that in which the plaintiff was injured may create sympathy in favor of the plaintiff, yet evidence of this fact, in so far as it bears on the issues of the defendant's negligence, is admissible.227 Likewise though the fact that a defendant is insured against such negligence as is. now'alleged in the present suit, is not admissible to show his negligence, and though mention of the fact that he is insured may tend to lead the jury to be more liberal in the setting of damages, yet mere mention of the fact that the defendant is insured does not conclusively require that a verdict of the jury favorable to the plaintiff, be set aside.228 So where a plaintiff's

I. Best evidence rule. The best evidence rule is usually assumed to apply to exhibits only.281 It is therefore considered at length under writings.232 There is authority, however, for the application of the rule to all evidence. Thus the rule without limitation to exhibits, has been stated, "Where it is incumbent on a plaintiff to prove a fact, and he refuses to prove it by the best evidence which is open to him, all other evidence may properly be excluded and the plaintiff's case will fail for lack of evidence."' 238 If this rule still applies to evidence other than exhibits, its enforcement in a particular case lies in the trial court's discretion.234 The examples under this rule, and its effect and modifications as applied to writings and exhibits, hereafter is considered at length.285

3. Application of the rule: Signatures. A signature to an instrument declared on or set forth as a cause of action or as a ground of defense, or set off, shall be taken as admitted unless the party sought to be charged thereby files in court within the same length of time after such instrument is pleaded as is allowed for an answer, a specific denial of the genuineness thereof and a demand that it shall be proved at the trial.245 

4. Application of the rule: Corporations: Highways: Exec utors: Trustees: Etc. If it is alleged in any civil action or proceeding that a party is an executor, the administrator, guardian, trustee, assignee, conservator, or receiver, or is a corporation, or that a place is a public highway, such allegation shall be taken as admitted unless the party controverting it files in court within the time allowed for the answer thereto or within ten days after the filing of the paper containing such allegation a special demand for its proof.2 246

6. Application of the rule: Agency of automobile driver. In all actions to recover damages for injuries to the person, or to property, or for death of a person, arising out of an accident or collision in which a motor vehicle was involved, evidence that at the time of such accident or collision it was registered in the name of the defendant as owner, shall be prima facie evidence that it was then being operated by and under the control of a person for whose conduct the defendant was legally responsible, and absence of such responsibility shall be an affirmative defense to be set up in the answer and proved by the defendant.248 

7. Application of the rule: Allegation of damages. If spe cial damages are claimed, this fact with full allegations must be set forth; 249 if no special damages are involved the general allegation such as "to the damage of the plaintiff as he says" is sufficient. Hence in cases which arise out of a collision of automobiles, an allegation that the plaintiff's automobile was greatly damaged is sufficient to admit evidence that the plaintiff lost the use of the automobile while it was being repaired;250 and in an action for trespass general allegations of damages admit evidence of the natural and necessary direct damages, but do not admit evidence of injury to the plaintiff's house caused by the trespass.251 It seems that if one count of a declaration alleges special damages and another does not, if evidence of special damage is admitted, and later the count which contains that allegation is stricken out, if no further action is taken to restrict this evidence or to strike it out the jury may include as a part of their verdict on the other count, damages for this special injury.252

I. Introductory. In the preceding chapter the general principles on which the rules of evidence are founded in the trial of cases at law and in equity are set forth. In "Part III" which follows the exceptions to these rules are considered. Here we treat of proceedings in which these rules and exceptions are inapplicable. Evidence admitted under the exceptions to the rules of exclusion are not to be confused with evidence admitted in spite of those rules. Though offered testimony may be admissible under an exception to a rule, that does not mean that the rule is not recognized and in full force. We now consider the cases wherein the rules and exceptions are not recognized. 

II. Boards and tribunals other than courts. As has been pointed out heretofore the rules of evidence do not apply to hearings before boards, bureaus, administrative bodies, and many other tribunals. The rules of evidence set forth in the preceding chapter apply only to proceedings before courts and their delegated and allied tribunals. 

III. Agreements of parties: Stipulations. Though parties probably may not agree in advance that certain inadmissible evidence shall be admitted or excluded in any possible future 

1 Part II, numbers 9 to 98. 

343

dispute, and be held to such agreement, yet by agreement or stipulation after suit is started parties may formerly agree that certain facts are the facts of the case, or that certain evidence shall be received as if testified to. Such agreements or stipulations when properly made and filed are binding on the parties. 

They are usually required to be in writing or to be made in open court.5

IV. Calling on party to admit facts. Similar to the above is the procedure by which one party calls on the other to admit certain facts. This statutory procedure permits the proof of facts by methods other than those established by the rules of evidence; but the relevancy of the evidence is still an issue at the trial. By 

By admitting the facts a party does not admit their admissibility.

V. Failure to object. In order to raise a question of the admissibility of evidence under the rules and exceptions, a party against whom the inadmissible evidence is offered must duly and seasonably object. Otherwise the evidence though inadmissible may be admitted; if admitted and relevant, it usually has probative force." Though the general rule is that matters

VI. Depositions. If a commission is issued to take depositions on written interrogatories, objection to the questions must be taken before the commission is sent out and must be noted in the commission.10 The objection cannot be taken for the first time at the trial." If no objection to a question is made before the commission is sent out, a responsive answer, though inadmissible on proper objection under the rules of evidence, and though objected to at the trial, is admissible. Objection to evidence or to the competency or credibility of a witness who testified by depositions, if the depositions are not taken upon written interrogatories attached to a commission, may be made at the trial.12

I. Introductory. Usually one is responsible for only one's own acts, and evidence of what others said or did when offered against a party usually is excluded as hearsay or res inter alios. 

A person may act, however, through agents and such acts, if authorized, are admissible against that person. Under modern business organizations the evidence of agency has assumed great importance. Corporations and large organizations operate almost exclusively through agents with the result that in trials. a party frequently finds himself confronted suddenly with an unanticipated set of facts tending to establish or limit an agency. 

Such facts may not raise questions strictly of evidence but because they are presented suddenly and the party may seek to learn during trial what inferences may be drawn from them, this chapter deals with such questions as are most likely to arise.

AGENCY 

355 II. Pleading. What may be done by one individually usually may be done by his agent, and little distinction is made in law between the doing of an act by the principal and by his authorized agent. The declaration, criminal complaint or indictment may allege that the act was done by the party to the suit therein named and without variance the proof may show that an agent performed the act.¹ By Acts of 1928, ch. 317, in suits which arise from collisions involving registered automobiles, chauffeurs are assumed the agents of defendants, if the registered owners, unless their agency is denied in the answers. 2 III. 361 C. Control of premises as proof of agency. One in apparent charge of a place of business may be found an agent of the person whose place of business he occupies, and within the scope of his employment when he there transacts business which naturally would be transacted there. So it has been held as to a clerk in the office of a gas company,35 and a cashier and other persons in a dentist's office, one in the transmitting office of a steamship company," an employee of an express company in charge of a shipment, one who unloads packages on the premises of an express company, the manager in complete charge 

38 

35 Person in charge of office. Evidence that assistant tree warden called at the defendant's office and spoke to a girl who was the only person in charge of the office telling her that he wanted to see the superintendent and that trees on Pleasant St., the highway in question, 'were dying,' was admissible. The office which apparently was the defendant's place of business was in charge of a person ostensibly employed there to look after its affairs, and notice to her of the condition of the trees, the jury under the circumstances could say, was notice to the company. Twombly v. Framingham Gas etc. Co., February 27, 1924, 248 Mass. 53. 

86 The defendant represented by signs that it was conducting a dental office; plaintiff desiring dental advice and assistance, entered the office, where, after stating his condition to the cashier, he sat down and waited until a young man came out of a side room and talked with him. Dr. Campbell then came in, called and told 

Friedman "to take care of him."

After examination Friedman extracted the tooth. The plaintiff had the right to assume that Dr. Campbell and Friedman, who each wore dental uniforms, and the cashier were employees of the defendant engaged in conducting its business as advertised. The defendant however offered evidence that Friedman was actually employed only in laboratory work. But the jury were to determine whether as between the parties, Friedman was acting within his scope of his ostensible employment. 

The plaintiff could not be expected nor was he required to ask for proof of the authority of the cashier, or of Dr. 

Campbell, or of Friedman, all of whom he found at the office engaged in the manner previously described. He had the right to "trust to appearances and to the not unreasonable assumption that the defendant would not permit unauthorized persons to be so engaged."'

The defendant under such circumstances could not avoid liability by evidence that Friedman's authority was limited. (Citing Newman v. British & North American Steamship Co., 113 Mass. 362, 91 N. E. 220; Rintamaki v. Cunard Steamship Co., 205 Mass.

E. 

Drivers of vehicles. By Acts of 1928, ch. 317, in all actions "for injury to the person or to property or for death arising out of an accident or collision in which a motor vehicle was involved, evidence that at the time of such accident or collision it was registered in the name of the defendant as owner shall be prima facie evidence that it was then being operated by and under the control of a person for whose conduct the defendant was legally responsible and absence of such responsibility shall be an affirmative defense to be set up in the answer and proved by the defendant." Even in such accident and collision cases, under proper pleading the defendant may show that the driver of his automobile was not his agent or within the scope of his employment. In all cases not within the statute agency of a chauffeur or driver is not presumed. Before agency and authority can be found in such cases there must be some evidence 55

Ex- amples:- 

A mechanic in a garage selling cars on commission after working hours with authority to demonstrate them without special permission, found within the scope of authority when demonstrating a car; important facts were:- (1) the driver had authority to sell cars for the defendants out of working hours" (2) "had been to the Ross home two or three times to sell a car to some member of her family,' "" (3) "on one of those occasions, he had demonstrated one of the defendants' cars to Miss Ross," (4) "later in the year the defendants sold a Nash car to some member of the Ross family, and (5) talk on the trip about automobiles." Jury could infer that when "Dorsey took Miss Ross and Ledoux for a ride on the night in question, he was trying to promote the sale of an automobile of the defendants, either by demonstrating the Flint car in which they were riding, or by using that car in furtherance of his efforts to sell a Nash car, and that in either case he was acting within the scope of his employment to aid the defendants in making the sale of an automobile." (Citing Ouimette v. Harris, 219 Mass. 466, 107 N. E. 435. Hoffman v. Liberty Motors, Inc., 234 Mass. 437, 125 N. E. 845. McDonough v. Voz zela, 247 Mass. 552, 142 N. E. 831.

even though with an agreement that he would not be responsible for accidents. The facts that the driver was alone in the car,68 that he was in the general employ of the defendant, 64 or in the employ of the defendant shortly before the accident and again shortly after it, that he had driven a team for the defendant until the defendant substituted an automobile, that the defendant had insurance against accident on the vehicle and that record books had been burned are all admissible to combine with other facts to show agency.65 Proof of ownership of the vehicle and of general employ is not enough to prove the agent within the scope of his employment.66 Evidence that the work which the driver is accomplishing is urgent and in the owner's business is admissible.67 The fact that an agent is not called to testify he made any reply." At the time of the accident the motor truck was being used to transport milk for the milk company. Held, that there was no evidence that the driver of the motor truck was the servant of the defendant, and that the plaintiff had no right to go to the jury; that, even if the silence of the defendant's manager was evidence of an implied assent to the proposition made to him, this was not evidence that the driver was the servant of the defendant, which never had hired him. While of course agency cannot be established by declarations of the agent, still they are admissible to prove that the agent believed himself to be the agent of a particular principal, and so held himself out, and that the third person dealt with him as such in good faith. G. Limitations created by writings-1. Generally: "Per proc"-seal. If a person relies on the authority of an agent, and seeks to prove that authority by a signed power of attorney he must show the signature within the authority of the person who purported to represent the principal in signing such power; 180 but though there is a written power of attorney which does not include the claimed authority of the agent the party seeking to establish agency though a party to the writing may show an oral modification of the writing, or if not a party to the writing, extrinsic facts which enlarge the written power. 181 If an agency is created solely by a written contract and there has been no modification of the writing and the suit is between parties to the writing the writing sets the scope of the agent's authority. Parties to it are bound by its terms. 182 But agency may be created and also proved either by actual appointment or by inference from facts or partly by each; 183 and when a person not a party to a writing who has no actual or constructive notice of any limitations seeks to hold the principal the apparent powers of an agent are his real powers 184 and the writing between the principal and the agent is then not conclusive of the agent's authority in favor of the principal.185 If the adversary relies on actual powers created by the written contract, of course it would be admitted; if he relies on apparent powers exclusively, it seems that the secret written contract might well be excluded.186 Authority of an agent in excess of that set by by-laws may be proved by parol evidence which contradicts the by-laws.187 So also of evidence outside of the records of a cor-

2. By-laws: Corporations: Public officers. The usual rules of evidence apply to corporate agency. K. Deputy sheriff as agent of sheriff. Proof that a tort has been committed by a deputy sheriff within the scope of his power establishes liability on the part of the sheriff. A sheriff is liable for the acts of his deputy performed within his duties as such deputy.265 As to what are acts within the scope of a deputy sheriff's duty, there are many decisions. Evidence that a judgment debtor, to avoid publicity of suit places in the hands of a deputy sheriff, personal property or negotiable instruments with instructions to sell them not by legal process is admissible to show that such sale is not within the deputy's scope and that his negligence in the sale does not bind the sheriff; but if the deputy actually sells the property and receives the cash, he must apply it on the execution or the sheriff may be held for his failure so to do.266 If a defendant whose property is attached and taken by a deputy sheriff assigns it and the proceeds thereof, the title to the proceeds vests in the assignee and if it be proved that the attachment is dissolved and that the deputy fails to turn over to the assignee the proceeds after notice and demand, the sheriff is liable.867 A sheriff is responsible for money actually received by his deputy upon process committed to the deputy officially for service though void on its face.268 If a deputy who has a writ for service and who has been authorized by the plaintiff to settle the suit by receiving an order on a particular person, receives the amount of the claim in money and does not pay it to the plaintiff nor serve the writ the sheriff is liable.269 Suit based on the deputy's official act should be against the sheriff. L. Surety as agent for principal in making admission. Whatever may be the rule when one becomes guarantor or surety for another by a separate obligation, it is probably law that when the principal and sureties are all bound by a joint obligation and the suit is against both the principal and sureties as joint defendants, the declaration and admissions of the principal debtor are admissible in evidence against the sureties.278 Hence to prove the breaches of a bond and to charge the sureties, admissions of the principal obligor, a cashier, as to the manner in which his defaults occurred, the extent of them, and the manner in which he concealed them have been admitted against the surety.277

"The defendants excepted to the testimony of Mrs. Kimball that she had a five gallon can on the platform of the store; that the can was empty and was not on the piazza the next morning. The exception to the admission of the testimony and to the refusal to strike it out was properly overruled. The circumstantial evidence warranted a finding that the person who asked for the gasoline was one of the defendants, John Dies. If the jury so found, the evidence of what he said and did at the time and place was incontrovertibly admissible against him, and against the other defendants if he was found to be acting in furtherance of their common purpose. Dies's connection with the endeavor of some person to get gasoline from the witness, could properly be found from the testimony of John J.

Indictment charging defendant in one count with burning a building and in another with being accessory before the fact. Defendant, was quitted on the first count and convicted on the second. The testimony of Collins and Wheelwright related to the acts of Frank Derry, defendant's brother. As to Frank the defendant's brother, the only evidence offered to show his connection with defendant's business or the intimacy of their relations was that he was a brother employed in defendant's factory at the time of the fire and for a number of years preceding; that at about six o'clock in the evening of November 21, 1911, he locked up the factory and that upon occasions previous to the fire he had used a key in opening and closing the door of the storehouse.

The government was permitted to show that Frank in September or October 1911, called at the store of Wheelwright and asked if he could let him have a dozen of cork stopples. This testimony in the absence of any evidence tending to show a common purpose or that Frank Derry was acting at the request of the defendant, was not admissible. At the close of the evidence the defendant moved for exclusion of testimony as to acts of 

Frank Derry on the ground that no such connection had been shown between Frank and the defendant or evidence of any such connection offered as to make the testimony admissible. 

No evidence had been introduced that as between the defendant and his brother there existed or had existed any business connection or interest other than such as naturally appertains to the relationship of employer and employee. There was no evidence showing the presence or absence of any unusual bond of sympathy such as sometimes marks near relationship. Assuming that Frank Derry purchased the corks and further assuming that they were used to plug the sprinkler heads by the defendant or by someone at his request, there is no evidence that Frank knew the purpose to which they were to be put or in any way participated in their use or in the setting of the fire. Commonwealth argues defendant and his brother Frank had entered into a conspiracy to burn the defendant's box factory and that the acts of Frank in the purchase and attempts to purchase corks were directed towards a common object, namely, preparations for the fire and setting the fire. "The short answer is that the defendant and Frank were not, and so far as appears, are not under indictment as conspirators.'' (If the jury might find that the corks were kept where the defendant might procure them, hence the evidence might be admitted as to the defendant in the question of means of committing the act.)

V. Exceptions to the general rules-A. Generally. There are certain relationships in which agency and responsibility for the acts of an alleged agent are not made out by proof of the same facts that would in other matters show agency. These are in instances involving "public officers" and "charities."

B. Public officers and municipal corporations-1. Generally. 

Though such evidence as appointment of, and paying of wages to, and direction of, an agent are usually evidence that the one appointing, paying, and directing is the principal, that conclusion does not follow in the case of "public officers." Frequently officers appointed or chosen by a city or town are not agents of that body-the municipality in appointing them acts merely as the appointing power and the officers are "public officers." So acts of selectmen such as arranging for the farming out of a pauper, or of "surveyors of highways" such as work on roads, or of a mayor in agreeing with a land owner to use land as a dump, are not admissions as against the town or city.378 Evidence that a city mentioned one as its superintendent of highways or road commissioner is not proof that such officer is the city's agent.374 "And on the other hand it is also established

Deane v. Randolf, 132 Mass. 475. "There are other cases of which the repair of roads and bridges furnish the usual example where a city or town by reason of its statutory liability for injuries sustained through neglect of keeping ways safe and convenient for travellers, and of the statutory penalties upon it for defective ways, as well as by reason of its responsibility for the cost of construction, incur a liability by undertaking the performance of a public work in which it has a direct pecuniary interest to see that it is done not only economically but thoroughly. In some of these cases the assumption of the work by the town itself has been voluntary, and apparently because it preferred that the work should be done by special agents rather than by surveyors or others upon whom in the absence of such special provision the law would devolve the duty of prosecuting it. But in all such cases a prominent element in the action of the city or town must have been with reference to its continuing liability to statutory penalties or responsibility in damages to persons who might receive injuries through defects in the highways. 419 Municipal Corporations. Char acter of two-fold. (1) As a convenient sub-division of government. (2) 

As ordinary corporation. Higginson v.

Treasurer & School House Commis sioners of Boston, 99 N. E. 523; 212 

Mass. 583; 42 L. R. A. (N. S.) 215.

Cities and towns are territorial subdivisions of the State operated as public corporations for convenience in the administration of government. They exercise only the powers which have been conferred by express enactment of the legislature or by necessary implication from undoubted prerogatives vested in them. They have a two fold character, the one governmental and the other private. In the one they execute the functions and possess the attributes of sovereignty which have been delegated by the legislative department of government; in the other they are clothed with the capacities of a private corporation, and may claim

ties delegated to it; in the second it has the rights and liabilities of a private corporation. When it operates not in a governmental capacity, but for profit it is liable for acts of its agents employed in the enterprise operated for profit as it would be were it a private corporation. Hence, liability for agents of a city acting within a profit seeking enterprise is proved by evidence that would prove liability if it were an ordinary corporation, when it operates voluntarily for possible profit 420 an electric lighting plant,421 engages in the business of selling gas,122 in opening house lots,423 in running a ferry,424 in renting a public hall for profit,425 in managing a farm partly for the support of the poor, partly for the maintenance of the highway department and partly for the production of income,426 in operating a stone crusher for profit 427 and in flooding with sewage land of another.428 It has been held not liable for acts of negligence in constructing a free public bath house, or subways though some revenue is received,429 for negligence of servants in setting off fireworks,480 for injuries arising from a general plan of drainage approved by public officers,431 for negligence of servants, in mainits rights and immunities, and are subject to its liabilities, Neff v. 4. Agent's liability: Implied warrant of authority to act as agent. Proof of an agency by proper evidence does not always establish the liability of the principal; and proof that one, though apparently an agent of a city, is in fact not such agent, cannot always be relied on to hold the agent personally liable on his implied warranty of authority.489 It is not reasonable that a municipality or a public officer who is engaged upon a public work conducted for the benefit of the people and not for gain, should be held liable for the negligence of his servants or agents under the doctrine of "respondeat superior." 440 Selectmen have been held not individually liable for negligence of the driver of a town ambulance operated ultra vires.441 However, any public officer is liable for active misfeasance committed by him in discharge of his ministerial duties as such and not as special agent of the municipality.442 Personal liability in such cases is not warded off by the "cloak of office" and good faith is no defence; hence field drivers taking cattle otherwise than as provided by statute, members of a board of health wrongfully causing the killing of an animal believed to have glanders,444 selectmen or members of an election or registration board wrongfully refusing to put a name on the voting list, or to allow one to vote,445 assessors making an illegal assessment,446 a superintendent of streets personally negligent in superintending the blasting of rock,447 and executive or administrative officers wrongfully removing an official are personally liable for their acts. Inferior tribunals and magistrates acting 448 without jurisdiction do not enjoy the protection of "the cloak of Public Office" though they are in the main public agents engaged in public business.449 In some cases, 27, 1911, 209 Mass. 259; 95 N. 5. Police officers: Constables; sheriffs; special officers. A police officer is a public officer and not the agent of the municipality 451 However, the municipality is charged with his knowledge as to defects in the highways. 452 Evidence that a police officer invades a person's premises and assaults him and robs him is not sufficient to hold the city liable. "Policemen when guilty of such wrongdoing do not act as servants of the city though they may have been appointed or elected by it." 453 "Police officers are state or public and not corporate or private officers. There is no such relation between the city and the officer which it is required by law to elect or appoint as will oblige it to pay compensation to them for their official services unless provision is made therefor by law, ordinance or contract."454 "The common law is that for the acts of a special police officer in apprehending or punishing a wrongdoer for an injury done to the public at large where he represents the public and not his employers the latter are not responsible unless they actively direct his movements. "'455 So evidence that a regular police officer was asked by the owner of a vacant building on his beat to look out for it and if he saw anyone "taking stuff out" to report it, or to keep an eye on the premises as the building had been broken into, falls short of warranting a finding that agency exists. "The common practice of an owner's notifying a police officer that his house or building is to be unoccupied with the request for him to keep an eye on it does not establish the relation of principal and agent. It is simply calling the attention of the public officer to a situation of property which may call for vigilance in the performance of his duty to protect property."456

445 skill. The digging of a trench may be done by an independent contractor.492 Evidence that the work is in the exclusive control of a person is evidence that he is an independent contractor. 

Hence the fact that a carriage was repaired at a repair shop in the control of the person making the repairs and that it could not have been taken away without breach of contract is admissible to show the repairer an independent contractor.498 One who does jobs driving and repairing for such persons as may employ him, and has a workshop of his own, has been found not the agent of the owner of an automobile when he drives it after repairs in "tuning it up. "404 Though an independent contractor or his servant is not the agent of the person employing the independent contractor, yet the person employing him is not absolutely free from liability. Evidence that the work to be done necessarily involved danger coupled with evidence that the danger was not guarded against, is frequently admissible to charge such person for resulting injury. One erecting a dangerous wall on one's land by an independent contractor may be held for damages from its fall.495 When lumber is piled in a street a defendant is not relieved from liability simply because he employs an independent contractor to pile it; if the evidence tends to show that the defendant controlled the action of the men and that he negligently performed the assumed duty of maintaining barriers, his liability is for the jury.496 A landlord who employs an independent contractor to lay pipe must guard a necessary trench or warn his tenants of its existence.497 Independent contractorship will not relieve one against liability for blasting near another's line,498 for installation of a drain which at high tide floods another's cellar,499 or for repairing an awning of such a nature that unless special care is taken, injury will result. It is well settled, however, that there are certain exceptions to this rule. For example, if the performance of the work will necessarily bring wrongful consequences to pass unless guarded against and if the contract cannot be performed except under the right of the employer who retains the right of access, the law may hold the employer answerable for negligence in the performance of the work.' 502 If a permit is granted to the principal contractor, and the independent contractor working thereunder opens manholes in a city street, the principal contractor is not excused from liability unless he takes precaution to guard against the natural injury which will result.503 The employer of an independent contractor perhaps may assume that he will act legally 504 and use care to protect the public if the work is not necessarily dangerous. Hence, if one using due care in the selection, employs a window washer as an independent contractor to do lawful work, one is not responsible for negligence of such contractor or his agents unless evidence is presented that from the very nature of the work a nuisance will be created or wrongful consequence be brought to pass if not guarded against.505

VII. Scope of authority. A.. General and explanatory. In dealing with the subject of proof of agency much naturally has been said of scope of authority. The Court does not always analyze the admissible evidence by distinguishing what is evidence of agency and what is evidence of scope. Hence, in the preceding sections are illustrations and rules which touch on the question of evidence admissible to show both agency and scope. This section deals with evidence showing only scope of authority. It assumes that agency for some purpose has been proved and considers in some circumstances what further powers result from the existence of those powers. 

B. Ostensible powers-1. Generally. 

Generally. "The ostensible powers of an agent are his real powers and limitations if any as between the principal and agent of an apparent general authority do not effect third parties where they have no knowledge of such restrictions."508 Secret limitations on an agent's apparent authority do not control an apparent general authority and the apparent powers of an agent are his real powers.509 It seems that evidence of such secret limitations should not be admitted.5 510

5. Miscellaneous. If an agent acts in a part of his master's business, doing what his duty requires, he binds his master. 

If the act is one outside of his duties his master is not bound. 

Hence a truck driver has no authority to invite guests to ride.562 

A conductor on the other hand can invite one to ride on a freight train;568 and brakemen may be found to have authority to remove a passenger or trespasser.564 A claim agent is not an instructor of his employer's servants, and hence is not assumed to have authority to issue orders or to explain his employer's rules.565 

A guard at a railroad station of an elevated railroad is not assumed to have authority to instruct a proposed passenger as to general methods of conduct at future times.566 Evidence tending to show that the act is done in performing the master's work, with purpose to accomplish the master's business even though it is a negligent act or one done by wanton and reckless purpose to accomplish the master's business is usually admissible.567 

Hence an agent authorized to do what was necessary in preserving order in running a hotel, or a department store, may be found

C. Agent's "frolic of his own." Though evidence has been presented that warrants a finding that one has been employed by another and has performed the kind of act which he was employed to perform, yet circumstances may exist that will make the employer not liable for those acts. Before the doctrine of "respondeat superior" applies it must appear by either direct evidence or by inference, that the alleged agent acts with a purpose to serve his master and not to serve himself.590 In other words to hold the master when all the evidence is in, it must be found that he is not on a frolic of his own. If the evidence of the plaintiff establishes that the servant of the defendant is on a frolic of his own, the defendant may rest. The plaintiff, however, may produce evidence that warrants a finding that the servant is an employee of the defendant and acting within his scope. 

To meet this, the defendant may produce evidence that the servant was on a "frolic of his own." The burden of proof is still on the plaintiff by the whole evidence to show the agent within the scope of his employment.591 A master is liable for the acts of a servant when the latter is acting in the main with the master's express or implied authority, upon his business, and in the course of the employment for the purpose of doing the work for which he is engaged. The master is not liable if the servant has aban-

471 X. Joinder of parties in actions. In contract a plaintiff may join a principal and agent in the same writ and later, with the Court's consent, discontinue as to one.677 In tort, however, the rule may be different. If a plaintiff in tort seeks recovery against two jointly the act for which he seeks to recover must be a joint act or the action cannot be maintained.678 A master, therefore, usually cannot be jointly sued and held in tort with his servants for the acts of the servant in the master's absence.679 

The liability is several and not joint. Were the master present and aiding or abetting, both could be sued jointly. Thus persons present and uniting in the abuse of a horse may be joined in one action of tort.680 A sheriff and his deputy cannot be jointly sued in tort for the act done by the deputy alone.681 If the act is done wilfully by the agent at the command or by authority of the principal it may be that a joint action in tort will lie.682 It has been said that it is settled at common law that a judgment without satisfaction 683 against one of two joint wrongdoers who are sued separately is no bar to taking judgment against the other; but that if they are sued jointly taking judgment against one not only operates as a discontinuance but constitutes a bar to obtaining judgment, against the other.684 

The cause of action being single has been merged in the judgment and the form of the action changed.685 It cannot afterwards be divided into two actions one on the judgment sounding in contract, and the other in the original tort.686 In actions upon a joint written contract it is provided by statute 687 that the plaintiff may have separate judgments if it is found that all that the defendant is in insolvency is not material to the question discussed.''

XI. Statements by agents-A. Introductory. When an agency has been established or is sought to be established 689 the question arises as to what statements of the agent are admissible against the principal. This is frequently referred to as the only question of agency which is a part of the law of evidence. 

When admissible the evidence must come within one of the exceptions to the rule excluding hearsay. In reality apart from statements admitted by some statutes 690 and rules of court,691 the same principle which apply to acts,692 usually apply to words—the statements of the agent to be admitted with probative force and not simply to affect his credibility must be within the scope of his authority, or a part of it.693 If admissibility of the evidence is determined strictly by the relation of agency, the proponent must show the statement within the agent's scope of authority.694 This scope may be shown by express authority 695 or in some instances by implied 696 authority. Implied authority usually does not include statements made before or after the act to which they relate.697 Statements made at the time of the act

473 with which they are connected if a part of it are admitted sometimes on the theory of implied authority, sometimes on the theory of "res gestae." 698 Some statements such as those of deceased persons, or of a superintendent in charge of the defendant's work made after the act and not expressly authorized, or of person negligently causing death 699 are admitted not on account of the authority of the agent to make admissions, but on account of statute, or to show a negligent manner of doing work or on account of some rule of common law apart from agency.700 Agency, however, is the basis of a well recognized exception to the rule excluding hearsay, and though perhaps other principles admit the statements of an agent, yet so to argue only tends to confuse. Briefly, then, the general rule of evidence is that statements of an agent before or after the act are not within his implied scope but statements at the time of the act if a part of the act which he is authorized to perform are within his implied scope. Among statements of an agent treated as exceptions to the hearsay rule, admissions are the most common.

B. Admissions-1. Generally. When a principal is a party, and the adversary seeks to introduce a statement of an agent favorable to the adversary's claim, the statement is admissible if it was authorized by the principal. The same rule applies whether the one making the remark is an agent, a co-conspirator, an associate, or one to whom the alleged principal has referred an inquiry for reply or report.701 Before an agent's state-

Commonwealth v. Dyer, 243 Mass. 472, 138 N. E. 296, this is true. Whether an alleged co-conspirator understood incriminating conversation, held with his associates in a foreign language has been held a question for the jury, Commonwealth v. Sokorelis, 254 

Mass. 454; 150 N. E. 197. The acts and statements to be admitted against a co-conspirator must occur during the continuance of the conspiracy, and the question whether the conspiracy still exists is first a preliminary question for the court, and then, if he admits it, for the jury. Commonwealth v. McDermott, 255 Mass. 575, 152 N. E. 704. It is well here to note that where defendants band together to commit robbery, their association may not end as soon as they have secured the money and left the building, and that if one then returns to the building and to remove the probability of their detection kills the watchman therein, it is not essential that the murder be part of the original plan; if it is one of the probable consequences all may be guilty of murder. Commonwealth v. 

Heinlein, 255 Mass. 575, 152 N. E. 380, A. S. 1415. A conspiracy or joint enterprise on the procuring of the desired result does not end so completely that all statements made thereafter are to be excluded. Hence in prosecution for conspiracy to commit larceny by false pretenses which concerned a building trust, a conversation with one defendant after the money to be stolen had been paid has been held admissible. 

Here the conversation was with one defendant only and related to statements by him which convinced the witness that the house for which he had paid would be completed shortly and that he should delay putting in his winter's coal at his present residence. The court says that the evidence is not prejudicial and implies that it would be admissible against the speaker. The mere fact that the statement was made after the money was paid does not exclude it. "The admissions of the defendants at that time might tend to prove the conspiracy alleged in the indictment." Commonwealth v. Knight, 257 Mass. 421, 154 N. E. 91. In the same case the admission of a conversation with one defendant in which he stated that he owned certain material land and that the defendants controlled it was not prejudicial error and evidence of the time of the foreclosure of mortgage was admitted to show the time when the witness had knowledge of the foreclosure. A questionnaire made use of in a conspiracy, given a police officer on his visit to the defendant's office, especially when its delivery is accompanied by a statement that it would explain the enterprise, is admissible. Commonwealth v. Knight, 257 

Mass. 421, 154 N. E. 91. The repeated presence of a defendant at a garage where liquor involved in a conspiracy frequently was transferred, his assistance occasionally on request in the transfer, the frequent driving by defendants who had pleaded guilty of automobiles in and out of this garage at night and in the early morning, proof that at another garage kept by this defendant and another person, a truck owned by one of the other defendants and liquor had been seized, and the illegal absence of a record of the entries of the cars above referred to at the garage first named which the defendant testified he managed during the day time unrefuted, rendered the evidence sufficient to connect the defendant with the conspiracy. Commonwealth v. Muchnikoff, 257 Mass. 181, 153 N. E. 460. In a trial for conspiracy to steal, and larceny a ruling admitting evidence of acts and statements of one alleged conspirator, is not subject to exception, though the count for conspiracy is later withdrawn. 2. Where authority to admit may be inferred: Similar cases where not inferred. An agent in apparent charge of a place of business has authority to make statements which are within his apparent scope; so of one in charge of a dental office 727 or a gas company's office.728 A receipt taken by an agent in the course of his employment is admissible against his employer,729 but if his employment has previously ended it would be excluded.789 

An agent usually has not implied authority to make admissions against his principal as to past events; 781 or as to matters not connected with his apparent duty. Hence, a man who comes from a stable on the land where the maker of a note lives, and not that he acted as an agent for a certain party, until by other evidence the latter fact is made out. The order of evidence is in the court's discretion:-Statements of Davy that he was the agent of Davison, authorized to bind him in the sale of stock to the defendant held competent. Mass. 563, 566; 104 N. E. 341. Ennis v. Wright, 217 Mass. 40; 104 N. E. 

430;) it was admissible to show that in what he did he purported to act for 

Davison and not for someone else. (Citing, Nowell v. Chipman, 170 Mass. 

340; 49 N. E. 631.) And this testimony was not the only evidence of agency; it could have been found from what the defendant said that he was bringing Davy into his business because he was a valuable man. The ruling made related merely to the order of proof to which no exception lies.

This testimony directly and unfavorably contradicted the plaintiff's assertion that the defendant's proposal had been accepted by Leventhal without qualification. Its effect, if believed, was to destroy utterly and beyond the possi-, bility of redemption the plaintiff's case. Held, "L" had no authority to bind the plaintiff by act or word, and as had been shown, "C" had none.

It follows that the admission of the testimony was error and the exceptions must be sustained. Exceptions sustained. Adams v. Frank, Nov. 24, 1915, 222 Mass. 215, 110 N. E. 290.

G. Other statements admitted by some rule of law. The rules of evidence do not require the exclusion of statements of agents simply because they are agents, if the statements are admissible under the general rules of admissibility.798 Hence statements to show knowledge, fraud or mistake,794 state of mind or body,795 records of corporations,796 statements in the course of duty,797 statements to contradict testimony 798 and many other statements and documents 799 are admissible when they fall within the rules admitting such evidence when the question of agency is not involved. 

XII. Form of objection and exceptions.. The usual rules of form of objection apply to agency. If at a hearing evidence as to an agent's statement is objected to and is wrongfully admitted, and an exception is taken, if the judge in his finding sets forth the objectionable evidence as admissible, the injured party must again except or lose his rights.800

II. Definitions: Confessions: Admission. A confession is a direct acknowledgment of guilt; 2 it is to be distinguished from the ordinary admission. An admission in criminal law is an acknowledgment by the accused, direct or implied, of facts pertinent to the issue and tending in connection with proof of other facts to prove guilt but of itself insufficient to authorize a conviction. An admission in a civil case is any word, act or omission adverse to a party's interest. wealth v. Reibstein, 257 Mass. 436, col lecting cases. The right to a preliminary hearing exists only with reference to a confession as that word is accurately used in the criminal law; that is, to an acknowledgment by the accused in express words of the truth of the guilty fact charged. It does not exist in case of mere incriminating admissions or declarations of subordinate or independent facts which may tend in connection with other facts and circumstances to prove the defendant's guilt, but do not constitute an acknowledgment that he is guilty of the precise crime with which he is charged." "The distinction between a confession and an admission, as applied in criminal law, is not a technical refinement, but is based upon the substantive differences in the character of the evidence educed from each. A confession is a direct acknowledgment of guilt on the part of the accused, and by the very force of the definition excludes an admission which of itself, as applied in criminal law, is a statement by the accused, direct or implied, of facts pertinent to the issue, and tending in connection with proof of other facts to prove his guilt, but of itself insufficient to authorize a conviction." The right to a preliminary hearing exists only with reference to a confession as that word is accurately used in the criminal law, that is to an acknowledgment by the accused in express words of the truth of the guilty fact charged. If you make a statement you do so voluntarily, as any statement you make can be used either for or against you in court," that person made a statement in which he denied his guilt but without acknowledging guilt, admitted facts from which inferences unfavorable to him might be drawn. At the trial the statement was admitted in evidence subject to the defendant's exception. Held, (1) not a confession and the rule which excludes a confession of guilt by a defendant who was induced to make it through fear of personal injury or hope of personal benefit, was not applicable; (2) the statement clearly was admissible in evidence; (3) even if the statement of the defendant to the captain of police while in custody were treated as in fact a confession of guilt, it was not shown that he was induced to make the confession through fear or hope of reward; the preliminary warning given by the captain of police was neither ambiguous, misleading nor improper; (4) a confession made to a person in authority by a defendant in an indictment while under arrest is presumed to be voluntary and if the defendant objects to its admission in evidence on the ground that it was made because of a threat or a promise, he must show

Even though the confession were wrongfully obtained, facts disclosed by it may be proved to convict." If the accused is wrongfully induced to make a confession by a promise of leniency so that such confession is not admissible, but later when not under influence of that promise of leniency or when the promise has been realized, he voluntarily writes out a story confessing the crime, this story may be admitted. If the accused is not induced to confess by threat, promise or other wrongful act or deed the confession is admissible.⁹

"The principle undoubtedly is that if a confession is procured by threats, all subsequent confessions of the same fact are to be excluded; and the reason given is that the subsequent confessions may be presumed to be induced from the same motive of fear or hope, and therefore, if it is shown that such motive has been removed before the subsequent confessions are made, this will rebut the presumption, and render the subsequent confessions admissible."' 10"The ground on which confessions made by a party accused, under promises of favor or threats of injury, are excluded as incompetent is not because any wrong is done to the accused in using them, but because he may be induced by the pressure of hope or fear, to admit facts unfavorable to him without regard to their truth, in order to

actual or apparent authority 11 whose words or acts influence 12 obtain the promised relief or avoid the threatened danger, and therefore admissions so obtained have no just and legitimate tendency to prove the facts admitted.'' Commonwealth v. Morey, 1 Gray 461 at 462. "The test of exclusion thus would be:

Human nature being what it is, were the prospects attending confession (involving the equalization or averaging of the benefit of realizing the promise or the benefit of escaping from the threat, against the drawbacks moral and legal of furnishing damaging evidence,) as weighed at the time against the prospects attending non-confession (involving a similar averaging) such as to have created, in any considerable degree, a risk that a false confession would be made? Putting it more briefly and roughly, was the inducement such that there was any fair risk of a false confession?" Wigmore, section 824, paragraph 937. 

The kind of fear must be something more than the fear which is produced by the fact that the defendant was accused of a crime and was arrested or taken into custody. Commonwealth v. 

Preece, 140 Mass. 276. Commonwealth v. Smith, 119 Mass. 305. Commonwealth v. Mitchell, 117 Mass. 431. "A threat of corporal violence is the clearest case of an inducement that may vitiate the confession. To escape the disagreeable consequence of silence, whip, gallows, or rack, the threatened person naturally prefers to utter what his tormentors desire to hear, a confession. He trusts to chance to enable him to repudiate his untrue avowal and vindicate his innocence; or perhaps, under the violent pain of the rack, he thinks of nothing but the present relief from agony which his confession will gain him. Yet not every threat of violence is necessarily sufficient to cause distrust of the confession which follows it: 'I shall put you out of my house unless you confess yourself guilty of this murder' has obviously no tendency to cause a false confession. But the typical cases of such violence in legal annals, the rack of the inquisitor, the whip of the slaveowner, and the slip-noose of the jail breaking mob, serve as the clearest and usually the least questionable instances of an inducement which vitiates a confession for evidential purposes. That a confession obtained by the rack, or a threat of the rack is inadmissible was apparently never judicially decided; that it would be inadmissible is of course unquestioned to-day. Confessions obtained from slaves under the whip, or a threat of the whip, have usually been excluded upon the circumstances of the case presented. Confessions made in fear of a mob are usually made under circumstances calculated to educe a false confession; and in almost all the instances brought before the courts, they have been excluded, usually with propriety upon the facts of the case. Other instances of violence or physical intimidation, by starvation or otherwise, would invalidate a confession; but the term is often exaggeratedly applied to any form of solitary confinement and does not then signify such intimidation as would exclude a confession.” more, section 832, paragraph 948. See also section 829, paragraph 941. Wig- 

Thayer distinguishes confessions induced by mob violence and other illegal duress and considers them inadmissible “irrespective of the technical doctrine of involuntary confessions."

D. Withdrawal of. If a confession is procured on the promise of leniency and with the agreement that the defendant will stand by his confession for the conviction of his accomplices, and the confessor while the promise of leniency is still in force attempts to withdraw his confession and rely on the representations which induced it, his withdrawal is ineffective. His refusal to testify permits the confession to be introduced against him.59
