G. Pleas of guilty. Pleas of guilty are confessions of the facts properly set forth in the complaint or indictment to which the plea pertains, and may be admissions or confessions.67

IV. Admissions-A. Generally. Admissions, distinguished above from confessions, are admitted under the same rules in criminal as in civil cases, with two exceptions,-first, when statements are made in the presence of the accused who is under arrest, and he remains silent. or unequivocally denies their truth, the statements are not admissible; 68 and second, in prosecutions under sections 1 to 22 of General Laws, Chapter 273, by sections 7, 16, and 22 admissions and confessions in private communications between husband and wife are not privileged.69

B. By words; unrefuted statements-1. Generally. Words spoken by or in the presence of a person may constitute an admission against him. A person against whose interest a statement is made, if he hears it, is bound usually to deny it, or, on failure to do so, to run the risk that it may be taken as true. 

Whether he heard it, or understood it, if it was within his hearing and uttered under such circumstances that the court reasonably can infer that he understood it, is for the jury.70

2. Material and immaterial statements. Conversations with, and remarks by, or in the presence of, a party, as has been said, are usually admissible against him. The statement may be in any form of words, if material to the issue; but if not material to the issue, it is to be excluded. Illustrations are found in many common controversies. Hence when the issue is undue influence, unrefuted statements, made in a party's presence even if by near relatives, offered merely to show animosity; or on issues of negligence, warnings given of present dangers to attentive drivers by persons riding with them, merely to show want of due care; or on issues of the defendant's libel, advices to the plaintiff to stop drinking, in a matter where drinking is immaterial; or on issues of value statements of "assessed value," to show true value; or on any issue, conversations with persons of the same family name as that of a party, but not identified as the party, have been excluded. Cases so holding and other similar illustrations of less common occurrence appear in the notes."¹ furniture for wife admitted, Sherry v.

4. Direct confession of fault: Offer to pay damages: Fraudulent or unconscionable trick or proposal. A direct material confession of fault such as "I am to blame," or "it is my fault" without further particularity, though it sounds in opinion and tends to establish a degree of care which should be determined by the jury only, seems admissible against a party. A promise made to an injured person immediately after an accident to adjust damages to his automobile, is an admission of the agency of the speaker's chauffeur and of his fault and is not privileged as an offer of compromise." Such offer made even to a third person likewise is admissible.78 If the offer is manifestly a fraud and unjust or involves a highly unconscionable trick, it is clearly admissible. The distinction between such offer and a charitable expression of willingness "to take care of" or "look after" an injured employee is close; such evidence is to be excluded.78 In criminal law the rule is the same; in prosecution for abortion a defendant's offer to adjust the damages with the victim is admissible.78

5. False Name: False story or accusation of others: Other matters. Giving a false name, telling a false story or making an untruthful accusation, or by silence condoning such conduct by others, if wilful and wrongful, is some evidence of liability or guilt.74 Other matters which involve admissions by words are so involved in admissions by conduct that they are considered under that heading. 

C. By silence and failure to act 1. Generally. As has been said, in civil cases, and, subject to the exceptions later set out, in criminal cases, a total or partial failure to respond to a charge or statement made in the presence and hearing of a person, renders that charge or statement admissible in evidence against him if the circumstances are such that he could and should have replied. Failure to reply if the circumstances are such that a reply should be made permits the jury to consider the statement and its truth.75 Whether the statement was heard 76 by the accused or in a language which he understood 77

The same rule that applies to statements in the presence of an accused who remains silent, seems to apply to acts.94 A recent decision which might suggest a contrary rule does not seem an authority to admit evidence of such acts; and other decisions are explainable on other grounds.95 

D. By conduct-1. Generally. A party's 96 conduct before and after an event if it tends to show material conditions, state of mind or other facts, or to explain his acts, is admissible against him.97

3. Attempt to escape. 175 Actions arising from collision. 

Defendant had interview with the plaintiff's attorney in which he was informed that the plaintiff intended to bring an action. Plaintiff permitted in cross-examination of the defendant to show that immediately after this interview, the defendant conveyed his homestead to his daughter, that no valuable consideration was agreed upon and that the defendant continued in occupation. 

Defendant testified that the understanding was that he should pay rent, to be deducted from the purchase price, and conveyance was a distribution of his estate in accordance with the wish of his deceased wife at her death; he, a part owner, by operation of law had become the sole owner before the transfer was made. An inference and finding were warranted that the house constituted all of the defendant's property which could be attached and that it was conveyed to avoid an attachment in the impending action of which the defendant had been fully informed. Portland Gas Light Co. v. Ruud, 242 Mass. 272.

7. Actions near scene before and after crime. The actions of a defendant at or near the scene of a crime before or after its commission are admissible at least within the rules of discretion when they tend to show notive or preparation or otherwise indicate guilt.176 

8. Acts showing motive, interpretation, understanding, knowledge, bad faith. A party's mental state is not easily discovered. His acts and failure to act may betray a state which he seeks to conceal. Hence when motive,177 interpretation of ambiguous contracts,178 knowledge,179 and like matters will assist in fairly disclosing the truth, his revealing acts and failure to act are admissible against him.180 

9. Reports of, failure to report, accident, failure to stop and make self known. If statute requires that one who causes an accident shall report it and the purpose of such statute is that he who is injured may learn who caused his injury, failure to report is evidence of fault. 181

3. Effect of receiving unanswered letters. "It is settled that failure to answer a letter is not an admission of the facts stated in it.''234 "Self serving statements" therein "are incompetent and failure to reply to them does not amount to an admission."'235

Hence an unanswered self serving letter, not referred to in later conversations, is not admissible to serve the writer; 286 there is no inference from the fact that the recipient did not reply.287

4. Similar matters distinguished. If it appears by the writing sent a party that a charge is being made or will be made against him on the assumption that he is the one liable his failure to reply may be found an admission of his liability.242 A partnership by similar evidence has been proved.248 This rule however so far is confined to matters involving charges of a strictly pecuniary nature.244 A letter received by a party from his attorney under unusual circumstances and for limited purposes has been admitted against him though he has not replied thereto.245 Usually however a letter though vitally affecting the case, 241 A bishop attempts to deliver to a communicant a letter setting forth the attitude of his church toward her; leaves it in her vicinity where it disappears immediately thereafter; letter admitted in evidence. 242 Credit-Consented to continuance of by silence,-Plaintiff each month sent a statement to the defendant, the father of a girl to whom merchandise delivered. At second month and at the third month plaintiff wrote defendant seeking payment and finally wrote demanding payment. Defendant made no reply. Such evidence tended to show defendant had notice that the credit was being given to him on his daughter's behalf; and that he by his silence assented to its continuance. A finding for the plaintiff as to all items of charge after those of the first month was warranted, although the reason that the defendant did not reply was a mistaken understanding on his part that his daughter was of age. Auringer 

V. Cochrane, 225 Mass. 273. 

Compare; a bill sent father, bill charged to son. Stimpson v. Hunter, 234 Mass. 61 at 62.

1886, c. 140). These two statutes last cited gave an option to proceed by an action of tort as well as by an indictment in cases against railroads and street railways, Hudson v. Lynn & 

Boston R. R., 185 Mass. 510, 515, but abolished the remedy by indictment as to death caused by other common carriers and through defective highways.

The damages awarded by the last two of these statutes, namely, for death occasioned by an employer, (see St. 1887, c. 270, s. 3) and by all others not otherwise made liable, (see St. 1897, c. 416, St. 1898, c. 565), never have been recoverable by indictment. But these statutes always have required the amount recoverable to be assessed' with reference to the degree of culpability' of the person liable, or his servants or agents, which are the same words used in all the other death statutes. These are the decisive words. They stamp the character of the damages awarded as punitive rather than compensatory. 

The use of these words puts all these statutes in the same class and renders them harmonious and consistent." 

Boott Mills v. B. & M. R. R., 218 Mass. 582. 

It is well to note that though an action for death by negligence existed under these statutes, if the death was caused by intentional, wanton and reckless misconduct, the same statute did not apply. Prondecka v. Turner Falls 

Power El. Co., 241 Mass. 100; Cotter 

Petitioner, 237 Mass. 68 at 69. See

At the trial evidence was admitted that "In September or October, Frank Derry, the defendant's brother and employee at the factory attempted to buy from one 

Wheelwright a number of dozen cork stopples of the half pint bottle size.

This was testified to by Wheelwright and by Collins," and "Around October," Frank bought of one "B" "Some cork stopples' "_"it might have been a dozen or two," that the clerk, "could not say whether it was three or four dozen.'' They were "small corks for half pint or pint bottles." 

After the fire sixty-three of the two hundred fourteen sprinkler heads of the system of sprinklers with which the factory was equipped were found plugged with corks of the half pint size. The Commonwealth argued that this evidence of the sales to Frank was rightly admitted because the defendant and his brother Frank had entered a conspiracy to burn the factory and that the acts of the defendant, and the acts of Frank in purchasing and in attempting to purchase corks were "directed toward a common object, namely, the object of making preparations for the fire and setting the fire." The court holds the evidence not admissible on that ground because the defendant and Frank were not and "so far as appears are not" under indictment for conspiracy. Frank, and that they naturally were kept in a place accessible to the defendant. The evidence therefore was admissible as tending circumstantially to show that the defendant had the means and the opportunity of procur ing corks of the kind used without direct purchase." As to the evidence of

Under "Witnesses" privilege is considered more fully.345 Here it is well to point out that private communications, and hence admissions, between husband and wife are absolutely privileged;346 to this there is but one exception.347 In a criminal case neither spouse can be compelled to testify against the other.348 To this, again, is an exception created by statute.849 To refuse to testify is the privilege of the spouse called as a witness and not of the defendant.350 

The defendant's failure to call his wife as a witness may be commented on in argument.850 Privileged admissions to a party's attorney are excluded at the client's instigation.851 Here also are exceptions.352 If the attorney acts not as an attorney but as a conspirator, there should be no privilege.353 Repairs and precautions taken to avoid accident are frequently spoken of as privileged.854 To this also there are exceptions. M. Certain statutory. Admissions by pleading or failure to plead 376 may be finally binding on parties; but these are of a different nature from the ordinary evidential admission.877 It is well, however, here to point out certain statutory provisions. 

To dispute the genuineness of a signature of a document relied on, it is necessary to deny in proper manner its genuineness, and to demand proof thereof.978 Like provisions apply to allegations that a party is an executor, administrator, guardian, trustee, assignee, conservator, receiver or corporation or that a place is a public way.379 To fail to deny such facts or statements and to demand proof admits, against him who so fails, the truth of the allegation. Certain agreements between counsel must be in writing, 880 and on a "case stated" the court may draw inferences.381 A statute passed in 1926 supersedes former similar acts,882 and the rules of court,888 and provides that a party at law or in equity may call upon the other party to admit for the purposes of the case material facts, or the execution of any material paper or document; if no answer is filed within ten days or within such further time as the court may allow on motion, the truth of the facts and the execution of the paper shall "be held to be admitted." Such notice in so far as it relates to a material fact or document and any answer filed in response thereto shall if offered by the party who filed such notice be admitted in evidence. I. Classes of opinions A. Introductory. Matters sounding in opinion may be considered as divided into four classes. First: 567

those opinions to which anyone, even without expert knowledge, may testify. Second: those to which no one may testify. Third: those to which one qualified may testify within the discretion of the court. Fourth: those to which one qualified regardless of discretion has the right to testify. These classes are now considered.

B. Opinion and conclusions as to which any person may testify. "It is the general rule that opinion evidence from one having no special qualifications by experience or study is not admissible. 

Exceptions to this rule exist where the facts about which the witness is asked to express an opinion are such as may be comprehended by persons of ordinary capacity and cannot be reproduced and described to the jury precisely as they appeared to the witness at the time of the event. The exception is founded on practical necessity in the administration of justice, where matters as to which in the common affairs of life such expressions of opinion convey definite conceptions of actual facts, and where otherwise evidence might be difficult or impossible to obtain.”

Hence a question, "In your opinion did the deceased speak loud enough for the operator of the car to hear her?" has been held admissible. This is said to be not a mere opinion. How-

9"The exception comprehends a wide range of subjects. It was said by way of illustration in the thorough and full discussion of this general subject in Com. v. Sturtivant, 117 Mass. 122 at 133. 'Every person is competent to express an opinion on a question of identity as applied to persons, things, animals or handwriting.' It is plain from the connection. in which that sentence occurs, that it was not intended to lay down an unvarying rule that everybody might under all circumstances testify, whether in his opinion a disputed signature was genuine. Where the controversy is whether a lost document was in the handwriting of a certain person, anybody familiar with that person's handwriting may testify, although he pretends to no skill in the matter. So where one has considerable familiarity with the signature or handwriting of a person growing out of numerous observations, he may give his opinion even though unable to read or write.' (Citing Foye v. Patch, 132 Mass. 105, 108.) "Where undoubted standards of handwriting as well as the questioned signature are before the jury there is no occasion for the testimony of one who is neither an expert nor possessed of considerable familiarity with the handwriting of the person whose signature is under examination. 

The opinion of the jury is quite as good as that of the witness of ordinary experience. There is, under such circumstances, no occasion for the opinion of the outsiders of only ordinary intelligence." (Citing Whalen v. Rosnosky, 195 Mass. 545. Com. v. Tucker, 189

Speed of car,-expert and laymenrefusal of judge to allow preliminary examination:-As the testimony was not offered as the opinion of persons who by reason of education, of observation or of experience were peculiarly qualified to speak, the defendant had no right to a preliminary examination. 

Speed is determined in the absence of a speedometer by observation of surroundings and conditions which often times are complicated. Were a rate of speed a matter exclusively for experts it would be impossible for persons to recover for injuries predicated upon running vehicles negligently or in violation of statutory speed laws. That a proposed witness is without experience or is not accustomed to the use of his facilities in observation of speed goes to the weight and not to its admissibility. Defendant was not deprived of his right to cross examination. Johnston v. Bay State St. Ry. 

Co., 222 Mass. 583. Plaintiff in direct said car was going at a very good rate."' Asked what he meant by "a very good rate,' ," he replied, “Well, it was going so fast that a man could not cross the track at the rate it was going." The defendant asked to have the answer stricken out. Answer conveys very little, if any information; it did not tend to show the speed at which it was moving and we do not thing the defendant was harmed by the answer. Godfrey v. Old Colony St. 

Ry. Co., 223 Mass. 419. Mahoney v.

Plaintiff called a witness fourteen years old when the accident happened, whose attention was called to the defendant's automobile by its lights one hundred and sixty feet from the point of collision, and who had it in view until plaintiff and the car came in contact. He testified that he had driven for about 5,000 miles. He referred to his personal experience in driving, although his age forbade holding of an operator's license. In direct he was asked the speed of the vehicle. The question was excluded subject to exception. Thereafter an offer of proof was made that the witness would testify that the rate of speed of the car when he saw it was twenty miles per hour. After this he testified that he observed the speed of the car, he was then asked "What speed was it (the defendant's automobile) going?" This question was excluded subject to the plaintiff's exception. The record cannot be fairly construed as limiting the proffered testimony to the expression by this youth of an expert opinion concerning speed. Actual experience may well add weight to such testimony, but it does not warrant its rejection, at least where the evidence is not offered as that of an expert. 45 Fugitive from justice not opinion. 

Petitioner contends no evidence that he is a fugitive from justice; he claims that affidavits of the prosecuting attorney state merely a conclusion of law from undisclosed facts. It is a question of fact whether one is a fugitive from justice that is whether having actually and not merely constructively committed a crime within another state, he has departed therefrom and cannot be found there to answer to a prosecution for his offense. 

The question is not whether he has consciously and literally filed from trial, but whether he is a fugitive from justice. In re

DP bor NI It ere 6 It has been said as to this kind of evidence that the competency of this evidence rests upon two necessary conditions, first, that the subject matter to which the testimony relates cannot be reproduced or described to the jury precisely as it appeared to the witness at the time; and second that the facts upon which the witness is called to express his opinion are such as men in general are capable of comprehending and understanding. When these conditions have been complied with or fulfilled in a given case the court must then pass upon the question whether the witness had the opportunity and means of inquiry and was careful and intelligent in his observation and examination. It is not. the mere qualification of the witness, but the extent and thoroughness of his examination into the specific facts to which the inquiry relates, and the general character of those facts as affording to one having his opportunity to judge the required means to form an opinion that constitute the test.47 

Lay witnesses to wills testifying as to sanity, 48 owners of property testifying as to value,19 and those familiar with a man's handwriting or who have corresponded with him testifying as to the genuineness of his writing, 50 are in a class slightly different from the above. They are more like experts, for some specific qualifications, namely that they were witnesses to the will, or owners of the property, or familiar with the writing, are required before they can testify. One who carries on a conversation with another in a foreign language may testify in English as to what was said though one is not qualified as an interpreter.51 Doubtless much must rest in the discretion of the trial court and many of the illustrations herein resemble those in the part of the text marked III following.

of insane persons.75 There are doubtless light shades which separate a case within this division from those wherein a layman's opinion is admissible, and these may be still lighter as we approach the field of expert testimony. No set rule can be formulated in advance for all cases.76 However it is well to remember that the objection that a question calls for an opinion or a conclusion which the jury is asked to reach as a part of its verdict is not always fatal to the admission of a question." "Any expression of opinion which will aid a jury necessarily in- volves the consideration of questions which are similar to that in issue, and sometimes of those which include it. But that alone does not render the evidence incompetent, if the witness is not permitted to express opinions upon evidence, and if the questions are so framed as to confine him to a statement of his conclusions as an expert and not to submit to him the precise issue which is presented to the jury. Indeed, we are not prepared to say, if everything else is eliminated except that upon which the witness is competent to give an opinion, that a questo be narrated in evidence (excluded).

Glass Co. v. Lovell, 7 Cush. 319.

77 Soundness of mind. "He was childish." To a witness who had great opportunity of observation, this question was put: "Taking the time immediately after the death and just before January, when this codicil was signed, what did you notice, that is what facts did you notice to show as to whether he was easily influenced?" she answered "He was childish." The answer was stricken out. It was a fact, a conclusion of fact the resultant of data collected in the observation of the decedent for a considerable period. In arriving by inference at a conclusion of fact, opinion and judgment necessarily play their part and a statement in truth a fact is not necessarily to be rejected because involving an opinion. The vital question was whether the facts were so complex and difficult to state as to make their presentation to the jury impracticable; if so the testimony should not have been rejected. If not, especially when the conclusion of fact is most material to the fact in issue, the facts and the inferences to be drawn therefore were in the province of the jury alone to determine. Following the rejection the witness apparently stated all facts from which she drew her conclusion; they appeared neither complex, difficult of statement or description nor full of minute detail. It follows that there was no error and the exception must be overruled. Johnson v. Foster, 221

Judge refused to allow a medical electrical specialist to testify that in his opinion the cause of the physical condition into which the plaintiff was thrown was an electric shock. Exceptions by proponent of a will; issue whether the testator was unduly influenced by the beneficiary and executor; exceptions to the allowance as a "preliminary question" of a hypothetical question, put to an expert and specialist in mental and nervous diseases, which assumed the truth of certain facts stated, and directed the attention of the witness to the day when the will was executed (six weeks and one day before the death of the testator) and asked, "What is your opinion as to whether his mind at that time was in a normal condition?'' 

Exception also to the admission in evidence of the answer, "It was not in normal condition.'' Both exceptions must be overruled, where it appears from the entire testimony of the expert that by his answer he intended only to say that the mind of the testator was more susceptible to influence and was less able to function normally than would be the case had he not had cardiac-vascular-renal disease. Becker v. Becker, 238 Mass. 362.

If plaintiff's tuberculosis was caused by this accident it would have been an element of damages; so if induced, without any intervening cause, by her weakened condition or her loss of blood, itself directly caused by the accident. 172 Action for price of "Aroostook'' potatoes; dispute as to the condition of the potatoes. Plaintiff called witness as expert as to the fair market price in 

Worcester. In a preliminary examination, the witness testified that he was a paper hanger and painter; had not been in the potato business since 1914; had bought and sold potatoes in 1913 and 1914 and had raised some in 1914; between 1914 and 1919, when he "made this transaction" with the defendant, he had not raised, bought nor sold potatoes; that at the time he sold the potatoes to the defendant he familiarized himself with the state of the market in potatoes, and in reply to the question, "Did you while you were in 

Worcester?" said "I did. That was practically the first thing I did, I went around familiarizing myself by asking the dealers the prices of potatoes that they offered to jobbers, the 'Aroostook' potatoes," and that he was familiar with the terms and terminology of the potato trade. The witness was allowed to testify. Held (1) All the evidence material to the finding of the qualification of the witness being in the bill of exceptions, the decision of the judge was reviewable; (2) The witness was qualified by a general experience in the potato trade which enabled him to apply the information, obtained by him on inquiring from jobbers, and from following the market, to the determination of the market value of the potatoes which he sold to the defendant. 

Shaw v. Keown & McEvoy, Inc., 243 

Mass. 221 at page 223. E. Electricity: Experiments: X-ray. Electricity is a proper subject for expert testimony;174 and though it has been held that when all particulars are before the jury opinion of an expert may be excluded 175 yet qualified experts have been allowed to testify as to the effect of electricity on the human body,178 that an electric light would not go out and remain out unless there was a defect,177 and that death was caused by an electric shock. An expert on electricity may testify to the last, as well as a physimony of the witness in the case at bar. (Citing, Whitney v. Thacher, 117 Mass. 

523; National Bank of Commerce v. 

New Bedford, 175 Mass. 257, 259.) Assuming the rule of qualification to be no broader than it is argued to be by the defendant, we think the evidence established that the witness had a general experience in the potato trade which enabled him to apply the information, obtained by him on inquiring from jobbers and from following the market, to the determination of the market value of the potatoes which he sold to the defendant. (Citing, Whitney v. Thacher, supra; National Bank of Commerce v. New Bedford, supra;

Barrie v. Quinby, 206 Mass. 259. Witnesses for the Commonwealth were cross-examined about their testimony in the Lee Police Court, to show that they were adding thereto. The defendant admitted that the judge was "familiar with the practice," but objected to the testimony. 

It was rightly admitted for the limited purpose of explaining away the inferences which the defendant was attempting to establish. Com. v. Williams, 244 Mass. 515 at 520.

IV. Opinion affecting due care. If a person involved in an injury acts in such way that he considers his conduct unsafe, the doctrine of "volenti non fit injuria" applies. If he acts in a manner that he considers safe, his so acting has bearing on his due care.

In the admission of direct evidence of the plaintiff's opinion at the time of his injury that he was acting safely, the court has discretion. A plaintiff may rely "to some extent" on the expectation that the defendant will exercise care not to in-

When it is simply a question of the plaintiff's reasonable conduct, evidence of his opinion as to his safety is admissible or excludable within the court's discretion; hence when one uses a diving chute his opinion that he was acting safely may be admitted or excluded as the court sees fit.252 A plaintiff has been permitted to testify that he did not realize a danger;253 yet his opinion as to the capabilities of his fellow workmen in handling a certain box has been excluded.254 In issues of due care arising from a plaintiff's crossing a street evidence that he thought that he had time to reach a place of safety before he might be endangered is usually admitted.255 What a plaintiff saw others do may affect his opinion in regard to what is safe. Acts of others are not only similar acts by others (see chapter 17 "Similar Circumstances, Events, Conditions and Acts") but are silent expressions of opinions as to what is safe conduct. Within the court's discretion such acts are admissible.256

"Exception to the admission of these questions must be sustained.

Expert witness cannot be asked or allowed to express an opinion founded in whole or in part on the evidence where, as in the case at bar, it was conflicting. The proper way to interrogate an expert to obtain his opinion is to put questions on hypothetical statements of facts or to ask the witness to give opinions founded on possible views of the evidence stating in connection with the opinions the hypothetical facts to which they relate so as to make them intelligible." Expert witness cannot be asked to give an opinion "founded on his understanding of the evidence against the objection of the other party, except in cases where the evidence is capable of but one interpretation," Questions must

ent question arises.275 As the jury is to pass on the entire question taking the opinion of the expert as one piece of evidence only, the facts on which he forms his opinion should be before them. The jury may fail to believe some fact or facts on which the expert bases his conclusion. In such case his opinion would be of no value to them. As the court does not pass on the truth of evidence he cannot exclude the question simply because it assumes the truth of some fact already in evidence which he does not believe. The jury alone passes on the truth of facts. Hence the facts on which the expert forms his opinion should be presented.276 Questions containing the clauses,277 "as testified to by the plaintiff," or "in the way that has been described," 278 have been admitted. The general rules have been thus summarized.879 "The competency of an expert witness to testify to his opinion rests upon unusual knowledge and extraordinary experience, superior to that of ordinary persons. The witness, being qualified in this particular, then may base his opinion upon facts observed by himself or within his own knowledge and testified to by himself, or upon facts assumed in the questions put to him and supported either by admitted facts or by the testimony of other witnesses already given or to be given at the trial, or upon facts be so framed that the witness will not be called upon to give an answer involving his opinion on disputed questions of fact which are not proper subjects for the testimony of an expert or to intimate to the jury his opinion as to the credibility of any of the witnesses. derived partly from one source and partly from the other. It is not necessary in all cases that the facts be stated in the form of an hypothetical question, although this is generally permissible. Where an opinion is sought upon substantially uncontradicted testimony heard by the witness with or without personal observation on his part, the question may be asked upon that express or implied assumption without reciting the testimony in the question. Where there is conflicting testimony, a witness, who has been present in court and heard it, may be asked if he has formed an opinion as to a material point, respecting which his skill gives him requisite qualifications to express an opinion, based upon that testimony or parts of it. If his answer is in the affirmative, then he may select and state the facts given in testimony which in his opinion, if true, are most significant and pertinent as aids in the formation of an opinion and to what conclusion his mind is led by the consideration of such facts. In the trial of a criminal or other case, it is permissible to ask an expert witness if he has formed an opinion from his observations and examination and from testimony heard in court as to the point in issue about which he is qualified to give evidence. Upon answering in the affirmative he may be asked to state that opinion. The direct examination then may stop, leaving the other side to develop the reasons in whatever detail may be desired. The forms of question given in decided cases may not be exclusive of all others. It is essential, however, that in giving testimony the expert witness should not undertake to pass upon the truth of the fundamental hypothesis upon which his opinion rests unless the facts assumed are within his own observation and knowledge. He simply must assume those facts as the basis of his opinion. It is the province of the jury alone to decide whether those facts are established. If they are established in substance to the satisfaction of the jury, then and not until then can the value of the expert evidence be taken up by them. If such facts are not so established, then the jury does not reach at all the consideration of the expert testimony. Manifestly an opinion not grounded either upon facts observed by the witness or upon facts assumed and specified in the question or upon facts in evidence through other witnesses, but based upon facts taken on the hearsay of others out of court and not in evidence and not put in the form of a supposition in the question, is not admissible in evidence. Such an opinion would or might well be founded upon facts, the truth of which could not in the nature of things be established to the satisfaction

of the jury because no competent evidence respecting them would be before the jury. As to the order of introduction of evidence and the form of questions much must be left to the discretion of the presiding judge." The discretion of the court may permit a hypothetical question to be put though it does not contain all the facts,280 or though it contains only facts sustained by the plaintiff's testimony," or if its impropriety is not specifically pointed out by the opponent on request,282 and may exclude it if it assumes facts not in evidence, 283 or wrongfully assumes liability 284 If the grounds of exclusion do not appear exceptions will not be sustained.285 281

C. Cross examination and impeachment of experts. In all cross examinations much is left to the court's discretion.302 An expert may be asked in cross examination the ground of his belief,303 and as to the material details of his interview with a party at the time of his medical examination of that party. 304 

He may be asked as to his employment and his interest 305 and bias. A question asking whether the plaintiff had no money with which to pay her doctor has been excluded.306 Questions tending to show that an expert in a personal injury case wherein the defendant is insured is in the employ of the company which insured the defendant, are not usually admitted.807 Questions as that if there was a violent explosion near the sidewalk in front of the house which caused the plaster and shelves to fall and part of the cellar wall to become broken, such conditions would be noticeable for years provided no permanent repairs were afterwards made.

Although the admission of this evidence was not preceded by proof that the condition of the house in 1921 was the same as immediately after the explosion, it was rightly admitted, as there was other evidence tending to show that the conditions found were not due to shrinkage or to the natural and usual settling of the house, but were such as would result from a violent explosion near the house, and would be consistent with the explosion described to have occurred in 1914. 

Whether the evidence was too remote was within the sound discretion of the trial judge, which was not exercised wrongly. Goldman v. Regan, 247 Mass. 

492, at 493 and 494. Exceptions to evidence which arose from the admission of questions calling for expert medical opinion. In dealing with such questions much must be left to the discretion of the trial court; and his rulings will not be revised unless they are plainly prejudicial to the rights of the excepting party. IX. Doctor's opinion as hearsay. A doctor's statement out of court of opinion or diagnosis, is mere hearsay and not admissible.818

X. Experts in criminal cases. The rules as applied to civil cases apply also to criminal matters. The Commonwealth, however, in criminal cases owes a duty to present as witnesses only competent experts.

XI. Objectionable evidence not objected to. Though the general rule is that objectionable evidence not objected to has probative force, this may not apply to all expressions of opinion. 

An opinion given casually has been held not to override better and more explicit evidence.820 When expert evidence is before a jury certainly common knowledge cannot override the expert believable evidence to the extent of creating liability on a finding contrary to the truthful expert evidence.821 juries received in 1919. Defendant offered in evidence a statement signed by a physician, deceased, concerning an injury received by the plaintiff in a station of the defendant in 1910. Judge remarked that the requirement of the statute was that the deceased must have made the statement of facts of his own known knowledge before the beginning of the action and in good faith.

In these circumstances the ruling that whatever the plaintiff stated to the decedent might be read, imported a finding of the preliminary facts required by G. L. chapter 233, section 65. (Cit ing McSweeney v. Edison Electric Illuminating Co., 228 Mass. 563, 564. 

Eldridge v. Barton, 232 Mass. 183.)

The fact that the statement was made by the plaintiff, and reduced to writing and signed by the decedent, ten or twelve years before the trial, did not render it incompetent. The statement was introduced in evidence only on the question of damages. The jury returned a general verdict for the defendant.

I. Generally. At common law hearsay evidence is not admissible. The reasons are four,-that the statement is not under oath;¹ that the adverse party has not had an opportunity to cross examine, that the repetition of a statement is likely to be inaccurate, and that the honesty of the speaker who has not appeared before, and been observed by the trier of facts, cannot be fairly passed on. When a second trial of the same issue between the same parties occurs the evidence of a witness given at the first trial is not subject to all the objections which apply to the ordinary hearsay statement. Such evidence has been received under oath, and the adversary has had the opportunity of cross examination. In two particulars, however, the former evidence still is objectionable-its repetition may be inaccurate and the jury has not seen the witness. If the witness can give his evidence again, a fair trial should require his presence. So says the first case decided in Massachusetts. If however he cannot testify, is the exclusion of his former evidence a lesser evil than its admission? That is the question which confronts the court in admitting evidence of testimony at a former trial given by one now unavailable. Two of the objections noted above then, namely that this hearsay is not under oath and that the adversary has had no chance to cross-examine seem sufficiently satisfied to allow the admission of the evidence. The court tries to eliminate the third objection to this hearsay, by

CHAPTER 10 DYING DECLARATIONS IN HOMICIDE AND UNDER STATUTE 

I. Generally, pp. 624-625.

II. The Rule, pp. 625–629. 

A. Generally, pp. 625-627. 

B. Civil cases, p. 627.

I. Generally. A dying declaration, repeated in court, is hearsay. As has been said in the preceding chapter the objections to the admission of any hearsay are that it is not under oath, that the adversary cannot cross-examine the speaker, that repetition leads to inaccuracy, and that the trier of facts cannot judge the speaker's truth by his appearance. Permitting repetition of a dying declaration in court is contrary to all these objections; yet, at common law in homicide, the court admits it, and by statute the common law doctrine has been extended to criminal prosecutions for procuring miscarriage which result in death.

The necessity of the evidence to prevent a murderer's escape, especially when he alone is responsible for the silencing of the most important witness, has established this exception.¹ In establishing the rule admitting such evidence the courts seem to consider the motive for speaking the truth at the time of such declaration as powerful as the motive to testify truthfully under oath. If one regards an oath as sacred, the probability is that in one's last moments, when one has abandoned all hope of recovery, one will not accuse another falsely of one's death. 

1 Wigmore, section 1433, quoting 

State v. Bohan, 15 Kan. 418. 

2 See Maxwell v. Hardy, 8 Pick. 559 at 561. See also Wigmore, section 1438. 

8 They are admitted on the ground that the solemnity of impending death is equivalent to the solemnity of an oath, in restraining one from falsehood. 

Commonwealth v. Roberts, 108 Mass. 

296 at 301. 624

DYING DECLARATIONS IN HOMICIDE 

625 Were the oath required only as a threat of imprisonment the rule might be different; but when the doctrine of dying declarations arose, in about the 17th century, the punishments for perjury in the hereafter seem more frequently to have been brought to the attention of the courts and witnesses. The logic then that one about to die would state truthfully the important facts, seemed to dispose of the necessity of an oath. Though there is no chance to cross examine, yet the aim of cross examination is chiefly to procure the exact facts and to test the witness's credibility and accuracy. In dying declarations the statement on account of the speaker's physical condition, usually contains only the important facts, and the circumstance of his facing the hereafter, warrants the assumption that he is doing his best to tell the truth. The reasoning does not convince that cross examination might not assist in the search for justice; but the case where the statement would be false would be rare, and the probability of the defendant's guilt, indicated by the statement, seems to overcome the presumption of innocence to the extent of allowing the jury to consider the evidence. The objection that repetition may lead to inaccuracy seems of less weight than in ordinary hearsay. The tragedy of the situation calls forth the hearer's most careful attention, and the seriousness of the crime, and death seem to indicate that chances for inaccuracy are diminished. The last reason for excluding the dying declaration as hearsay, namely that the jury cannot see the witness to judge his veracity, seems outweighed by the awfulness of the crime, and the danger that a murderer by his own act in destroying evidence shall go unpunished. The rule, however, is a limited one. Massachusetts cases disclose only a working rule.

III. Court's discretion in excluding evidence to offset facts in dying declaration. Although in many matters the court in its discretion may exclude evidence to explain or impeach were the evidence not produced by a dying declaration, the fact that evidence thus produced violates the hearsay principle, seems to require that the court exercise this discretion to exclude with caution. The jury generally should consider carefully the weight of the evidence. "It is to be considered," says Mr. Greenleaf, "that the particulars of the violence of which the deceased has spoken, were in general likely to have occurred under circumstances of confusion and surprise, calculated to prevent their being accurately observed; and leading both to mistake as to the identity of persons and to the omission of facts essentially important to the completeness and truth of the narrative." The jury might be so instructed. Such evidence should not be allowed to prejudice unjustly against the defendant. Every precaution should be taken to protect the defendant's rights. If a deceased in a dying declaration identifies the defendant as her assailant, the court cannot in his discretion exclude evidence of occasions wherein the deceased mistook others for persons whom she knew, and evidence that she was in the habit of so doing. I. Generally. Pedigree constituted another limited exception to the hearsay rule. Since the passing of Acts of 1889, chapter 

100, now General Laws, chapter 233, section 65, admitting statements of deceased persons made in good faith before trial, and on personal knowledge questions involving this exception to hearsay are of less importance. Evidence offered of one Hughes offered by defendant that deceased had said that she was pregnant by one T. and that if T. did not remedy her condition she would do so herself. Evidence excluded. "It is not easy to see how any question of pedigree can be involved in this case." "It is not enough that the declarations tendered may relate to some question of pedigree, nor is it enough that a question of pedigree may be relevant and pertinent to the issue. The exception relative to the admissibility of hearsay evidence because it relates to pedigree, is only when the question of pedigree is itself in issue. When declarations in relation to pedigree are proved to have been made by a person who might properly make them, it is indispensable that they be made before the question in issue arises."'

CHAPTER 12 MATTERS OF GENERAL AND PUBLIC INTEREST 

I. Generally, pp. 635-636. 

II. The rule, pp. 636-638. 

A. Stated, p. 636.

B. Proof of general repute, pp. 636-637. 

C. Matters to which the rule applies, pp. 637-638. 

D. Private boundaries, p. 638.

I. Generally. General repute usually is not admissible. The theory of a trial is that matters shall be examined in the light of facts presented by those who know them. Hence unless a material fact is common knowledge its existence must be proved usually by evidence of those who know it at first hand. Hearsay is not admissible. Yet, under conditions of necessity and death, hearsay of some matters of general and public interest, anciently current in a community, seems admissible to prove the fact recited in the hearsay. This is a recognized exception to the hearsay rule. The exception seems to have been confused with other subjects, namely the proof of the location of private boundaries,¹ ancient and recorded documents, res gestae and statements in disparagement of title by a party's predecessor in title.

I. Generally. The hardship of proof to establish the genuineness of documents over thirty years old at the time of the trial, has led to an exception to the rule against hearsay,¹ and the rule affecting res inter alios. This rule allows the admission of such ancient documents. Our registry system with the admission of certified copies therefrom and the statute admitting certain statements of deceased persons,* make this common law rule of less importance. The rule nevertheless is still a fairly active one. It is to be noted that the rule admits the documents if material, in favor of all persons," not merely in favor of or against parties or privies.

VII. Illustrations of the rules, pp. 666-668. 1 I. Generally. Entries of various classes made in the course of duty are admissible though hearsay and unsupported by judicial oath. This chapter does not deal with all such entries. 

For clearness the classes should be distinguished. Outside of the present subject are those public records made by public officers which are admissible by statute,' those public documents admissible at 2 common law and those private recorded documents admissible under the recording acts. The documents in those classes are usually admitted regardless of the fact that the person signing them and the person certifying the copies are living, sane and available as witnesses.

under other rules. Our definition of private entries in the course of duty is too narrow to include these. It applies to matters where the duty arises through some business custom and duty, or custom and duty of equal ethical force." The definition includes shop books but also includes other entries made in the course of duty. The Massachusetts rule has been from time to time in a state of considerable confusion 10 and exactly what its final outcome would have been if statutes 11 had not superseded partly the common law rule is doubtful. The rule seemed to be merging into consolidation, affected by three independent principles,-first the Colonial Rule 12 admitting entries made by a party in his books, second the common law 13 exception admitting entries made in the course of duty when the entrant was dead, insane, or unavailable on account of absence from the jurisdiction, and third a principle which seems a corollary of both, the admission of shop books wherein the entries were not made by a party personally, when the entrant was not available. 14

I. Introductory. Several important exceptions to the rules of exclusion have been created by statute. Most of these create 669

exceptions to the rule against hearsay, but some admit evidence though self serving, transcribed or secondary. They are considered below.

II. Declarations of deceased persons under general laws, chapter 233, section 65-A. The statute annotated. "A dec laration of a deceased 2 person shall not be inadmissible in evidence as hearsay if the court finds that it was made in good faith before the commencement of the action and upon the personal knowledge of the declarant."8 5 3 4

"By the true construction of it, Revised Laws, chapter 175, section 66 authorizes the admission in evidence of a statement of a deceased person where the statement concerns a fact of which the deceased had personal knowledge. IV. Dying declarations in prosecutions under general laws, chapter 272, section 19. In criminal prosecutions for alleged abortions, in which the death of a woman is alleged to have resulted from the means described in General Laws, Chapter 272, Section 19, her dying declarations shall be admissible in evidence, 100 

99 Loweth v. Bradford, 227 Mass. 584. 

100 General Laws, Chapter 233, sec tion 64; Revised Laws, Chapter 175,

Section 65; Acts of 1889, chapter 100. 

See "Dying Declarations.'' "While at common law dying declarations of a deceased person were confined to prosecutions for homicide the Statute of 

1889, chapter 100, now Revised Laws, Chapter 175, section 65, makes such declarations admissible in the prosecution of the crime for which the defendant is indicted. (Cases cited.) 

Before such declarations can be admitted the judge must be satisfied of the declarant's belief in the certainty of approaching death and that the statements made are material and relevant to the issue on trial. (Cases cited.) 

The preliminary inquiry made in the absence of the jury showed, and the judge by admitting the evidence, found that the decedent realized that all hope of recovery was gone, and the fact that she held up her right hand and repeated to one of the attending physicians, 'I say this realizing I am about to die and this is true so help me God,' did not render her declaration that he performed the operation merely a statement under oath and inadmissible as hearsay. True she made contradictory statements as to the person responsible for her pregnancy but the change of names in the accusation went to the weight and not to the competency of the evidence when submitted to the jury. (Cases cited.) The jury was instructed to disregard this evidence unless satisfied of the defendant's identity beyond reasonable doubt." 

Com. v. Turner, 224 Mass. 229. 

Indictment for attempting by the use of instruments to procure miscarriage in consequence of which decedent died. 

The dying declarations made when she fully realized that she had no hope of recovery, contained in the form of answers to questions in a paper subscribed and sworn to by her before a justice of peace, who testified to having taken down the answers as nearly as he could in writing long hand, are admissible in evidence and the presiding judge properly may allow the contents of the paper to be read to the jury. Statements of the woman contained in such a paper which describe her purpose in seeking medical advice and assistance from the defendant and her conversations with him, are competent evidence to which the declarant could have testified as a witness if living. Commonwealth v. Wagner, 231 Mass. 265. 

The woman's dying declarations written and verbal were admitted. She said that defendant had performed an abortion upon her. Besides a general exception to the admission the defendant specifically excepted to these statements. He contends that these were merely her opinion or conclusion that what the defendant had done had caused miscarriage and had been done. for that purpose and that if she had been a witness she could have stated merely what the defendant had said and done and only the jury could have drawn inferences therefrom. Her dying declarations were admissible only to those things to which she could have testified if she had been living and had been sworn as a witness. In common language and in its legal acceptation the word "abortion" means simply a miscarriage, the premature delivery before capable of sustaining life. It does not of itself import a charge of any original intent. Com. v. Smith, 213

V. Foreign laws. By Acts of 1926, chapter 168, the court takes judicial notice of certain foreign laws. 101 Hence various sections 102 relating to foreign laws are almost obsolete. 

VI. Public and quasi public documents. Oaths and affidavits administered or taken by a notary public of any other state or government, under his seal,108 acts of incorporation,104 printed copies of all statutes, acts and resolves of the Commonwealth, public or private, published under its authority, copies of ordinances of a city, the by-laws of a town or of rules and regulations of a board of aldermen attested by the clerk of such city or town,105 copies of books, papers, and documents and records in any department of the Commonwealth duly authenticated 106 when material, by statute have been made admissible. These are considered more fully under "Public and Quasi Public Acts and Documents, 107 and "Entries in the Course of Duty." 108 

VII. Accounts of certain banks. Copies of the records, books and accounts of a trust company, national bank or savings bank, doing business in the Commonwealth, shall be competent evidence in all cases, equally with the original thereof, if there is annexed to such copy an affidavit, taken before a clerk of a court of record or notary public, under the seal of such court or notary, stating that the affiant is the officer having charge of the original records, books and accounts, and that the copy is correct and is full so far as it relates to the subject matter therein mentioned.109

2. Interpretation of statutes. In reading the cases the predecessors of this statute should be borne in mind. Acts of 1905 

Chapter 330, Section 1, required certain hospitals to keep records, Section 2, stated that they should be in the custody of the person in charge and "admissible in evidence in the courts of the Commonwealth as to all matters therein contained." 118 

Section 3 provided that they should not be subject to inspection and regulations as were "public records" under Revised Laws, Chapter 35, section 17, but enacted that "they shall not be open to public inspection until they are produced in court by the person having custody of the same." 119 This statute did not admit hospital records made before the statute was passed.120 Acts of 

1908 chapter 269 extended the provisions to records made before the enactment of 1905.121 This permitted records made before the enactment of the statute to be admitted.122 In 1912 by chapter 442, section 1, the former statute which required hospitals to keep records of the "history" of the cases, was amended so that the "medical history" only was required; 128 by this section also a clause in earlier statutes requiring the records such hospital, and in compliance with the terms of such order, such records may be inspected and copies furnished on payment of a reasonable fee."

By section 2, the clause in earlier statutes making the record evidence "as to all matters therein contained" was stricken out and the records were made evidence simply "so far as such records relate to the treatment and medical history"; and it was enacted that "nothing therein contained shall be admissible as evidence which has reference to the question of liability." 124 

As to what is a part of the "medical history" and what is inadmissible "as evidence which has reference to the question of liability," the court has refused to accept the view that the hospital record is inadmissible if it may have reference to the question of liability even though it directly relates only to the treatment and medical history of the case.125 A reasonable interpretation must be given to both these clauses in the statute. 

Apparently the legislation making this hearsay evidence admissible was enacted primarily to relieve the physicians and nurses of public hospitals from the hardship and inconvenience of attending court as witnesses to facts which ordinarily would be found recorded in the hospital books. It is argued that under the broad language of the original act (Statute 1905, chapter 330) making the "records of the case" admissible as evidence "as to all matters therein contained," plaintiffs in personal injury cases were sometimes confronted at the trial with hearsay statements in hospital records which related solely to the cause of the accident. However that may be, the amendment 126 of 

1912 defined what the record should contain and limited its admissibility as evidence. Under the present statute only such portions are admissible as relate to the treatment and medical history of the patient.127 A reasonable and practical construction of the statute requires that a record which relates directly and mainly to the treatment and medical history of the patient should be admitted, even though incidentally the facts recorded may have some bearing on the question of liability. The improper application of the facts recorded can be prevented by

I. Introductory. In judging the guilt of another we frequently deduce from his past acts the degree of his wickedness and hence the probabilities of his commission or failure to commit the present offense. In the trial of cases this process of deduction is not encouraged. The theory of our system of trial is that a man shall be tried, at one time, for that offense only which is set out in the pleadings. In criminal cases the constitutions provide that the crime shall be clearly set forth. In civil cases the reason for the declaration or bill and answer is to set clearly definite issues for trial.5 Many other reasons are given for the exclusion of such evidence, that it complicates or would involve the issue, would create prejudice," would cause a verdict in the present case because the defendant had escaped a verdict in another matter, would tend to surprise the adversary, and would lead to other wrongs. Each of these in proper cases is

Poorvu, 249 Mass. 88. There is a probative effect resulting from continuance of a scheme and in the doing of other acts in pursuance of it. It is somewhat of the nature of threats and declarations of intent but more especially of preparations for the commission of the crime. "If for instance it could be shown that a defendant had formed a settled purpose to obtain certain property which could only be gotten by doing several preliminary things the last of which was criminal the government might show on his trial for the commission of that last criminal act that he had formed the purpose to accomplish the result of obtaining the preliminary things which were necessary to that end. This purpose might be shown by clear direct evidence as a letter, or by circumstantial evidence as by other acts. And in such case it makes no difference whether the preliminary acts are criminal or not; otherwise the greater the crime the greater his immunity. Such preliminary acts are not competent because they are criminal, but because they are relevant to the issue on trial; and the fact that they are criminal does not render them irrelevant." (Fraud, Sibley v. Garland, 239 Mass. 20. Feinberg v. Poorvu, 249

the Ya fraud 17 or other like matter 18 is required, considerable leeway is allowed in the proof of similar events.19 In most crimes and in many torts, one's state of mind is material. 80 Petition for damages from setting street line. City established a building line. The petitioner brought this petition under Statute 1917, chapter 344, Part 2, Par. 73, to recover the damages.

The respondent was permitted to show that although no building line had been established on Main Street, certain specified bank and other business buildings erected or reconstructed within the past fifteen years, had been set back from the street line distance varying from two to six or eight feet. The apparent purpose of this testimony was to have the jury infer that whatever damage the petitioner might suffer by being prevented from erecting structures on this five foot strip of its front yard 30 would be offset by the advantages thereby accruing to the lot; and in proof thereof that property owners on Main Street, had voluntarily set back their buildings from the street line. The judge's charge emphasized this purpose. 

This evidence was inadmissible, and considered in the light of the charge was prejudicial. Te record does not disclose that the owners of lots on Main Street set their buildings back voluntarily; they may have been compelled to do so by reason of restrictions in their deeds. Nor was it shown that the two streets were so similar in character, use, and other circumstances as to warrant an inference that what was advantageous to one street (assuming that it was) would necessarily be advantageous to the other. (Citing Campbell v. Russell, 139 Mass.

46 The plaintiff excepted to the testimony as to the manner in which the defendant operated his automobile during the two years after the accident which resulted in the death of the testatrix. The fifth count contained an allegation that injuries were caused by reason of the defendant's careless and negligent operation of said automobile as well as by his physical unfitness to operate an automobile.'' The evidence showed that the defendant wore an artificial leg, and that at that time his left leg was withered. The plaintiff contends that there was no evidence to show that the physical disability of the defendant was the same two years afterwards as at the time of the accident, and that consequently this evidence as to the manner in which he operated his automobile, aside from other reasons, was incompetent. The jury fairly could have assumed that the condition of the right leg had not changed during this period. Besides the defendant testified at the trial, and was subjected to certain tests in the presence of the jury as to the use which he had of both legs, from all of which the jury could have found that the defendant's physical condition had not materially changed. We are of opinion that the allegation in the fifth count of the declaration was in effect an allegation that the defendant was physically unfit by reason of his infirmities and disabilities to operate an automobile. In view of this allegation in the fifth count we are of opinion that evidence was admissible to show the manner in which the defendant operated his automobile within a reasonable time before and after the accident not for the purpose of showing that he did operate it carefully at the time of the accident, but for the purpose of rebutting the inference that he was physically unfit to operate, stop, regulate or control an automobile at the time of the accident on account of his disabilities. O'Hare v. Gloag, 221 Mass. 24.

55 The defendant contends that if its offer of proof had been admitted in evidence the jury would have been warranted in fiinding the fire had been set by a son of the plaintiff or at least sufficient doubt would have been raised to overcome the burden of proof. But in the absence of any direct evidence connecting him with the occurrence, the defendant endeavored to show from incidents in his early life that he had acquired а disposition which had ripened into a habit to set incendiary fires whenever the opportunity offered.

A habit of this character is abnormal, and it may be criminal. The defendant was required to satisfy the presiding judge, that the course of conduct on which it sought to predicate the commission of an affirmative wrongful act of the character claimed had become so continuous and systematic that the setting of the fire in question would follow as a reasonable and probable consequence. (Citing Shailer v. Bum stead, 99 Mass. 112. Thayer v. Thayer, 101 Mass. 111, 113, 114. Commonwealth v. Abbott, 130 Mass. 472, 473. Hathaway v. Tinkham, 148 Mass. 85. Lane v. 

Moore, 151 Mass. 87, 90. Edwards v. 

Worcester, 172 Mass. 104. Wigmore on 

Evidence, sections 92, 376.) 68 Speed at one place as evidence of speed at another. The first contention of the plaintiff is that the car was approaching Judson Street at a rate of speed prohibited by law. He put in an order passed by the Board of Mayor and Alderman as revised by the Board of Railroad Commissioners which order reads "No street railway car shall run at speed exceeding twelve miles per hour when crossing another street and in no instance exceeding twenty-miles per hour.''

It appears by uncontradicted testimony that between Ashland and Judson Streets its rate was about fifteen miles per hour; it also is not disputed that the motorman shut off the power, reversed his motor and put on his brakes before the car reached Judson Street. No witness testified as to the rate of speed upon crossing Judson Street, but the reasonable inference is that concurrently with the throwing off of power with the reversal of the motor and the application of the brakes the speed of the car lessened. The burden was upon the plaintiff to establish by a fair preponderance of the testimony that the rate while crossing Judson Street was in excess of twelve miles an hour. Burden not sustained. Sibley v. Garland, 239 Mass. 20. "** "Within two years before the beginning of his relations with Mrs. Rogers, Farmer had made to two other persons false representations of a kindred nature touching the sale of extremely valuable publications to persons of great wealth. This testimony was limited strictly to the issue of Farmer's intent in his personal transactions with Mrs. Rogers. The principle of law governing the introduction of evidence of this kind has been discussed with fullness and accuracy in Commonwealth v. Joffries, 7 Allen 548, and in Commonwealth v. 

Jackson, 132 Mass. 16. Summarily stated it is that it is not competent to show one crime committed by a defendant for the purpose of prov ing that he committed another distinct crime. Guilty conduct in one instance does not follow from like conduct on another occasion. It is not fair that a

event are admissible against one; so to some extent 92 of matters defendant should be called upon in the course of a trial to exonerate himself from offenses not charged against him in the indictment. But commonly it is necessary to prove a particular intent as an essential ingredient of the crime alleged. The thought of the human mind is not capable of direct observation. It can be determined only from external signs and from the knowledge the person is proved to possess. Some offenses are not so plain and distinct and so connected with visible facts that the accompanying intent can be inferred without further aid. Obtaining money or property by fraudulent pretenses under some conditions belongs to this class. Conduct of one on another occasion reasonably near in time under similar circumstances it appearing to be parts of a comprehensive scheme by which different persons are to be defrauded may have an important bearing upon his purpose in doing a particular act. (Citing, Commonwealth v. Stuart, 207 Mass. 568. Commonwealth v. Dow, 217 Mass. 473. King v. Boyle (1914) 3 K. B. 339, 347. Makin v. Attorney General (1894) A. C. 57, 65, and cases cited in each opinion.) This principle was not narrowed by the decision nor by anything said in Noyes v. Boston & Main R. R., 213 Mass. 9. Although the facts bring the present case close to the line, no reversible error is shown in admitting the evidence. It had some tendency to show a fraudulent intent on the part of Farmer."

99 Cadieux in December 1912, sold a parcel of real estate to Schusler and in that sale the defendant Fuchs acted for Schusler and the defendants Quinn and Berman acted as real estate brok ers. Evidence of representations made to Cadieux was offered to show that the conduct of the defendants at that time was similar to their conduct in this case that the sale occurred at about the same time as the sale by Bullard and that similar representations were made in both transactions. This evidence was offered to show the intent of the defendants in their dealings with 

Bullard. "Conduct of one on another occasion reasonably near in time, under similar circumstances, if appearing to be part of a comprehensive scheme by which different persons are to be defrauded, may have an important bearing upon his purpose in doing a particular act." (Citing Commonwealth v. 

Farmer, 218 Mass. 507, 512. Commonwealth v. Riches, 219 Mass. 440.) There is no evidence to show that Cadieux was defrauded, or that the sale of his property was not perfectly fair transaction. The sale was fully consummated, and so far as appears in the record, there is nothing to indicate that Cadieux was induced to part with his property by reason of any fraud practiced upon him. For these reasons the evidence relating to the sale by Cadieux was incompetent, and the exception to its admission must be sustained. Commonwealth v. Quinn, 222 Mass. 504.

101 Illegal practice of medicine:-The 

Commonwealth elected to rely on the 

24th and 30th of November, 1914, respectively as the days upon which the offences were committed. Against the defendant's exception the Commonwealth was permitted to introduce evidence of the defendant's acts and conversations on different days between

April 1913 and November 1914. While 

Commonwealth is not allowed to introduce evidence of other crimes with the purpose of showing the defendant to be guilty of the offense charged, evidence of other crimes and acts is admissible when they are a part of a common purpose where the plan or scheme of the defendant is a material circumstance and when the course of the defendant's business is a matter of importance in passing on his guilt or innocence. Where the several visits and consultations of a patient with one from whom she is receiving medicines, are but parts of the same course of treatment where the speech or conduct of the defendant on one of the occasions may be equivocal, and it is essential to determine the dominant purpose of the defendant on the day of the offense, then the conduct of the defendant on other days, and as a part of the same transaction, may be a matter of great importance and therefore of probative value. (See Commonwealth v. Dow, 217 Mass. 473.) The defendant contended that in delivering the medicine to the various witnesses he was acting not as a practitioner of medicine, but as an agent or salesman for the Dr. Willard M. Lindsey, Inc. or the Magnetic 

Sanitarium Company. Assuming that he could sell and deliver drugs and medicines without violating the particular statute, the Commonwealth had a right to meet this defense by showing the plan and purpose of the defendant as well as his method of business in order that the jury might determine whether on November 24 and November 30, he was acting in the capacity of a salesman or a physician. As sales of liquor at other times than that alleged to have been held admissible as showing the intent with which the specified liquors have been kept, so the intent with which the defendant disposed of his medicines on the days in question whether as sales of goods to customers or as medicines prescribed by himself, might be shown by his conduct respecting people and medicines in his office on other occasions. Commonwealth v. Lindsey, 223 Mass. 392. (A majority decision.) (Citing Cases.)

At a time previous to the present accident, the intestate had met with an injury in which his skull was fractured. The defendant offered to show by expert testimony that a fractured skull impairs equilibrium; that alcoholic habits or habits of drinking, whether constant or intermittent, still further impair equilibrium, and that the intestate since the fracture had drunk intoxicating liquors and had been drunk from time to time. No evidence was offered of a universal and unvarying rule that loss of equilibrium follows, without exception, every frac ture of the human skull regardless of its nature and degree, nor was there evidence to show the nature and the degree of the fracture of the skull of the intestate, or to prove that he had in fact a balance of mind and body less than normal, or that at the time of the accident he was intoxicated or under the influence of liquors. ¹¹7 F. 

Similar acts of crowds or mob. If a person has the duty to protect another the fact that a boisterous uncontrollable crowd frequently and previously has gathered at a place to which the protection should extend cannot be ignored; and if at a later time such crowd does gather and does injury to that other without his fault, in a suit for that injury evidence of the previous gathering and conduct is admissible, when it tends to show that the defendant should have realized the danger, as evidence of the defendant's reasonable notice of the danger.118 

G. Similar acts to show incompetency. When the declaration alleged merely negligence of a servant on a certain occasion and does not charge incompetency, the proof should be confined to his acts on that occasion;119 but if it is alleged that he is a careless and incompetent servant as the master well knew or in the exercise of care should have known, other facts are admissible to prove that allegation.120 Generally.

VII. Similar acts by privies. As was pointed out in "Admissions" the acts of a party's privy in title sometimes affect the party, and then are admissible against him. If he deals with the same subject matter under those circumstances, the method in which the matter was then treated may show the true privies of the parties and is admissible.185

172"That other employers furnished similar appliances for use in similar work and that the tongs were purchases from a reputable maker do not as matter of law relieve the defendant, if the appliances furnished, although perfect in mechanism, are found to be unsuitable and unsafe, which condition the defendant knew or in the exercise of reasonable diligence should have known. Carpenter against his employer, before the workmen's compensation act, plaintiff was injured when he was at work piling sawed hard pine by means of an engine, a derrick, and a pair of tongs, and one of the timbers slipped from the tongs and struck the plaintiff on the head. The tongs were unsuitable for hoisting such timbers, being intended for use only in handling round logs, and the only safe tongs for such timbers, were chain tongs, which easily could be had in the open market. The jury found in answer to special questions, that the tongs supplied by the defendant were in common use for the purpose for which the defendant used them and were used commonly by contractors and builders for such work. The jury returned a general verdict for the plaintiff but the judge ruled that on the special findings the action could not be maintained. Held, that the ruling was wrong because if the tongs were unsuitable and unsafe and the defendant in the exercise of reasonable diligence should have known this, it was no defense for him that he had proceeded in the usual manner pursued by other builders under like circumstances. Wilson v. Alexander, 230 Mass. 242.

In the former as bearing on the negligence of the defendant in permitting the swine to be at large on the public street, evidence was admitted to show that they had been frequently seen at large outside the defendant's premises previous to the plaintiff's injury. It was held that the evidence limited as it was by the instructions of the court was admissible. In that case the important question was the negli gence in failing to keep the swine safely inclosed; and as tending to show that proper care was not taken, and that they did not escape by pure accident, the evidence was admissible. In the case at bar the conduct of the plaintiff in caring for his horse at the time of the accident, and not his conduct at another time, was the question 1
