XIII. Previous and subsequent conditions or use of premises and machinery. The movements of a machine, and the condition of premises, before and immediately after the event in issue, may be admitted to show its defective condition or (if previous and under such conditions that the party to be charged should have known its condition) notice thereof; likewise purposes for which premises have been customarily used, may tend to show the purpose of their present use." The trial judge has discrebefore the jury. In Johnstone v. Tuttle, the plaintiff while at work on a street lamp, was standing on a ladder, one end of which rested on his wagon; his horse started because frightened by the defendant's dog. The defendant contended that the horse had a habit of starting and that this was the cause of the plaintiff's injury. To prove that the cause was not the defendant's fault, it was proper to show the habit of the horse. That case is not applicable to the case at bar where the issue involved was the care of the plaintiff at the time of the accident, not the habit or disposition of the horse. The plaintiff admitted that at the close of his day's work he took the harness from the horse and turned it into a field and that the last he saw of the horse, it "went into the highway" and out of his sight. In view of this testimony even if the evidence of the plaintiff's daughter were not believed, it was of no material importance that at other times the horse was seen at large on the highway, and there was no reversible error in excluding the evidence.

XIV. Value. Actual sales of other similar land in the vicinity, made near the time at which the value of the land in question is to be ascertained, are admissible to show its value.232 Though the court has discretion as to the remoteness of such land, that discretion is not unlimited.238 Value in other years of land a quarter of a mile distant has been held not too remote.234 In taking by eminent domain, when the issue is the value of the land after the taking, evidence of the selling price of some of the land after the taking is admissible, to show the value of the land which the petitioner owned after the taking, but not the value of the land before the taking.235 Evidence of the assessed value of land nearby, offered after the assessed value of the land taken had been admitted, has been held rightly excluded.236 

Values of the other land may be given in values per square foot.287

A price for other like land paid in compromise by a city is not admissible to show market value.238 In determining the value of services, the price paid for the same services between the parties, at other times, may be shown.239 The market value of like standardized articles is admissible to show their value;240 and the sale price at a fair sale shortly after a conversion may determine the value at the time of conversion.241 If there is no ready market, the time of such sale may be more remote.242 The periments shall be admitted must be left largely to the discretion of the trial judge. XV. Cross examination. The extent of cross examination, though usually within the court's discretion in matters involving similar circumstances, is limited.246. If the similar matter is part of the act to be proved, a considerable latitude in cross examination doubtless will be allowed.247 When a second offense of a criminal defendant is directly in issue, he may be cross examined as to whether he previously pleaded guilty to a complaint which charged him with the previous offense, and as to his serving sentence therefor,248 the record need not be produced.249

The record would be required as the best evidence if the attempt were to impeach the witness;250 and the attempt to discredit a defendant on trial for larceny by showing on cross examination, particularly when the evidence is offered without the record, that the defendant was charged with other crimes such as with the sale of narcotics, and that he was licensed to operate an automobile in a name different to his, is not allowable.251 When the other crimes are part of a general scheme, cross examination may show them so.252 Though the court has wide discretion to allow more after the material date, Woonsocket Machine & Press Co. v. I. Introductory: What is value. When value of an article is to be proved if it has a clear market value, and can be purchased at a staple price, that price is usually its value.¹ Sometimes however an article at the place where located has no set market value; perhaps it cannot be duplicated and may be most valuable when employed with other property. "Its value when thus employed might be much greater than the price at a possible auction if sold separate from the other property. The test then, is the "highest price which a normal purchaser not under peculiar compulsion will pay at the time and place in question in order to get the thing."" Purchasers might buy with intent to adapt the property to other uses, or might buy with the hope of acquiring other property or rights which have been used with the property to enhance its value.

The plaintiff who was the owner of the dye was a dealer in dye stuffs at the place of shipment; evidence that he personally packed the dye; that he had dealt considerably in the particular kind of dye stuff that was shipped; that he was familiar with the value of dye stuffs at that time and that although he had made no examination of the contents of the keg he had taken a sample of the contents of the keg in question, had examined it and had had it tested. 

Subject to an exception by the defendant the plaintiff was allowed to testify as to the market value of the lost dye. 

Held, that (1) where the value of property, real or personal, is in controversy the owner thereof may be presumed to have such familiarity with it as to be qualified to express an opinion as to its value; (2) The evidence apart from the fact that it was the testimony of the owner warranted a finding that the plaintiff was competent to give his opinion as evidence upon the subject of the market value of the lost dyc, Meyer v. Adams Express Co., 240 Mass..

E. An unaccepted offer and willingness to pay a proper price. 

Evidence of unaccepted offers 52 and willingness to pay a certain price 58 unless admitted by some other rule of law 54 are not evidence of value. When however one qualified testifies that he was willing to pay a certain price and that this was the market price there is not harmful error in admitting the evidence as evidence of the market price.55 

F. Auction. Prices obtained at a fair open public auction are evidence of value.56

G. Mortgage security. What the value of property is for mortgage purposes has little bearing on its market value and dence upon the question of value. But in a market regularly attended by buyers and sellers, an offer as well as a sale of an article of recognized uniform character, constantly bought and sold in that market so as to have a place upon the daily price current lists may serve to show the market value of that article did not exceed the price at which it was offered. It is admissible because of its publicity and the presumption of the presence of dealers ready to purchase and who would have done so if the offer had been below the market value. That dealers are themselves guided in these transactions by such indications of the state of the market makes the fact one that may properly be considered in evidence.

Holmes, in Braithwaite v. Hall, 168

The general rule of damages in trover and in contract for not delivering goods, undoubtedly is the fair market value of the goods. B. Profits-1. Generally. The question whether the profits which a plaintiff would have made had the defendant's wrong not intervened, may enter the consideration in setting the value of the article damaged or withheld, is not without complication. 

The law generally does not favor the jury's consideration of possible profits in setting values. 122 Two principles of law usually exclude prospective profits,-first the rule of avoidable consequences and second the rule against admitting of testimony based on guesswork and surmise. It is well to consider both.

3. Indefiniteness. An optimistic plaintiff who has lost his property through the defendant's wrong is sure that had he possessed the property in time to put through proposed transactions, he would have made a large profit,-how large depends on his optimism rather than on facts within logical sequence. 

Hence the court rules as a matter of law that in certain cases evidence of prospective profits is not admissible because they can not be established with sufficient exactness to warrant their consideration as evidence.¹ 132 rections, then the one guilty of negligence is liable for the resulting injuries, even though a higher degree of medical skill might have minimized the injuries. If the appearance of the patient's body resulting from the defendant's wrong, together with an honest and fair statement of his feelings and sensations, are such as sometimes in common experience might cause an attending physician, selected in the exercise of reasonable prudence in view of the seriousness of the injury, to believe that a certain physical condition existed, and to give treatment in accordance with that belief, then the defendant will be responsible, even though subsequent developments may demonstrate that the supposed physical condition in fact did not exist, and would not have been supposed to exist by a physician more skillful, experienced or highly trained, and even though the injury may be aggravated by the treatment in fact given. The causal connection is not broken under these circumstances, though one or even two surgical operations may have been performed. This is substance of Hunt v. Boston Terminal Co., 212 Mass. 99.

Further cases to same effect concerning physicians, see Garrahan v. N. Y.,

771 4. Uncontemplated. In actions of tort based solely on negligence in determining the defendant's liability to the plaintiff, the question whether the injury to the plaintiff was reasonably foreseen or foreseeable is important. If it was probable according to common experience 188 that the injury would follow from the defendant's wrong, the result is not too remote to constitute liability in damages; and in testing the defendant's liability one material question is whether the injury could have been contemplated reasonably.184 If some injury to the plaintiff was reasonably foreseeable it is immaterial that the exact damage done was not contemplated.185 When a duty owed the plaintiff by the defendant has been established, damages for its violation seem to include compensation for injuries which were not in the contemplation of the defendant at the time of the injury, if they were the natural proximate result. The defendant's "actual contemplation" of the damage is not important.186 In contracts 'contemplation" is of more importance. If a plaintiff in making a contract will receive special damage such as a direct loss of profits from its breach by the defendant, before the contract is made he should call to the defendant's attention the damages which will result in case of breach. If he fails to do so and the defendant is ignorant of the special circumstances, the loss of profits though a direct result and though ascertainable with mathematical certainty, is not "within the contemplation of the 

Damages, though difficult to estimate, still must be ascertained. Chamberlain

5. When admissible-a. Generally. Though the cases have not so stated, questions which involve profits are really questions of value. The question to be decided is what is the value of the chattel or contract in regard to which the defendant's wrong has arisen. That value may be affected by the profit which could be earned if the chattel or contract were available in the condition in which the defendant's duty required it to be.189 To determine this value profits may be considered in the following cases. b. Injury to an established business. Boston Elevated, 221 Mass. 116, reviewed as follows: The principles upon which damages for personal injury caused by tort are to be assessed are settled. In general the plaintiff is entitled to such sum of money as will compensate him for the loss actually sustained by the injury to his person. It is personal and not property damage which may be recovered. As bearing upon the question of compensation, disability and impaired capacity are to be considered. 

If one received wages or a salary, the amount lost in this regard from the enforced inability to work is a proper element to be considered in assessing damages, but it is not strictly recoverable as wages or salary. The loss of time and the diminution of earning power in the past and in the future are to be considered in estimating the damages. Sibley v. Nason, 196 Mass. 125, 131. Profits hoped to be derived in the future from a business are too remote and uncertain to be regarded as an element in estimating damages. Ballou v. 

Farnum, 11 Allen 73, 76. That is not a personal injury, but a property damage. Decrease in income is an element to be weighed, when it arises from inability to exercise personal effort or especial efficiency directly producing the income; but not when it is interwoven with profits derived from a business in which capital is employed and to the success of which the service, skill and zeal of others contribute. Personal earnings may be considered, but the more or less uncertain profits from a business venture arising from an investment and from ability in employing and managing labor cannot be taken into account. 

Where the element of personal expertness is the essential and dominant factor and the capital invested is insignif-

142 The rule of Hadley v. Baxendale, 9 Ex. 341 is accepted and approved in 

Massachusetts. Mather V. American 

Express, 138 Mass. 55. The rule of that case may be summarized thus:- "Where two parties have made a contract which one of them has broken, the damages which the other party ought to receive in respect of such breach of contract should be such as may fairly and reasonably be considered either arising naturally, i. e. according to the usual course of things from such breach of contract itself or such as may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of

The usual profits which the plaintiff, as a dealer would have made directly from the performance of the broken contract and as a part of it, if the defendant had performed, are an element of damage on the defendant's breach. They arise from the both parties at the time they made the contract as the probable result of the breach of it. Now, if the special circumstances under which the contract was actually made were communicated by the plaintiff to the defendant, and thus known to both parties, the damage resulting from the breach of such a contract which they would reasonably contemplate would be the amount of injury which would ordinarily follow from a breach of contract under these special circumstances SO known and communicated." Hadley v. Baxendale, 9 Ex. 341.

Massachusetts cases hold that loss of prospective profits may be allowed as an element of damages in an action for breach of contract where it appears (1) that the loss was a natural, primary, and a probable consequence of the breach, and (2) that the profits arising from the performance of the contract or the loss likely to result from its non-performance were within the contemplation of the parties, and (3) that the profits are not so uncertain or contingent as to be incapable of reasonable proof. Gagnon v. Sperry, Hutchinson & Co., 206 Mass. 547.

IV. Value in issues other than damages-A. Generally. The proof of value usually is necessary only on issue of damages. Yet the admissibility of evidence of value is frequently considered when the value is offered to corroborate a claim of a party 166 to aid in the interpretation of a contract,167 to identify subject matter, 168 or in other issues.169 Some of these are now considered. 

B. Evidence of expenditures to corroborate party's claim. 

In the ordinary case a person's expenditure of large funds for the purpose of preparation to perform, or of performance of, a contract is not admissible to corroborate his claim that he was party to such contract or that the true construction of the contract was as he secretly interpreted it.170 The case is close to the principles which lead to contrary results set forth in the following paragraphs.

C. To impeach adversary's claim. Doubtless if an alleged claim is so inconsistent with fair value or reasonable dealing that the value of the subject treated will tend to show the claim unreasonable or absurd, evidence of that value may be admitted.171 

D. To prove contract or terms. There is some authority tending to show that when the "existence or terms of a contract are in issue" value of the subject matter covered by the contract may be admitted to assist in determining the existence or meaning of an agreement.172

F. Uncollectibility as evidence of no value: Injunctions: 

Preference. If the enforcement of a claim is enjoined in equity,17 or if a transfer such as would constitute a preference in bankruptcy turns out valueless,175 these facts may be shown to establish that the matter in suit was valueless. 

G. Value when terms clearly fixed. When by the terms of a contract a price is clearly fixed, apart from questions of identity, the value of the article mentioned, in the absence of fraud,178 is of little importance; a party should not be allowed to bolster up his claim by showing his contract fair by such evidence.177 

H. Price paid for services not indicating negligence. That a person contracted to work for an exceptionally low price, it seems, has not tendency to prove that he did not do his work carefully.17 

I. In criminal cases. Value is frequently important in criminal cases. Larceny may be a felony or misdemeanor dependent on value of the article stolen.179 So, too, to be the subject of larceny, the article stolen must have some value. If a paper stolen involves one's character, this may be considered, apparently, in considering its value.180 

J. Paper profits. In estimating value mere paper profits should not be given consideration as cash.181

I. Generally: Rule. "The business of the court is to try the case, and not the man; and a very bad man may have a very righteous cause." Such is the principle on which rests the general rule that proof of one's bad character is not evidence that one performed a disputed act. This rule is based rather on policy than on generally accepted logic. Out of court men frequently decide the truth or falsity of accusations by considera- 

1 Thompson v. Church, 1 Root 312, 

(decided in 1791.) 

2 Commonwealth v. Webster, 5 Cush. 

295. "The fact that a person's habits or character are such that he would be apt to do an act is not competent evidence that he did the act, Commonwealth v. Rivet, 205 Mass. 464 at 466, 

(Citing Commonwealth v. Worcester, 3 

Pick. 462. Ellis v. Short, 21 Pick. 142.

Tenney v. Tuttle, 1 Allen 185. Heland v. Lowell, 3 Allen 407. McCarthy v..

Commonwealth v. Rivet above.) 784

8 tion of the character of the accused. Should courts permit this method of deciding cases the trial would wander from the true issue; and losing sight of the main controversy, we should get lost in the past of the parties and the witnesses. The rule applies not only to evidence of the character of parties to a suit. but also to evidence of the character of a third person when it is offered to prove performance of an act by that third person. 

Hence comes the general rule that "Doing an act cannot be proved in either case by evidence that from the habits of the person in question he would be apt to do it."" 

Several subjects in evidence frequently referred to, and sometimes confused, namely character, reputation, habit and custom, should be distinguished. A man's character is what he is; his reputation what he is said to be; his habits, what he customarily does; and his customs, those habitual institutions so connected with his duties that the two form a complete general system. 

Of these four the latter two are considered elsewhere." Here we treat only character and reputation. In all it is well to remember the general rule again stated in another form. "For the purpose of proving that one has or has not done a particular act, it is not competent to show that he has or has not been in the habit of doing other similar acts.'' This principle as applicable to character and reputation is now considered. 

II. Character to prove performance of acts. In criminal cases one's character cannot be proved to establish that he is the sort of person who would perform, and therefore who did perform, a certain act. B. In criminal cases. In criminal cases the Commonwealth cannot present evidence to show a defendant of such bad character that he is probably guilty.18 The defendant however may present relevant evidence of his good character to show that he is innocent of the crime charged.19 This principle was not established without dissenting opinions.20 At first it was stated that such evidence was to be considered only when the defendant's guilt or innocence was doubtful,21 but this theory later was such promise or statement shall be admissible," the evidence offered was admissible, the court did not find necessary to consider. The evidence should be confined to reputation among the defendant's neighbors and members of the community.2 29 IV. Character to show probable cause, knowledge, state of mind, malice, self defense. Though juries may not consider a person's bad character in reaching its conclusion of his guilt, yet a man who is making up his mind whether he shall institute proceedings to bring another whom he suspects of crime into the law's custody, must consider what he knows of the character of the suspected criminal, or suffer the consequences if he is later sued for malicious prosecution.80 Such evidence of a plaintiff's good character in actions for malicious prosecution is admissible only when the reputation is known to the defendant. 

The reason is that, although commonly in civil cases evidence of reputation is not competent as bearing upon liability for a particular act, yet in an action for malicious prosecution the burden of proving want of probable cause lies on the plaintiff, and "the same facts which would raise a strong suspicion in the mind of a cautious and reasonable man, against a person of notoriously bad character for honesty and integrity, would make a slighter impression if they tended to throw a charge of guilt upon a man

VII. Character in impeaching a witness. "A witness may be cross examined, in the discretion of the judge, to test not only his accuracy and credibility, but also to shake his credit by injuring his character and for these purposes his way of life, his associations, his habits, his prejudices, his physical defects and infirmities, his mental idiosyncrasies, if they affect his capacity, his means of knowledge, powers of discernment, memory and description may be relevant.''49 A wise discretion should limit this form of inquiry that injustice may not result from prejudice.50 The cross examiner and adversary should remain within his rights and not attempt to create unfair inferences,51 to introduce evidence in inadmissible form,52 or to suggest, without money. In direct examination the defendant's counsel was allowed under the plaintiff's exception to ask the defendant how much of a family he had, and he testified that he had a wife and five children. The presiding judge told the jury that this evidence as to the families of the plaintiff and the defendant was admissible in order to enable the jury to get in a general way "what sort of a man is on the witness stand," that it was competent for that purpose and that purpose only. He told them in terms that "Luiz in this case doesn't get any more or any less compensation because he has a wife and children in Portugal." His right to damages is not affected by that feature of the case, and that "Favley's responsibility, if he is responsible in your judgment, is in no way affected, one cent either way, by the fact that he has a family of children." As matter of practice it is usual to allow parties to ask such question. As matter of law it is within the discretion of the judge to allow such testimony. Luiz v. Falvey, 228 Mass. 253. See and compare, Commonwealth v. Gleason, Jan. 9, 1928, 262 Mass. 185; 159 N. E. 518.

C. Defamation. In libel the defendant may be permitted to show in mitigation of damages that the plaintiff's general reputation was bad, and that his character was bad in the particular in which it was assailed; 81 but he cannot show a mere rumor of bad character pertaining to a single transaction of the plaintiff.82 Rumor that the plaintiff committed a crime charged against him by the libel, or even general reputation to that effect, may not be shown.83 Particular instances of misconduct by the plaintiff usually are excluded.84 The defendant is not permitted to show his own character bad,85 or the bad character, moral or intellectual, of those to whom the libel was issued.86 

The plaintiff may repel the inferences of the defendant's slanderous words by proving his own good character.87 Rumor of the plaintiff's guilt does not justify the defendant's accusation; 88 but that the plaintiff's general reputation was bad before the libel is admissible, even though it be in another place and ten years before.90 The pleading need not set forth that the defendant intends to put in issue the plaintiff's character.91 89 D. XVIII. Objectionable evidence not objected to, p. 889. 

I. Generally. There are some matters which cannot be observed directly by the senses. In proving these the courts are compelled to resort to a kind of evidence different from that admitted in most matters.¹ A man's intention, knowledge, or motive cannot be observed. It is known to the man himself only, yet the mental state frequently displays itself in outward signs. Certain desires of the normal mind produce certain results and these results may be observed. Indirectly then the existence of these desires may be proved. The same general principle applies to physical condition. If one is in severe physical pain, such pain probably will cause expressions of the face, or exclamations, or some other outward sign of inward sensation. A third person observing such may testify to his observation and the jury may draw conclusions. The general rule, however, is that narrations out of court of past sensations or past conditions of the body made to a layman cannot be introduced in evidence.5 

1 It has been said "The existence of many bodily sensations and ailments which go to make up the symptoms of disease or injury can be known only to the person who experiences them. It is the statement and description of these which enter into and form part of the facts on which the opinion of an expert as to the conditions of health or disease is founded. As they can be proved only by declarations of the party whose bodily condition is the subject of inquiry, such declarations must be admitted or the proof of them would fail altogether." Barber v. Merriam, 11 Allen 322. 

2 See charge of Judge Thayer, Commonwealth v. Sacco, 255 Mass. 369 at 394. "In Bacon v. Charlton, 7 Cush. 581, 586, it was held that a party to an action might give in evidence his own complaints, exclamations and expressions such as usually and naturally accompany and indicate bodily pain or injury,'' but all statements of facts and narrations of prior occurrences though connected with the occurrence are excluded unless made to a physician who testified as an expert. Barber v. Merriam, 11 Allen 322. 

4 Statement by plaintiff that his back was broken and he would die admitted to show his mental suffering. ""There was no error in the admission of the testimony to the effect that the plaintiff's intestate said, before the bringing of the present action that his back was broken and he knew that he was not going to get better. As appears from the tenor of the question it was offered not for the purpose of proving the physical condition of the intestate but his state of mind, and by inference his mental suffering. This was admissible under Revised Laws, Chapter 175, section 66, which has been liberally construed." Buckley Adm. V. Boston

A person may testify as to his present or past pain, sensations or condition.14 He cannot, however, draw medical conclusions not within his personal knowledge.15 In attending a patient to ascertain his ailment, a physician properly procures the history of the case and the medical history of the patient.16 

These histories are considered by him in his diagnosis. It would be unreasonable to permit a doctor to state the result of his examination and not to permit him to give his reasons for his opinion. The patient when consulting the physician has every railroad train running at great speed. 18 See Chapter 8 on "Opinions and

The defendant contended that the Conclusions."' plaintiff's testatrix never became entitled to the legacies because she did not survive her husband. It appeared that the husband was eighty and the wife seventy-three years of age and that at the time of the accident the general condition of health of the wife was much better than that of her husband; that they were sitting at some distance apart on the rear seat, each in the respective corner, the husband at the extreme right and the wife at the extreme left hand side of the motor car; that the motor car first was struck by the engine of the train on its rear right hand wheel; that the right hand side of the car was crushed; that the left hand side was comparatively uninjured and that the chauffeur who was driving on the left hand side was injured only slightly by being thrown out; and there was evidence on which it could have been found that while the husband was killed instantly by the engine, the death of the wife was not caused by contact with the engine but was caused after the collision by having the top of her skull cut off by some part of the motor car when she was thrown to the ground. 17 The opinion of a surgeon or physi cian is necessarily founded in part on the statements of his patient, describing his condition and symptoms and the causes which have led to the injury or disease under which he appears to be suffering. This opinion is clearly competent as coming from an expert.

But it is obvious that it would be unreasonable if not absurd to receive the opinion in evidence and at the same time to shut out the reasons and grounds on which it was founded. Such a course of practice would take from the consideration of a court and jury the means of determining whether the judgment of the expert was sound and his opinions well founded and satisfactory. Certainly it ought not to be left to the option of the adverse party to determine whether the elements on which the conclusions of a medical witness are based should be drawn out on cross examination. The party producing the witness and who relies on his

reason to tell the truth.18 Hence his statement, though not supported by oath, differs from the ordinary hearsay. It is made, it is said, to a man of skill who may detect an untruth, with the hope that the facts disclosed will lead to the patient's relief or to improvement of physical condition.19 At any rate, whatever the cause, it is well established that statements to a qualified physician who is making an examination with the hope of curing or relieving a patient may be repeated by him on the witness stand, as explaining his diagnosis of the case, his prognosis and his opinion.20 This much was established by early cases, and the courts based the decisions on the fact that the patient consulted the physician in good faith, attempting to procure a cure. 

Later cases have established that such examination need not be solely for the purpose of cure, and that it may be made after suit is started, even though the physician intends to testify at the trial.21 Such statements are admissible for the purpose set out above though they are self serving and relate to past events and not to mere present sensations.22 If such statement of physical or mental condition is made as a narration of past sensation to one not a physician it cannot be admitted.23 This applies to opinion should be allowed the privilege of showing that his opinion as an expert is the result of due inquiry and investigation into the condition and symptoms of the patient both past and present. "The state of a man's mind is as much a fact as the state of his digestion, ,, 34 and a "man's intention is a matter of fact, and may be proved as such." 85 Hence a man may testify as to his knowledge, reason,37 intent,38 fear,39 or other mental attitude.40 He may present living for the term of seven years, the presumption of life then ceases and that of death arises. B. Direct evidence: Writings an exception. Usually when state of mind is a material fact the person whose state of mind is in question may testify to the fact even though such testimony is self serving. An exception to this rule covers writings. The intent of a writing, if it is not ambiguous, must be drawn from its contents. If it is ambiguous the intent is to be drawn from all the attendant circumstances.50 Apart from writings the material intent, motive, cause of action, or other state of mind may be testified to directly.51

C. Indirect evidence-1. Statements of person whose mental state is in issue. A person's intent may be learned from his statements out of court. Words or writings of a person spoken or written out of court though self serving, if made in good faith and as part of business or of other important transactions, have been admitted as evidence of his state of mind at the time of the statement when that is material.52 Thus instructions to a person's lawyer have been admitted on an issue of mistake and waiver.53 A letter from a husband, who lives apart from his wife, wherein he urges her to return to him, though self serving, is admissible in his behalf to show that he desires her to live with him,54 and a notice of injury required to be given by statute may be so obviously honest, that though inaccurate it of itself shows no intent to mislead.55 Hence it may be found sufficient within the wording of the statute which requires that if it be inexact, the person giving notice must show it given in good faith and without intent to mislead.56 So when the issue is good faith, one may show that one's acts were performed on the advice of experts,57 or in certain cases, of attorneys.58 Reasons

Hence in assault, on an issue of who was the aggressor, a conductor's statement that he was going to assault some one, if not a part of the res gestae, or made when the plaintiff was on the car,66 is not admissible against his employer, a street railway company.67 If the passenger had been on the car at the time of the remark and the remark had just preceded the assault the case would lie between two principles,-the one which admits a declaration which tends to show a present material intent coupled with a later condition,68 and the other which excludes statements of an agent not within his scope.69 The case however is to be read in the light of the fact that the plaintiff was not on the car at the time of the remark and that the statement related to an intent to assault another.70 Hence on the facts the transaction is res inter alios. Other cases which hold that evidence of an agent's running away after an accident, is not admissible against his employer," support this decision. The agent's state of mind is no more material than the state of mind of a by-stander who expresses fear of an impending collision. Such evidence is inadmissible.72

E. Inattention as affecting witness's ability to testify, It is well here to point out that mere negative evidence is not admissible to prove that an act did not happen, unless the witness who testifies is shown to have been attentive to the circumstances, or at a place, and in a state of mind, where he would have known of the happening of the event, the occurrence of which is in dispute.81 As an example, one busily engaged in work at a distance from a railroad track with no reason to listen for the ringing of an engine's bell has not been permitted to testify that no bell was rung. 

82 On the other hand one passing on a railroad crossing using care to protect oneself may testify that he heard no bell and this may lead to an inference that no bell was rung. 

Numerous cases exemplify the rule.84 One particularly is

Administratrix against a street railway company for death.-The intestate alighted from a street car, passed to its rear and was crossing double tracks when he was struck and killed by a car coming from the direction toward which the car from which he had alighted was going. The plaintiff contended that the ordinary headlights, as distinguished from the searchlight, and a lantern were not lighted. The defendant asked for, and the judge refused to give a ruling, that there was no evidence to that effect. Three men, who had alighted with the intestate and had preceded him across the tracks and were in a position on the tracks to discern easily what lights were on the approaching car, all realized the peril ous position of the intestate and two of them tried to warn him. They testified that they did not see the lights upon the car although two of them testified that they had seen its searchlight before it was turned off. Held, that it was proper to refuse to give the ruling asked for by the defendant.

Now that the defendant himself is admitted as a witness it must be competent for him to testify directly to that which is a subject of proof or disproof in indirect evidence.8 .87 Though motive of a defendant may not be a part of the crime of which he is charged, or necessary of proof for conviction, yet its admission in the trial of indictments against an accused is usually unquestionable.88 The court, however, may in his discretion limit such evidence.89 When the accused seeks to prove his lack of motive or intent, and for that purpose offers to show his movements and plans at about the time of the offense, he is not permitted thus to confuse the issue. Hence, his planning and preparations to be at another place on the night of the murder of which he is charged, has been excluded.91 Even if on claiming an alibi he has testified that he was not at the place of crime, and now in bolstering this claim by evidence of another, seeks to show whom he met and what was said, the court at least in his discretion, may exclude the testimony as to what was said.92 When a witness has testified directly to a fact from the experience of his own senses, the extent to which he shall be allowed to testify to circumstances, corroborative of the truth of what he thus has sworn must rest in the discretion of the judge who tries the case.99 One cannot fortify one's case

When intent is sought to be proved by indirect evidence, if the person whose intent is to be shown does not know of the facts which are offered to prove the basis of the intent, the jury cannot infer that his intention was as the true facts would indicate; 106 but one's erroneous belief in the truth of facts which do not exist may be the basis for the conclusion that he had a present intent or motive.107 The motive of parties in bringing a present suit usually is not admitted to prove the suit groundbeen found to have been a desire on the part of the defendant to cause a financial gain to his Aunt, Orphia A. 

Marsh, to whom he appeared to be deeply attached. As bearing upon this issue, the Commonwealth offered in evidence through a witness Crane, a deed from the deceased to Orphia A. Marsh of property of considerable value, together with a letter directing the witness Crane to deliver the deed at the death of the deceased, if that event occurred prior to July 20, 1915. Marsh discussed the escrow deed good many times in the presence of the defendant, and that once he spoke of it to the defendant. Manifestly, knowledge of the substance of the two documents introduced in evidence was brought home to the defendant and that being so, they became competent evidence.''

119 Here is a state of matters, a "tangible circumstance" which is to be explained; two sets of facts appear. 

Either if believed would be sufficient to show the cause of death. If coupled with the one there are motive and intent, the motive and intent are material. The following quotation seems worthy of consideration as setting forth a similar condition. "Where an act is equivocal in its nature and may be criminal or honest according to the intent with which it is done, then other acts of the defendant and his conduct on other occasions may be shown in order to disclose the mastering purpose of the alleged criminal act. Where the intent of one charged with crime is to be proved a greater range of evidence is allowed than in support of other issues.'' Commonwealth v. Dow, 217 Mass. 473.

Later in the text it is attempted to be shown that evidence of statements of present intent is admissible though it is not explanatory of a state of matters or coupled with any transaction. It seems that the true test of admissibility is whether the present intent is material. If it is material and not excluded by some positive rule of law it should be received. The question of materiality is for the trial court. If there is a state of matters which is to be explained, and two sets of facts appear, each of which would be sufficient to permit the jury to find that the state of facts arises from the intentional act of different persons, and evidence of statements of intent of one of these persons made at or before the time of the act is then offered; and if these are not too remote; then as a matter of law the court is obliged to find the statement material. Compare 

Commonwealth v. Caruso, 251 Mass. 362 which applies when all persons concerned are not shown to be connected with the transaction.

In an action for alienation of affections by a wife, against her husband's parents, the plaintiff was allowed to testify that two weeks after she received a letter in which the husband declared his separation, he said to her that the defendants had told him he was not the father of her child. Held, that this was error. Gilmore V. Gilmore (S. 

Dak.), 173 N. W. 865.

The court based its decision on the ground that the statement was not part of the res gestae. But there are two other classifications of declarations ad, mitted in such cases to which the term res gestae is sometimes loosely applied: (1) A direct statement of mental condition per se, an exception to the hearsay rule; (2) A statement proving mental condition by inference, to which Dean 

Wigmore points out, the hearsay rule is not applicable. See 3 Wigmore at 1715. 

See also Eustace Seligman, "An exception to the hearsay rule," 26 Harvard Law Rev. 146, 150. So in this case the alienation of husband's affections and what caused such alienation, are questions of states of mind, and the husband's declarations should have been admitted to prove them. Bailey v. Bailey, 94 Iowa 598; 63 N. W. 341; 

Williams v. Williams, 20 Colo. 51; 37 Pac. 

614. For the purpose of proving the defendant's agency in causing this state of mind the declaration comes within no exception to the hearsay rule and is therefore incompetent. Elmer v. Fessenden, 151 Mass. 359. Of course evidence not admissible for all purposes may yet under proper instructions be admitted for the purpose for which it is competent. See 1 Wigmore 13. This it seems would have been the proper ruling to have been made in the prin cipal case. 33 Harvard Law Review 315.

to procure a miscarriage in consequence of which death occurred, the defendant sought to prove that shortly before the alleged offense, the deceased had said that she was pregnant, that her condition was caused by one other than the defendant, and that if he did not procure a miscarriage she would perform the operation herself with a lead pencil. "It appeared that said declarations neither accompanied nor were explanatory of any act done by her." The court referred to the evidence as "what is recognized as hearsay evidence" and excluded the statement because it did not come within any exception to the hearsay rule, especially pedigree. Such evidence has since been said not to be hearsay.182 The court further says "The fact that the purpose and intentions of the deceased would be, if known, a material aid in coming to a correct conclusion does not permit such purpose and intentions to be found upon incompetent evidence. Indeed the more important the fact to be proved is, the more important it is that it be proved by proper evidence." "It accompanied no act.188 It gave character to no transaction. "It is mere recital." "The only apparent objection to the rejection of the evidence is this: the fact, if true, is an important fact; the deceased knew whether it was true or not; being now dead she cannot speak; in her lifetime she said it was true. The same suggestions may be made in reference to every fact material to any issue afterward tried, known to any person deceased at the time of the trial, and this alone is sufficient to establish the wisdom of the rule." 9.9

The court refuses to confine admissible verbal statements to speech which is wholly involuntary, but brands as admissible certain conscious voluntary declarations stating that although such evidence "has in it some of the elements of hearsay, yet it closely resembles evidence of the natural expression of feeling which has always been regarded in the law, not as hearsay, but as original evidence." 144 The opinion mentions the fact that because the declarant is dead this evidence is the "best" that can be procured.145 The cases up to that time seem to have involved largely statements by deceased persons, 146 but not exclusively so.147 The fact that the statement of the deceased was not made by a party to the case and hence was not an admission was disposed of by the court on the authority of Commonwealth v. 

Abbott, 130 Mass. 472.148 In commenting on that case several matters of importance are pointed out. The court says that the conduct or declarations of a party both before and after a crime if sufficiently near in time, and sufficiently significant of motive or intent, are relevant against him; that the mental and moral condition, intent and disposition of any person whether a party or not, can be ascertained from acts and declarations; that the court has discretion to exclude such evidence if it is too remote, or because a material change of conditions has taken place.149

The court in the Trefethern case does not attempt to lay down a general rule.157 Some passages however indicate the probable developments. "The fundamental proposition is that an intention in the mind of a person can only be shown by some external manifestations which must be some look or appearance of the face or body, or some act or speech; and that proof of either or all of these for the sole purpose of showing state of mind or intention of the person is proof of a fact from which the state of mind or intention may be inferred." 158 "On principle therefore we think it clear that when evidence of the declarations of a person is introduced solely for the purpose of showing what the state of mind or intention of that person was at the time the declarations were made, the declarations are to be regarded as acts from which the state of mind or intention may be inferred in the same manner as from the appearance of the person or his behavior, or his actions generally. 3. Cases enlarging and limiting Commonwealth v. Trefe thern. From the point of view of justice Commonwealth v. 

Trefethern was a necessary decision. It augmented a doctrine of res gestae adopted in this Commonwealth, so narrow that our courts excluded important matters admissible elsewhere. No sooner was the decision rendered than its effect was evident. 

The decision was handed down on October 19th; within a month 

Viles v. Waltham 162 was argued. The rescript filed in the following January tends to explain an anomaly in our doctrine of res gestae, the domicile cases. Statements of persons as to change of domicile even though remote from the acts of moving, always had been admitted as part of the res gestae.163 In Viles v. Waltham the court says, "Declarations of a person accompanying a change of his abiding place have always been competent to explain the change as a part of the res gestae; but declarations in such cases are often admissible on a broader ground than as a part of the act of moving from one place to another. The intention of the person removing is competent to be proved as an independent fact, and anything which tends to show his intention in making the change may be introduced, if it is free from objection in other particulars. The intention may be inferred from acts and conduct, and conduct which tends to

Declarations which indicate the state of mind of the defendant naturally have a legitimate tendency to show intention.'' 164 The court however sets limits to this general doctrine. Self serving 165 statements by parties are excluded, first if they are narrations of past events, for then the speaker's truthfulness can not be relied on; or second, if they are declarations of purpose, intent or feeling made after controversy has arisen, for then they are affected by interest; or third, if they are declarations of intent or state of mind of parties, unless made under circumstances which give them corroboration. In general such corroboration is found in the fact that they accompany and explain acts material to the issue of which they are a part. To the second, says the court, there is an exception for expressions of pain or other indication of one's mental or physical condition that may be treated as symptoms are not excluded.166 The case tends to consolidate this doctrine with the doctrine of res gestae.167 

There is no present tendency to consolidate these two distinct principles, but the clause "accompanying an act" so frequently referred to, has illogically been affixed to the doctrine of Commonwealth v. Trefethern. This clause arose from the attempt to distinguish Commonwealth v. Felch and doubtless was included in the bill of exceptions in that case so that the doctrine of res gestae might not be relied on by the defense. That a declaration of mental state, made when one "completes a transaction," should be distinguished from such declaration made when one fails to complete a transaction, is illogical. Particularly is this so when the transaction is separate and distinct from the intent. If one hears "A," at a place where he cannot be observed, while he performs no special act, say "I am going to drown myself" and later at a time not too remote "A" is found drowned this evidence should be admitted as readily as if the statement had been made by "A" while he was making a purchase or completing any other independent transaction.

What the court doubtless means by the "completing of a transaction" or by an "accompanying act" in Commonwealth v.

Trefethern, and other cases, is that if the statement of intent

"There was testimony that the street railway could be seen from the intestate's house, and that less than a quarter of an hour before the accident the intestate looked out in the way he always did, to see if the electric cars were there and then left in a hurry saying that he was going to take the train as there were no electric cars running.' "If either his intent or his belief that no electric cars were running was material, his statement at a moment when he had no interest to make evidence was admissible to show the state of his mind within the established exception to the rule against hearsay." (Citing Commonwealth v. Trefethern.) "Certainly his belief, especially when shown to have been correct, was material as it would have the taking of the steam cars for its natural consequence and so would show the probable intent with which he got upon them.

His intent so shortly before the act to be interpreted being in accord with what was to be expected from his belief, also was admissible and might have been presumed to continue as indeed it might have been found to exist, without direct evidence." 172

Here it is to be noted that the statement was favorable to the legal representatives of the speaker; that though not directly connected with an immediate separate transaction, it tended to explain the speaker's later position; and that it was of such nature that it evidently was made in good faith.

Alone it does not prove that a person performed an alleged act, 182 4. Present rule arising from doctrine of Commonwealth v. 

Trefethern. The probable rule then seems to be this. Whenever motive or intent is material, oral expressions of present motive or intent are admissible, by whomsoever made to show the speaker's motive or intent provided that they are made in good faith, made before controversy arose and are not too remote in time or circumstance.188 What is remote is a preliminary question to be passed on by the court before the evidence is admitted.184 If a condition of things exists which may have been caused by the act of any of several persons, expressions of present intent, and probably expressions of present motive, to perform the act, uttered by any of the several persons, and made before the act, are admissible, if such intent or motive continued to exist to the time of the act; 185 but mere expressions of intent or motive to do an act are not evidence that the speaker performed the act; 186 they only confirm inferences that might otherwise be drawn. The expressions may be self serving and may be by a third person and against the interest of the defendant even in a criminal case. The statement probably must accompany some act though this condition seems illogical.

A married son lived with his father, who has suffered a shock and whose property was in the charge of a conservator. The son daily and nightly rendered necessary services and incurred expenses including payment for the services of a housekeeper and a nurse. He never spoke to his father nor to any other person about expecting pay until after his father's death and he never kept any book account or memorandum of the payments and services. The son was appointed one of the administrators of his estate and filed a petition asking to be allowed individual payment for his services and expenses. 

The father's only property was the building in which his tenement was and the land on which it stood. The income was not sufficient to pay the interest on the mortgage and for water rates, taxes, repairs and insurance, but the equity of the property was worth at least $3,000. The petitioner testified that he did not render the services as a gratuity to his father. There was evidence of facts and circumstances warranting a finding that the father in his unspoken acceptance of the benefits conferred on him understood that his son expected to be paid for his services and disbursements and that the father received them with that understanding and with an intent that there should be pecuniary recompense. In explaining his intention the son said, "Of course I realized there was an estate there." The state of mind, that is, the purpose and intent of the petitioner at the time when the services were rendered in behalf of the father was material upon the issue whether such services and expenditures were made and received as a gift to the father or whether both parties at the time the services were performed and the moneys were paid contemplated or intended pecuniary recompense. VI. Consciousness. That a person spoke at a certain time may be shown to indicate that he was then conscious.218 In cases involving conscious suffering, groans, remarks, exclamations and like sounds may be admitted for the same purpose.214 The for what purpose this testimony was admitted. XI. Malice. In showing malice, acts and statements of him who is accused of malice, which tend to show his malicious state of mind, are admissible against him.227 Statements by a defendant to the effect that he would get even with a certain party who failed to honor his note, to show the material malice of the speaker, have been admitted, even though the count under which this evidence was admissible was later withdrawn.228 

XII. Mental distress. When mental anguish is material a plaintiff may be permitted to testify that his feelings were hurt,229 and in certain cases what people said to him, if this tends to affect his mental state.230 A doctor has been permitted to state that his patient's good spirits were affected by a dog bite.231 

XIII. Self defense. A defendant who seeks to justify his blow as one struck in self defense, may testify that he intended to strike only such specific blow as would beat off his assailant.232

XV. Insanity: Mental weakness: Undue influence. There is a prima facie presumption of sanity 244 which like any other presumption may be met and rebutted.245 When sanity is in issue the burden of proving sanity rests on him who alleges it.846 In the proof of wills the burden of proving testamentary capacity 47 is on the executor.248 Although the executor has the burden of proof upon him, to satisfy the jury that the testatrix was of sound and disposing mind and memory at the time of the execution of the will, there is a presumption of sanity and that presumption stands until it is met by evidence to the contrary.249 In proving insanity statements by the alleged lunatic are admissible when not too remote if they tend to show his sanity or insanity. These are not admitted as evidence of the truth of the facts stated, but as evidence which indirectly or circumstantially shows his mental condition.250 The general doctrine is "that the appearance, acts, conduct and declarations of one whose mental condition is in issue may be put in evidence if they are of such character as to throw light upon that question, and if they are not too remote in time; and whether they are too remote in time is a question which must be determined who participates in fraud, of intent to draw instrument and date it back, Tremont Trust Co. v. Tucker, 237 Mass.

Stuart, 201 Mass. 288.

XVII. Common illustrations of principles-A. Introductory. 

The principles above set out have been applied frequently in important criminal and civil matters. A few of the more important decisions are reviewed. 

B. Mental state and condition in criminal law-1. Generally.

In criminal matters when intent, motive, and like matters are involved a greater range of inquiry is allowed in admitting indirect evidence thereof, than in ordinary matters.318 A criminal attempts to conceal his crime, and were it not for the principle which allows the presentation of such evidence many crimes would go unpunished. The defendant is likewise given considerable leeway in proving the intent and purpose of others who are shown sufficiently connected with the commission of the crime to have been its perpetrator.319 If others had opportunity

To commit a crime a person must be mentally capable of having the mental intent which constitutes part of that crime. Persons over fourteen years of age are prima facie assumed sane and criminally responsible. The law conclusively presumes children to the age of seven mentally incapable of committing such offense. From the age of seven to fourteen apparently there is a prima facie presumption that a child is incapable of forming a criminal intent. The presumption does not apply after a child is beyond the age of fourteen. This responsibility does not depend upon "the mental age of the defendant nor upon the question whether the mind of the prisoner is above or below that of the ideal or of the average or of the normal man, but upon the question whether the defendant knows the difference between right and wrong, can understand the relation which he bears to others and which others bear to him, and has knowl- edge of the nature of his act so as to be able to perceive its true character and consequences to himself and others". "Constitutional or other inferiority is not the test of criminal responsibility. 1821

b. Evidence showing mental incapacity: Insanity: Drunk enness. Any evidence which tends to show a defendant insane is admissible in a defense in a charge for murder.336 It is important to contrast the effect of drunkenness of a defendant in murder with its effect in larceny. In murder, even if committed in an attempt to rob, if there is malice afórethought, drunkenness is no defense.337 In Commonwealth v. Taylor 338 the defendant was charged with murder, and the Commonwealth to show the required mental guilt relied on the attempt to commit robbery and rape on the victim at the time of the offense. The defendant relied on his drunkenness to establish that he had not sufficient mental capacity at the moment to have any intent to commit robbery or rape. The trial court charged as follows: "Intoxication has been frequently referred to in this case. Every man is presumed to be sane. There is no contention in this case that the defendant is insane, that he had any mental disease. And also every one is presumed to intend the natural consequences of his act. The mere fact that one who killed another was intoxicated does not necessarily indicate that the killing was not done in a deliberately premeditated manner. Drunkenness cannot be converted into a shield to protect from punishment a serious crime. Many crimes are committed under the stimulus of liquor. 

And the effects of liquor upon the mind and actions of men are well known to everybody. Voluntary intoxication is never an excuse or a palliation for crime. It would be subversive of all law and morality if the commission of one vice like drunkenness, or crime as it is under our statute here, should be allowed to excuse another crime. One may be perfectly unconscious of what he is doing and yet be responsible for his conduct during drunkenness. You will consider what evidence there is in this case as to how drunk the defendant was that night. It is urged upon you by the Commonwealth that the contention of the

Motive based on erroneous assumption of facts. On the issue of motive, the defendant's belief that certain facts exist which do not exist, will not lessen the admissibility of such evidence to show the motive. Hence, his belief, even if erroneous, that he or another friendly with him, would gain pecuniary advantage from the murder, is admissible. 6. Obtaining under false pretenses. In trials for obtaining money or property under false pretenses two principles should be noted, the required element of the defendant's knowledge of the falsity may be inferred from statements which are inherently false,368 and the defrauded person may testify that he relied on the false statements in parting with the property, that these were the sole inducement which led him to part with that property, and that he would not have parted with the property had he known of the falsity.369 

7. Extortion. In extortion the defendant's mental attitude may be inferred without direct evidence. His wrongful presence at a place where the crime is alleged to have been committed has bearing on his intent.370

A defendant tried on charges of making a certain specific sale of liquor cannot be convicted on evidence that he at other times made another sale.391 Yet when the intent with which liquor is delivered is involved evidence of other sales is not always excluded.392 If the question is whether there was an intent to make a sale evidence of other sales at the time of the delivery of the liquor in question has been admitted to prove an intent to sell.393 

The principle which excludes similar crimes to prove a present crime,394 has an important bearing on the general admissibility of this evidence and hence even on the issue of intent another sale unless approximate to the offense should be excluded. The court should exercise its discretion as to remoteness, favorably to the defendant.

When the charge is maintaining a liquor nuisance 395 evidence of acts which tends to show the business done and to establish the nuisance is admissible.396 This tends to prove intent as well as the other elements of the offense. It should be noted that evidence of one sale will not establish this offense,897 and that evidence of sales outside the period alleged for the continuing offense, will be admitted only for limited purposes.998 On this issue intent also may be inferred from the condition of the premises.399

In all liquor cases certain presumptions as to intent arise from certain signs and from delivery under certain circumstances.406 

An illustration of the principle 407 which permits the proof of present acts and words to show physical condition arises in liquor cases when the issue is whether the liquor is a "beverage." Evidence that persons who drank the substance were made sick has been excluded in the trial court, but the supreme court not passing directly on the question has held the exclusion harmless because other evidence of such nauseation was admitted without objection.408

That a flavoring extract which constituted a beverage that violated the liquor laws was manufactured under federal permit is not admissible to show a defendant's good faith.409 

The intent of the person who manufactured a liquor to mix in it a substance that would make it usable as a beverage is not material.410

One case bearing on intent in a liquor prosecution is worthy of note. The principle on which it rests lies between "res gestae" 411 and "actions near scene before and after crime." 412 A defendant's premises were about to be searched by the police for liquor. C. Mental state and condition in civil and equitable matters. 

The same general rules apply in civil matters. Where mental state is material any fact or set of facts which does not violate the above principles may be considered. Instances in some of the more common cases follow. 

1. Malicious prosecution. In malicious prosecution, the defendant's malice is material. Hence any fact which tends to show malice or lack of malice is admissible. Advice of counsel is material and may be proved to show that the defendant acted in good faith.480 So the defendant's animosity may be shown to establish malice, and to show this, his conduct in matters which tended to injure the plaintiff, if not too remote, may be admitted.481 On the matter of damages mental anguish and feeling of humiliation may be proved.482 

2. Deceit and fraudulent representations. In fraud and deceit, in the absence of a fiduciary relationship,188 a representation as to opinion is not such fact as will sustain the action.484 

In determining whether a statement is one of opinion or of present fact the speaker's state of mind as well as his words may be material. If a person lies about his present intention, this is a statement of fact and not of opinion.485 Hence when a defendant falsely represents that he intends to publish a manuscript which he purchases, this is a statement of fact and may be the basis of an action for deceit.486 One's intended fraud may be inferred from one's acts.487 So hurrying an adversary's signature, with other facts, has tended to establish fraud.438 Expressions of determination to validate a title by drawing a document alleged to be fraudulent and by dating back, is admissible as an

5. Matters involving husband and wife. When in cases arising from nonsupport, alienation of affections, or other like matters, the mental attitude of one spouse toward the other is in issue, acts and statements to show animosity are frequently admitted. The time of such acts or statements is material. "In actions for depriving of consortium, a letter written by the husband to his wife after difficulties arose, and statements by the wife in the husband's absence which tend to show their affection or animosity have been admitted. ''468 When, however, the date of the wife's decision to leave her husband precedes the date of the act offered in evidence and she then files suit for divorce, evidence of subsequent events to show the state of her affection toward him at that subsequent time, is to be excluded.464 Her state of mind apparently up to the date of the suit was material, and could be shown by her statements, written or oral, even though made in his absence.465 These statements properly are not evidence of the truth of facts stated therein, but only of the speaker's state of mind.466 That she had no affection for her husband after that date is immaterial. Had the question been the damage to the husband who had been deprived of the association of his wife by alienation of her affections, his mental attitude, even after suit against the person who alienated her affections, would be material and an attending physician might testify to his mental state.467 When the issue is whether the husband was willing to support his wife his statements and letters wherein he offers such support if she will return to him, though self serving, are admissible to show his state of mind and willingness to support.468

9. Minor with dangerous weapon: Animals. In an action of tort against the parents of a minor who has done damage with an air rifle, the issues in regard to knowledge are whether the defendants knew or ought to have known that the minor had such gun and whether they knew or ought to have known that it was unsafe and dangerous to permit the minor to have such gun. 

To prove this knowledge evidence of the boy's acts with the gun near the place of business of the father and in the presence of the mother is admissible.494 The minor's escapades with the gun which tend to show its wrongful and dangerous use, his age and conduct seem admissible to prove his unfitness, and in certain instances to show knowledge of his parents as to such unfitness.495 

Where the vicious acts of a domestice animal are in question, to show knowledge of viciousness, prior acts of the animal known to the keeper are admissible.496 In some instances knowledge of the owner or keeper is not a necessary element for recovery.497

1 10. Intent not to mislead in notices of injury. Several statutes require notice of the time, place, and cause of injury, as a condition precedent to suit.199 Such statutes usually contain clauses to the effect that no inaccuracy in stating the time, place and cause shall render the notice invalid or insufficient "if it is shown that there was no intention to mislead and that the party entitled to notice was not in fact misled thereby." When such notice is defective the burden is on the plaintiff to show that there was no intent to mislead and that the defendant was not misled. Intent not to mislead in some instances may be inferred from the notice itself;500 and evidence that the actual place of the accident was pointed out or orally described by the plaintiff to the defendant, when inaccuracy in stating the place occurs, is admissible likewise, apparently, to show good faith.501 Such evidence is clearly admissible to show that the defendant was not misled.502 If the defendant actually knew of the place of the injury, he is not misled by inaccuracies as to place.503

12. Injury to property: Trespass to machinery: Fires. When an issue is the wilfulness of injury to property as contrasted with accident, the mental attitude of the perpetrator of the injury is material. If he has animosity against the owner, this may be shown. His calling names to the owner in past years, his remonstrance with the owner in criticism in his legal acts even though somewhat remote, may prove the trespass wilful and not accidental.506 So when the issue is whether property damages by fire was damaged wilfully or accidentally, evidence of other fires under like circumstances at the same place if not 

506 Price v. Goldberg, 241 Mass. 465.

too remote may be shown to prove that the later fire was wilful and not accidental,507 13. Conversion. In conversion facts may be such that a material issue is whether a holder of property at a particular time used it with an intention to convert it to his own use. In such case this intent may be proved by any evidence in accordance with the rules above. His failure seasonably to return the property or unreasonably to do with it as instructed by the owner, or wrongfully to retain it on demand, is evidence of his intent to convert.508 510 

14. Due care in tort cases. In actions of tort for personal injury based on negligence, a plaintiff apart from statute is obliged to show his due care. This care requires reasonable mental alertness as well as reasonable physical alertness. Hence the state of the plaintiff's mind at the time of the accident in so far as it tends to show his due care or lack of it is admissible. 

So if the belief is reasonable, a plaintiff injured by collision in crossing a street, usually may testify that he believed that he could cross safely;509 and a plaintiff injured may testify that he did not anticipate that the defendant's automobile would come at a place in the street where it was not permitted to come." 

A warning of danger given a plaintiff is also material on his mental state of knowledge and caution.511 Though facts may be such that they may show that the plaintiff from them had warning of the danger, yet if the facts are such that a person reasonably would not suspect a danger, they do not constitute a warning. 512 

If a warning has been given a plaintiff and he has replied "I am not afraid", and has then performed the act against which he has been warned which has led to his injury, this evidence is admissible on the issue of his due care.518 What others did at the time and place of the injury is frequently material in showing the reasonableness of the plaintiff's act.514 That the plaintiff forgot that a dangerous condition of a highway existed, is admissible on the issue of his due care.515

15. Death cases and suits against persons who owe a high degree of care. In actions for causing death damages usually are based on the degree of culpability of the person at fault. 

Hence the degree of negligence of such person is a material issue. 

On his degree of culpability his knowledge of the dangers which resulted in the accident that caused the death, is material. To show this knowledge and the degree of his negligence, statements made by him, material on these issues, are receivable. These are admitted in a suit against an employer of the agent who caused the death, even though they are not within the scope of his employment.516 In actions of tort against a person who owes a plaintiff a high degree of care, a similar rule applies.517 

16. Cases involving gifts. When the issue is whether the title to property is in the possessor by virtue of a gift, the person alleged to have made the gift may testify directly as to the circumstances under which the property came into the hands of the possessor,518 and as to his intent to make or not to make a gift.519 "A witness may testify to his own intention when that intention is a material fact to be proved. 

Intent to make a gift is essential to its validity." 520 Cases which reach a different result rest on principles not here material.521 A donor's enfeeblement by age is material on the issue of validity of a gift of a large part of his estate, even though he is not of unsound mind and even though there is no fraud, misrepresentation, or solicitation by the donee. 522 Intent to make a gift without deliv-. ery or its equivalent will not complete the gift and pass the title. 523

25. Will cases: Sanity: Undue influence. Questions which frequently arise in "will cases" have been considered above.540 

Several additional important facts should be noted. The intent of the testator where a will admits of different constructions is to be learned from the whole instrument. This rule is stated as follows: "The will admits of different constructions. The court will 'ascertain the intent of the testator from the whole instrument, attributing due weight to all its language, and then give effect to that intent unless prevented by some positive rule of law.' It will not create an intent where none appears, nor permit some of the words of the will to defeat an intent fairly to be deduced from study of the will as a whole and of the circumstances in the light of which it was executed."547 It is the reading of the whole will and not of an isolated part that is to determine the testator's meaning,548 and the natural meaning of the words used construed in the light of circumstances known to the testator is to govern in disclosing his intent.549 When the intent is thus ascertained the will is given force unless some positive rule of law prevents.550 Statements of the testator to show directly his intent are not admissible unless the terms of the will come within the rule of "idem sonans" or a similar doctrine which is considered elsewhere.551 The burden of establishing by a fair preponderance of the evidence that the testator when he made the will understood the nature of the act and its effect, 544 Attorney General v. XVIII. Objectionable evidence not objected to.
