I. Generally. The admission of public documents, an exception to the rules against the admission of hearsay and in some cases against the admission of matters "res inter alios" and of self serving statements, constituted a principle of evidence long before the rules against hearsay, res inter alios, and self serving statements, and many other rules of evidence were formulated. 

Documents under seal in the earliest days were exhibits which passed to the jury. If the instrument were not under seal the attorney for either party might read it to the jury but such un- 

1 See Thayer's Preliminary Treatise on Evidence, 104-109.

sealed paper did not become an exhibit. A sealed instrument not only could be read to the jury, but becomes an exhibit. The seal supplied all the requirements preliminary to admissibility. 

The seal proved the document, and admitted it in evidence. The present rule which admits strictly governmental papers under the seal of the sovereign, is apparently a survival of the old form of procedure. Usually before a document is admitted in evidence some proof of its genuineness other than that which appears on its face must be presented to the trial court. If the document is a public document or in some cases a quasi public document or record, duly signed and under the seal of the sovereign, the seal and signature are judicially recognized, and the document is thus proved and admitted. In considering public documents it is well to have in mind that several classifications are to be distinguished. These classifications all are referred to at times as "public documents" or "public records," and the words are frequently used interchangeably. This leads to confusion. One should observe the following as separate classes.

Strictly governmental acts of public import embodied in writings; private papers recorded under governmental provisions and made open to the public; reports and documents of individuals recorded by public order; acts of public officers recorded for the public's information; acts of public officers recorded for limited purposes; and lastly acts and records of individuals who serve. the public but are not employees or servants of the government. 

Different reasons apply for the admission or exclusion of evidence in these classes and different results accrue from their admission. Then it is well to distinguish the principle which admits public documents because they are noted judicially, from the principle which admits secondary evidence of a recorded instrument, and some other instruments, without an excuse for failure to produce or to account for the originals.

Public documents of de facto governments.. The state papers of a de facto government have been admitted, particularly when taken under the protection of the established government, and placed in the possession of its officers as public documents.21

County and municipal records, votes, ordinances and by laws: "Practical Working Rule." Votes of County Commis sioners,50 votes of municipal councils, and ordinances of cities,61 and votes and by-laws of towns 58 within their respective jurisdictions are provable by certified copies of the record 5 or by the original record.54 Such documents are not like general statutes noted judicially, but when copies of the votes, ordinances, or by-laws are presented, with the proper seal and the signature of the custodian, they are admissible, if material, without proof of loss of the original.55 This does not mean that every document in the custody of a department and pertaining to its duties is admissible.56 In distinguishing what is and what is not admissible it is well to keep in mind the "practical working rule” referred to in Commonwealth v. Slavski,57 that "a record of a primary fact, made by a public officer in the performance of official duty is or may be made by legislation competent prima facie evidence as to the existence of that fact, but that records of investigations and inquiries conducted, either voluntarily or pursuant to requirements of law, by public officers concerning causes and effects involving the exercise of judgment and discretion, expressions of opinion, and the making of conclusions are not admissible in evidence as public records." 58 The distincowner's duplicate certificate shall be received in evidence in all courts of the Commonwealth and shall be conclusive as to all matters contained therein except as provided in this chapter."

VI. Recorded private documents of title-A. Explanatory. 

The preceding paragraphs apply to documents which are "public" in the sense that they are the acts of those who represent the government and its people. Those documents have a dignity which makes their accuracy and truth sufficiently apparent to admit them. Now we consider documents which record the doings of private citizens. The government and its officers do not create them, but the government, for the purpose of informing the public of the titles and incumbrances of property and of preserving plans, maps, and other documents, has created certain offices to which the public refer in guiding their acts, when such matters are material. To permit the public to guide their business by such records and then to exclude such records when material and shown accurate, would be inconsistent. Hence the general rule, subject to one exception, is that such original records are admissible. The government employs officers to copy and preserve documents of title in registries conducted for that purpose. These officers are disinterested officers of the state, usually sworn faithfully to perform their duties. That they are public officers, that they are sworn to perform their duties, that their attendance is needed at the work of the Commonwealth, and that cross examination would not tend, in the great majority of cases, to affect the admissibility or force of the record, are factors that lead to the principles established by common law or by statute, which admit certified copies of the originals, without calling the clerk who made the

VII. Reports, returns and petitions filed by laymen and corporations-A. General rule. By statute many individuals are required to file reports, and these in many cases are admissible in evidence.105 If they are open to public inspection 106 and required to be filed for the purpose of exposing the facts therein to the public, and not merely for the purpose of assisting some officer or department of the government,107 unless excluded by some other principle of law,108 when material, they, or certified copies of them duly authenticated,109 may be presented in evidence. Many forms of documents are included within this principle.

B. Certificate of condition of corporations: Income tax returns. Statute provides that certified and attested copies of documents filed in the executive or other departments of the Commonwealth shall be competent evidence equally with the "originals" thereof.110 This statute is interpreted to mean not only that the rule pertaining to the best evidence 111 is satisfied by a copy, but likewise that "a new source" of "primary evidence" is created.112 Hence though the document filed be a copy showing a variance. Ames v. Phelps, 18 Pick. 314. 

104 Morton v. Webster, 2 Allen 352.

C. Papers and returns filed with municipalities. The same statute that admits copies of documents filed in the departments of the State, admits copies of documents filed in any department of any city or town.189 These are admissible equally with the originals, but do not exclude the originals.140 The signature of the alleged signer or authority of the person signing to act for the purported signer need not be proved,-the document is assumed prima facie to have been executed by him who purports to execute it; 141 and there is sufficient evidence from the sameness of name to lead to an inference that the person who filed is 

Industries. But there is no provision in the statute giving the right to the public to inspect the reports or providing for their use except as declared in the statute; and the only provision relating to their availability is that referring to the State Board of Labor and Industries. These reports could not be called public records under General Laws, chapter 66, par. 10, requiring the custodian of public records to permit their inspection and to furnish copies thereof on payment of a reasonable fee. In many cases returns made to public boards by individuals are admissible in evidence when not made inadmissible by statute. (Citing, Brackett v. Commonwealth, 223 Mass. 

119; Union Glass Co. v. Somerville, 228 

Mass. 202, 204.) Schedules of an insolvent debtor in an action against him have been held to be admissible. (Citing Simpson v. Carleton, 1 Allen 109; 

Wellington v. Jackson, 121 Mass. 157. 

See Batchelder v. Home National Bank, 218 Mass. 420, 424. See also in this connection Casey v. Boston & Maine 

Ry., 231 Mass. 529; Commonwealth v. 

Slavski, ante.) The report however, was made to the Board by the employer merely to aid it in the administration of its duties; it was not intended that these reports of accidents should be used as evidence in independent proceedings, and the statements contained in them allowed in evidence as admissions against the employer when sued in an action at law. The information must be assumed to be of value and importance to the board. It relates to the time and place of the accident, the insurance carried by the employer and the reservation of common law right 

The wages of the workman if made. of the employee are asked for and the fullest details. It was required from the defendant under a penalty of $50. 

The defendant's report was in the nature of a privileged communication; and although not expressly privileged by the words of the statute, it was not intended that these reports should be availed of in an action at law arising out of the subject matter of the suit. 

Their purpose was fully served when the Industrial Accident Board received all information. It might cause serious embarrassment to the board in obtaining the necessary information, if these reports could be considered as admissions to the employer's prejudice in proceedings at law. VIII. Official documents prepared or filed by officials or limited classes of citizens-A. Generally. As a general rule the "record of a fact made by a public officer, whose duty it is both to perform and to record it is competent evidence of the truth of that fact.” For clearness in establishing the rule the following classifications should be considered.144

2. Reports made evidence in criminal cases: Analysis of liquor and drugs. Though the constitution provides that a criminal defendant shall have the right to meet the witnesses against him, face to face, yet statutes may be passed which enlarge the class of public documents admissible in criminal or civil cases. 

Here we should recall the "working rule" said to be not of universal application, and admittedly subject to some exceptions, to wit, "a record of a primary fact made by a public officer in the performance of official duty is or may be made by legislation prima facie evidence as to the existence of that fact, but that records of investigations and inquiries conducted either voluntarily or pursuant to requirement of law, by public officers concerning causes and effects and involving the exercise of judgment and discretion, expressions of opinion, and the making of conclusions are not admissible in evidence as public records." 180 

By statute 181 the department of public health is required to analyze all liquors sent it by licensing boards, selectmen, public officers and other officers authorized by law to make seizures of liquor, provided that the department is satisfied that the analysis is to be used in connection with the enforcement of the laws of the Commonwealth. Its certificate of analysis of such liquors is prima facie evidence of the composition and quality of the liquors. This statute is constitutional,182 and the principle on which it rests generally has been upheld in other states.188 

179 The character of the public records which at the time of the adoption of the constitution formed an acknowledged exception to the rule of Article 12 that in prosecution for crime "every subject shall have a right to meet the witnesses face to face," did not become rigid for all time for evidential purposes, but the General Court had power, to make, ordain and establish all manner of wholesome and reasonable laws not repugnant to the constitution to add to the varieties of public records admissible as evidence under the principles of law prevailing at the time of the adoption of the Con stitution. Commonwealth v. Slavski, 

245 Mass. 405. 

180 This is substantially the wording in Commonwealth v. Slavski, 245 Mass.

Analysts' Certificate in Criminal Prosecution as Violation of Right to Con frontation. A Massachusetts statute provides that a certificate of the analyst of the department of health "shall be prima facie evidence of the composi tion and quality of the liquors to which it relates" (1921 Mass. Gen. 

Laws, chapter 138, paragraphs 54, 56).

The defendant was convicted of keeping intoxicating liquor for sale. The only evidence of the alcoholic content of the liquor was the analyst's certifi cate in the form prescribed by law.

A similar statute has been enacted as to the analysis of drugs.18 184 E. Voluntary records and reports. Records and reports kept and made by a public officer not under obligation of law but voluntarily, usually are not treated as public documents within. this rule of evidence.185 Notes and maps of a city engineer 186 

Exceptions were taken to the admission of this evidence. Held, that the statute did not violate the constitutional right of the accused to meet the witnesses against him face to face. Exceptions overruled. Commonwealth V. 

Slavski, 245 Mass. 405.

The constitutional right of the accused to be confronted by his witnesses is not infringed by the admission of public documents as prima facie evidence of their contents. Heike v. 

United States, 192 Fed. 83 (2nd circ.); 

State v. Dowdy, 145 N. C. 432, 58 S. E. 

1002; State v. Donato, 127 La. 303, 53

So. 662. Contra, People v. Dow, 64 

Mich. 717, 31 N. Y. 597. In England an essential requisite of such documents is that the public at large shall have an opportunity to inspect them. 

See Sturla v. Freecia, L. R. 5 A. C. 623, 643. But this requirement does not obtain in the United States and the analyst's certificate is not objectionable on this ground. See 3 Wigmore Evidence, 2nd ed., par. 1634. It is significant, however, that the reports in question were prepared at the instance of the prosecution for use in this particular case and consequently the public document exception is not, as in the usual situation reinforced by the hearsay exception of entries made in the regular course of business. See Zachariah 

Chafee, Jr., "The Progress of the Law, 1910-1922: Evidence," 35 Harvard 

Law Review, 428, 442. For the reason that a certificate is strictly a document given out to an applicant for a particular purpose this objectionable lack of regularity of entry is not confined to liquor analysis; though in a situation such as that presented by the principal case, this objection is of particular force. Official chicanery presents itself as a possible danger. Without the "demeanor-evidence" brought out by cross-examination there is a tendency to jeopardize substantial rights of the accused. Only the countervailing necessity of conserving the time for public officials can justify the instant decision. 

Form of the Massachusetts statute has been upheld in Virginia. Bracy v. 

Comm., 119 Va. 867, 89 S. E. 149. See

"" Under Statute 1912, chapter 442, section 2, custodian of the records of the Danvers State Hospital, testifying as a witness, permitted to read from such records, portions showing the treatment and medical history of a patient admitted in 1896 and discharged in the same year in an unimproved condition. Raymond v. Flint, 225 Mass. 521. We cannot accept the view of plaintiff that hospital record is inadmissible if it may have "reference to the question of liability," even though it directly relates only to "treatment and medical history." The legislation was enacted primarily to relieve the physicians and nurses of public hospitals from inconvenience.

It is argued that under the broad language of the original act plaintiffs were confronted with hearsay statements which related solely to the cause of the accident. Under the present statute only such portions are admissible as relate to the treatment and medical history of the patient. It frequently must happen that facts stated therein, which deal in the main with the patient's medical history, may also be relevant to the issue of liability. For instance, statement of the location and nature of the patient's injuries, and essential element in the history and treatment, may incidentally tend to confirm or disprove his claim as to how the accident happened. So the condition of intoxication, in the case of a patient suffering from delirium tremens, would be important of his medical history and treatment; at the same time it well might bear upon the issue of liability. 

A reasonable and practical construction of the statute requires a record which relates directly and mainly to treatment and medical history be admitted, even though incidentally facts may have bearing on questions of liability. 

Improper application of facts recorded can be prevented by suitable instructions to jury. (Citing, Whipple v. 

Rich, 180 Mass. 477, 479.) Difficulty in the application of statute in present instance by reason of meagreness of record. Only objection made was a general one. Leonard v. Boston Elevated, 234 Mass. 280, at 482.

Plaintiff offered a part of the hos pital record. Following part was offered by the defendant and excluded. "Present illness, while patient was running along the road four days ago, she was run over by an automobile producing injuries as per local (left leg)"; offered under Statute 1905, chapter 330. 

Statute 1912, chapter 442. Clearly the purpose of the statute was to exclude any part of a record that referred to the question of liability; such evidence would be hearsay and contrary to a well established rule. Defendant relies on Leonard v. Boston Elevated Ry., 234

Mass. 480, an action for personal injuries, the recital “Odor of alcohol on breath." In the case at bar the complete record is annexed, from which it appears independently of the portion excluded that the plaintiff received an injury to her left leg; so much of the record as was competent was admitted and the defendant was not harmed by the exclusion. To have permitted the defendant to introduce that part which recited that the plaintiff was injured while she was running along the road" would have been in direct viola tion of the statute. XI. Military record. A certificate of honorable discharge from a proper military officer under statutes involving a soldier's settlement,256 has been held conclusive evidence of the cause of the soldier's leaving the service of the United States; it cannot be attacked collaterally to show that it was obtained by undue influence.257 The decision might have rested on the wording of the statute which the court interpreted 258 and rests in part on wording the United States Statutes at Large,259 then in force. However the court states "It is no new thing in law to depend upon military records as conclusive evidence of similar facts," and "It is more just to the soldier himself and more consistent with public policy and prevention of unbecoming litigation that the causes and motives of his leaving the service should be determined once for all, by the military officers of the government to which his service was due while the facts were recent and he had an opportunity to be heard, than that the question of his military loyalty or disloyalty should be left open to be collaterally contested between two municipalities in actions to which he is not a party and even after his death as often as any of his family may be so unfortunate as to fall into distress and need public assistance." 261 The honorable discharge was held "conclusive evidence of the cause and manner of his leaving the service." 262 If other records had been offered or if the soldier himself had been involved in procuring the certificate by fraud, possibly another result would be reached.263

XII. Acts of persons and corporations in public services—A. 

Generally. A presumption of regularity is attributed to acts of certain classes of persons in the public service. They and their agents though not sworn are under a duty to serve the public, and in the performance of that duty not to deceive or to act dishonestly 267 They are usually disinterested in the outcome of the controversy between the litigants and the public service is interrupted if they are compelled to attend at trial. The act to be proved in evidence in many cases is one which they could not recall, and their testimony if presented would consist of a statement that could well be assumed true in their absence,—namely that it was their duty to perform a certain act and that to the best of their belief they performed it. Cross examination could add nothing. The adversary is not injured by the absence of the various witnesses whose acts entered into the making up of the quasi public record. If he desires to present other facts in unusual cases he may call the required witnesses. This principle has been applied to carriers, to telephone companies, to the mails, and apparently to other concerns not so clearly within the public service.

XIII. Impeachment of public documents and acts-A. Ex ecutive and legislative acts.

A proclamation of the chief executive, 287 or an act of the legislature,288 or other body of the highest dignity,289 as set out in the official writing, is not to be impeached in a collateral proceeding by extrinsic evidence. The writing is the "act" of the state and as such is not to be offset by evidence of lesser dignity.

299 See following note. 

800 Credibility of witness for defendant attacked by evidence of conviction of assault with intent to kill, and sen tence to States Prison. Counsel stated in argument that "though the crime appeared to be a serious one on its face, and although the facts surrounding it could not be shown in evidence yet it might have been committed under circumstances which would not much affect the weight to be given to the testimony of the witness or his character for truthfulness. He then suggested a supposititious case to illustrate this argument "on objection the court refused to allow him to proceed on that line.'' 

This was held error. Though "no evidence is competent to explain the circumstances of the particular crime" and though "the guilt of the witness cannot be tried afresh and the record of conviction must stand" yet "Arguments of counsel concerning the weight which should be given to conviction of crime stand upon a different basis. It is permissible for them to magnify or palliate the moral degradation which as matter of sound judgment ought to be regarded as commonly accompanying the commission of the particular crime involved. Counsel may do this in any reasonable way.' 

Illustrations from drama, literature, history, personal knowledge, fancy and imaginary occasions "may be interwoven with fictitious inventions to point the argument. "Scrupulous care must be had not to suggest anything from which it might be inferred that the facts of a particular case or of any case are being stated." But so long as the argument is confined to hypothesis or imagery it is within the right of counsel. "It is possible that an exception to this broad statement of the rule may arise in an extraordinary instance of great public interest so widespread as to be matter of common knowledge." O'Brien v. D. Automobile registration. Though a registration of an automobile is to some extent an official adjudication and might be considered logically similar to a judgment in rem which could not be attacked collaterally, yet the court has decided that such registration may be attacked collaterally. Hence if an automobile purports to be registered in the maiden name of a married woman,314 its owner, or if the alleged registration certificate recites the wrong engine number,815 the alleged registration in the absence of statute is invalid. The substitution by the owner of improper number plates renders an automobile on which they are placed a trespasser in the highway.316 Substitution of a new motor after registration and many other acts and circumstances terminate or invalidate an alleged registration.317

E. Other documents. Usually certified copies of documents duly filed by individuals are but prima facie evidence of the contents of those documents and may be contradicted by proper evidence; but records of public boards and officers usually cannot be attacked collaterally.818 The various classes of documents have been considered heretofore in the text.

I. Introductory. The doctrine of Res Adjudicata constitutes an exception to the rules against the admission of opinion, of self serving evidence, and perhaps of hearsay. The phrase "Res 

Adjudicata" or "Res Judicata" is usually accepted as detached from the original quotations whence it has been abstracted. 

The entire legal maxim from which these words are taken is ,, 1 i. e. probably, "Res judicata exceptionem parit perpetuam, "A matter judicially decided creates a perpetual exception"; or "Res judicata facit ex albo nigrum, ex nigro album, ex curvo rectum, ex recto curvum, ," i. e. "A thing adjudicated makes white black, black white, the crooked straight, the straight crooked." Other latin maxims contain the clause." 

The law aims to end disputes. It gives a man his day in court; when he has had that day and has received a judgment of the court, that judgment carries with it the sanction and power of the state. When parties have litigated their disputes, and a final decree or judgment has been entered, that ends the suit, and by the result the parties are bound. If thereafter one party, being dissatisfied with the result, could again institute suit on the same cause of action, controversies might never end. Hence the law, when a controversy is determined by the decision of a court of competent jurisdiction," stamps the decision as "res judicata," and as between the parties recognizes it as final. If

issues materially involved in that adjudicated case again arise between the same parties or their privies," the court recognizes the prior decision as final and refuses to retry those issues. If a party relies on a previous adjudication as res judicata the burden rests on him to establish that the present matter in issue has been adjudicated. To establish a claim of "res adjudicata," the former judgment, the pleadings in the former case, the substance of the evidence, the judge's charge and any matter which logically discloses what issues were decided in that case, are admissible.10 The proof of these seems at first glance to violate the rule against the admission of hearsay." As far as the proof of the judgment itself is concerned this frequently does not violate that rule. But the evidence which explains the issues on which the judgment rests, though frequently consisting of repetitions of statements, and in that sense violations of the rule against hearsay, really is the best evidence and primary evidence in explanation of the meaning of the judgment, and hence not objectionable as hearsay. To establish what issues were decided by the former judgment these, whether strictly hearsay or not, are admissible.12 This kind of evidence, based as it is on the judgment of a judge, jury, or other officer or body, embodies an opinion and a conclusion,13 and hence violates another of the rules of exclusion.14 Such evidence also is frequently self serving and in that respect contrary to another rule.15 

Hence the principles of Res Judicata constitute exceptions to the rules of exclusion of evidence.16

The rule as to res judicata has thus been stated: "Res judicata is not a defense unless a judgment has been rendered on the merits. . . . A cause of action once finally determined, without appeal, between the parties, cannot afterwards be litigated by new proceedings either before the same, or any other tribunal." "The defense of res judicata is available when a judgment on the merits has been entered in an earlier action involving the same issues between the same parties." 29

The rule again has been thus stated, "The bar to a suit by a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction in another suit for the same cause of action between the same parties or those in privity with them, extends not only to those matters which were litigated and pleaded in the earlier suit, but also to those which might have been litigated or pleaded; but if the latter suit is upon a different cause of action the bar raised by the judgment in the earlier suit is limited to those matters which actually were litigated and determined." 80 The rule of evidence admits those facts legally provable which tend to establish the existence of the judgment, the sameness of the parties, the issues decided and such other matters as tend to show the judgment within the doctrine of res adjudicata. 30

A decision which summarizes in part the law and is frequently quoted is worthy of note. "Res judicata is not a defense unless a judgment has been rendered on the merits." . . . "A cause of action once finally determined, without appeal, between the parties, on the merits, by any competent tribunal, cannot afterwards be litigated by new proceedings either before the same or any other tribunal. But no such effect is attributable to a decree dismissing a bill for want of jurisdiction, failure of prosecution, want of parties, or any other cause not involving the essential merits of the controversy." 58 60 2. A judgment by a court of the jurisdiction in which the present action is tried, usually cannot be attacked collaterally. The court has expressed the rule thus: "It has long been settled in this Commonwealth that a domestic judgment rendered by a court of common law jurisdiction is valid as between the parties until reversed. Such a judgment cannot be impeached collaterally by the parties to it, the reason therefor being, not because of an apparent authority in the court to render the judgment, but because the remedy by review, or writ of error, is held to be more appropriate." 101 "The only remedy of a party who has been injured by a judgment erroneously rendered is by review, or by proceedings to reverse the same upon a writ of error." 102 "That a party to a judgment cannot impeach it collaterally, is well established in equity as well as at law." 108 The rule applies also to proceedings in the Probate Court and the

2. Method of attacking judgment collaterally. If the validity of a judgment is to be avoided by a collateral attack the proof must show that the court exceeded its jurisdiction of the subject matter,105 or that it had no jurisdiction of the parties,100 or that there was a fraud of which the judgment was a part.107 If an attorney without authority accepts service on a writ, the resulting judgment in some instances, may be void and attackable collaterally.108

D. Parties and privies-1. Meaning. In order to bind a party to the present suit, he and his adversary in the present suit must have been parties to the adjudicated suit,109 or in privity 110 with the parties. If all the parties, plaintiff or defendant, in the adjudicated suit are not parties to the present suit, apparently the doctrine applies only with limitations.111 

So a criminal conviction of a defendant is not admissible as res adjudicata in a later civil suit based on the same act.112

"In a suit in equity for an accounting brought against one of four tenants in common by the other two surviving tenants in common after the death of the fourth, the defendant filed a plea in bar setting up as res judicata a decree in a former suit in equity against the same defendant for an accounting, where it appeared that the plaintiffs in the two suits were not the same, the administrator of the estate of the deceased tenant in common having been a plaintiff in the earlier suit, and that the dates covered by the accounting in the earlier suit, which related only to the period terminating with the death of the fourth tenant in common, were none of them included in the second suit, it was held, that, not only were the items and the periods covered by the two suits different, but the parties were not the same and there was no splitting of a single cause of action, because the agency for which an accounting was sought in the first suit presumably ended upon the death of the fourth tenant in common, so that the plea of res judicata should be overruled.''

Decrees and judgments bind not only parties, but also their privies. The following quotations summarize the law and set out instances of privity. They indicate that mere interest in the outcome of a cause does not render parties privies. The first case summarized should be contrasted with those above. It involves a suit by an administrator who sues in his name as administrator, under Revised Laws, Chapter 171, Section 2, as amended by Statutes of 1907, Section 375, to recover for the death of his intestate under Revised Laws, Chapter 171, Section 2, as amended by Acts of 1907, Chapter 375. These acts are now em bodied in General Laws, Chapter 229, Section 5. The case holds that a "judgment obtained by the administrator of the estate of a woman in an action for personal injuries, which was brought by her in her life time and which the administrator prosecuted after her death, is not a bar to a penal action by the same administrator against the same defendant under Revised Laws, Chapter 171, Section 2, as amended by Statutes of 1907, Chapter 

375, to recover damages for causing, by the same injuries, the death of the plaintiff's intestate, to be assessed with reference to the degree of the defendant's culpability, to the use of the intestate's widow and children, or next of kin, there being no identity or privity between the administrator recovering compensation as the representative of the estate of his intestate, and the same administrator recovering the penalty for causing death as the representative of the widow and children or next of kin." 180 

The court in that case says, "These two divergent capacities do not come within any of the recognized classifications of privies. They are not privies in estate, as donor and donee, grantor and grantee, and such like relations; nor in is entitled to intervene in a bankruptcy proceeding. See Bankruptcy Act, sections 18b, 59f, 32 Stat. at L. 797, 30 

Stat. at L. 544. But these sections are permissive and not mandatory. See 

Gratiot State Bank v. Johnson, 249 

U. S. 246, 249. As to such creditors who are not parties to the proceeding an adjudication in bankruptcy is not res judicata as to facts or subsidiary questions of law on which it is based. 

Gratiot State Bank v. Johnson, supra; 

Manson v. Williams, 213 U. S. 453; In re McCrum, 214 Fed. 207 (2nd Circ.); 

In re Ulfelder, 98 Fed. 499 (N. D. Cal.);

They are as far from being privies as are administrators or executors of the same estate appointed in different jurisdictions."' 132 "They do not appear to be any nearer to privity than heirs and personal representatives of a deceased. They are not; and a judgment in a suit by a son against his employer arising from the employer's alleged negligence, is no bar to a suit by the father to recover for loss of the son's services, on account of the same negligence. The doctrine of res judicata does not apply.185

Method of proof. The burden is on the person who relies on res judicata to establish that the parties in the two cases are the same or in privity.142 In a small community, when the names of the parties in both suits are the same and somewhat unusual, a presumption may arise that the parties are the same. 148 Usually proof of the identity of the parties should be presented. Though the names of the parties are erroneously set forth in the suit in which the former judgment was rendered probably this, without amendment of the former judgment, may be explained in the later suit.145 When it is necessary to show privity, evidence of the facts which connect the privy with the party are admissible." 146

The principle which allows a party to identify the subject matter of a written contract under the Parol Evidence Rule,172 rests on the same judicial reasoning. In neither matter is the judgment or writing 178 avoided; it stands but its existence is explained and its subject matter identified. In the case of the judgment, no attempt is made to prove that the judgment is void; but the judgment alone does not establish all facts necessary to determine that the issues are res judicata.174 The party relying on that defense must prove that the issues now being tried previously were adjudicated.175 To do this he may present any available legal evidence.176 His opponent, on the same issue, to establish that the issue now on trial was not involved in the judgment, may show that the judgment was not a judgment on the merits, that the issues were not the same, that the suit was abandoned, or other matter which shows the adjudication not within the principle of res judicata.177 If these facts can be shown by the record, or a proper certified copy thereof, that should be produced; other evidence if the best evidence is not absolutely barred.178

F. Whether the suit in which the former judgment was rendered was instituted before or after the suit on trial. A former suit, when res judicata is involved, has no greater prestige than a later one.179 The adjudication, not the date of the writ, determines the finality.180 Hence, though the suit now on trial in which evidence of res judicata is offered, was pending before the suit in which that judgment was rendered was instituted, yet the judgment in the later case which covers the issues of both cases, is admissible in the earlier, and on those issues is final.181 There is but one variation to be pointed out. A clear case is one wherein a present defendant is sued on a policy of insurance issued under the Compulsory Automobile Insurance Law, or on a bond wherein he agreed to pay any judgment that might be entered in a former suit.194 (2) Disbarment. A similar case arises in matters of disbarment. If an attorney has been properly disbarred by the Federal Court, in proceedings to disbar him in the State court the judgment of the Federal court is entitled to weight. The State court will not re-examine the entire issue. It will inquire as to whether there was want of notice, or opportunity to be heard in the Federal court; and will consider whether there was "such infirmity of proof as to the facts found to have.established gross personal and professional misconduct and the want of private and professional character," as to give rise to a clear conviction on the part of the trial judge of the State court that he could "not justly accept as final the conclusion of the Federal court." The State court will also consider whether there is other grave reason for not recognizing the decree of the Federal court. If he is satisfied that there was want of notice and opportunity to be heard, or that the existence of said misconduct could not have been found honestly by the justice of the Federal Court, or that, for grave reason, recognizing the decree would result in injustice, he will not recognize as final, the decree; otherwise apparently he will so recognize it.195

No testimony, however, was taken or permitted by me to be taken at the hearing before me bearing on the merits of the issues presented in the proceedings in the Federal court. In determining the effect to be given to the judgment of disbarment in that court, I have adopted the rule prescribed in similar circumstances in the case of Selling v. Radford, 243 U. S. 

46, 37 S. Ct. 377, 61 L. Ed. 585.

(3) Guardian. The appointment of a guardian for an insane person is another matter worthy of consideration. "It is conceivable that one under guardianship may still have sufficient mental capacity to make a will, and, conversely, one whose guardian has been discharged may not have sufficient capacity to make a will." 196 A decree appointing a guardian, on similar issues, is conclusive only as to acts which are required to be done by a guardian and cannot be done by the ward. 197 It is to be noted that the parties bound by such decree are not necessarily parties to the action wherein the decree has been entered. 

Dismissal or appointment of a guardian, then, usually is not conclusive of the issue of insanity; but on that issue is probably admissible.198 conduct on the part of the respondent and the want of fair private and professional character, subject, however, to the limitations prescribed in the case cited, viz: (1) that there was no want of notice or opportunity to be heard in the Federal court; (2) that there was no such infirmity of proof as to the facts found to have established gross personal and professional misconduct, and the want of private and professional character as to give rise to a clear conviction on my part that I could not justly accept as final the conclusion of the Federal court; (3) and that no other grave reason exists which convinces me that to allow the natural consequences of the judgment in the Federal court to have their effect would conflict with my duty not to disbar except upon the conviction that under the principles of right and justice I am constrained so to do. The respondent admittedly had due notice and opportunity to be heard in the Federal court, was present and represented by counsel, testified at the hearing and was fully heard. The full transcript of the testimony at that hearing, which I had before me, the exhibits, the full and careful findings of the court and the arguments of counsel before me as to the strength and weight of the testimony, disclose no infirmity in the proof establishing the want of private and professional character and the guilt of giving misleading testimony with intent to deceive; nor has any reason been disclosed which convinces me that to allow the natural consequences of judgment of the Federal court to have their effect would contravene any principle of right and justice." There can be no successful contention to the effect that the trial judge did not follow governing principles of law as to the effect of the disbarment in the Federal court which he thus laid down for his guidance. There can be no doubt as to the soundness of those principles. We accept without further discussion the decision of Selling v. Radford, as stating the law of this Commonwealth. The differences between the facts of that case and those of the case at bar relate to immaterial details and do not affect the dominating principles set forth in that opinion."

(7) Discharge in bankruptcy. By the National Bankruptcy 

Act all creditors of the bankrupt duly scheduled,208 or notified," 1,204 who hold claims which are such as to be cancelled by a discharge,205 are bound by the decree of discharge,208 or by the acceptance and confirmation of a composition.207 The decrees of courts of bankruptcy bind all parties, privies, and persons within the above provisions.208 Hence a discharge, or acceptance and confirmation of a composition offer, is conclusive against the bankrupt's ordinary creditors that the bankrupt is not guilty of such acts as might cause under the act the refusal of his discharge.209 He cannot be sued in an action of deceit (a cause not dischargeable under the act),210 based on alleged fraudulent acts specified, but not proved, on a hearing wherein his discharge is as security for a loan and having paid the loan sued for the wrongful discharge of the mortgage. (9) Two persons found guilty of same offense: Similar civil cases. If two persons, not connected with each other as accomplices, conspirators, or otherwise, are found guilty in separate prosecutions of the same crime, the court tends to protect against this inconsistency and to grant, if possible, new trials to each.214 So of inconsistencies in civil matters. A party who claims that one defendant is liable for a transaction consummated by his agent, on procuring judgment against that party as principal, may not be allowed to recover judgment also against the agent as principal.215 (10) Other matters. If he declares on both notes, and puts in evidence of but one, because his pleading covers both, the judgment is res judicata as to both. He cannot later sue on the other note. He has had his day in court. If he puts in evidence of liability on both notes, but receives a judgment for but one the judgment is res judicata as to both. If he declares on "a note" and without objection proves or attempts to prove both, since the issue of both liabilities was tried and decided, the judgment is res judicata as to both. If he declares on but one, and "B" defends on the ground that both notes, at the same time and as a part of the same fraud, were procured by the fraud of "A," and "B" on that defense has judgment, the judgment is admissible in the later suit on the other note to establish the same fraud and it seems is res judicata.

I. Matters to be distinguished. Several matters similar to res judicata are to be distinguished. 

1. Stare decisis. A principle of law once decided by the court of last resort, unless clear logic requires a different conclusion, is not to be overruled. This is the doctrine of "stare decisis.' 

It applies regardless of who are the parties and what are the issues of fact. It applies to all decisions and all parties. It differs from the doctrine of res judicata for that principle requires that the parties and issues in the cases shall be the same.256 

2. Former jeopardy. Res judicata differs from the rule of former jeopardy; in that principle there need be no final judgment,—all that is required to bring a criminal defendant within the defense is that an attempt be made twice to bring him in "jeopardy of life or limb." Here it is well to note that if an offense is a continuing offense, extending over a stated period of time, no part of the period designated in the one complaint should cover the period in the other.857 

3. Impeachment by conviction: Proof of former conviction. 

A proof of former conviction of crime to attack a witness's credibility,258 is not based on the principles of res judicata. In a civil case as well as in a criminal one such proof may be presented. When the proof is presented in a civil case, of course, the parties are not the same. The method of proof of such conviction and the exception in cases in which a conviction may be proved by parol, are treated elsewhere.2 259 4. Law of the case-a. Generally. A ruling of law, if given over objection or perhaps if not objected to,262 rendered without exception, report, appeal or process of reservation for reconsideration by an appellate tribunal, though wrong, becomes the law of the case between the parties and they must accept it as final.268 

Illustrations clarify the principle. If parties try a case on the assumption that liability rests on certain principles, and the auditor who hears the case and the trial court so conclude, in the Supreme Judicial Court the plaintiff probably cannot establish his case on other decidedly different principles.264 "Rulings adopted by a trial judge at the request of a party and given by him to the jury as instructions become the law of the case, irrespective of whether they are too favorable to the party requesting them; and if, according to the law as thus stated to the jury, there is no warrant for a finding for the adverse party, it is error to submit the case to the jury." 285 A prior decision by the Supreme Judicial Court on the result of issues of fact as presented at a former trial, is final on those issues of fact; 266 hence when a court has determined that at the first trial the evidence showed a mortgage fraudulent, this establishes the status

The principle not only applies to rulings of courts. Decisions of the Industrial Accident Board,282 verdicts of juries, and finding of facts by the court,288 have a like effect. If at a first trial of a case certain rulings are made subject to exception, and before these exceptions are heard in the Supreme Judicial Court, the case is again tried, the rulings formerly made bind at the second trial; they are the law of the case until reversed. If they are later reversed the second trial is a mistrial and exceptions based on its impropriety will be sustained.284 This is because a material ruling in a case, though not in accordance with the law, binds the parties.285 If the Supreme Court of the United States, while a case which involves the same Federal question is pending in the State court, renders a decision on such Federal question contrary to the ruling of the State court, the result on the proceedings in the State court is at least doubtful.286 In the regular course of procedure errors could be corrected by declaring the trial in the State court a mistrial as indicated above.

The doctrine of the law of the case is not clearly defined or at present definable. Certainly every remark and ruling of the court which passes without objection and exception should not finally bind the parties.288 

Clearly if a party has two rights, though they are similar and arise in the same case, refusal of the court to recognize one as valid, does not bar the other; and a party who insists that his proper procedure in establishing his right is by one method, on receiving an adverse ruling, is not barred from procuring by another form of procedure, the desired result.289 There is no legal objection to the allowance for proper cause of the renewal of a motion previously denied.290 So also "mistake of a judge in failing to follow a rule of law, erroneously adopted, to a decision contrary to the rights of the parties on facts found to be true, does not require a new trial where it is manifest that a just decision, in the light of the governing correct principle of law, has been made." 291 Even a petitioner's attitude in pressing contempt charges as criminal, following a ruling of a master

I. Introductory. The administration of justice is greater than any code of law. Jurists attempt to reduce justice to rule. 

Practitioners seek rules of evidence. Some kinds of evidence have such unquestionable relative probative value, that though their admission violates fundamental principles which generally 985

guide a court in admitting or excluding evidence, yet justice requires that they be presented and considered. There has been a tendency by some courts to admit certain evidence of this kind under a doctrine termed "Res Gestae." It would perhaps be disrespectful to suggest that certain jurisdictions have used the phrase as a "catch all" to justify the admission of inadmissible hearsay,¹ yet certain jurists have, in admitting evidence, given to the words a meaning which they scarcely imply. 

The clause res gesta, the forerunner of the clause "res gestae," first appeared in the cases in about the year 1600. The words literally translated mean "the thing or things done” and imply the thing or things completely presently consummated and performed. Yet the term in other jurisdictions has been taken to admit evidence of words said long after the act in issue." 

This is a misconception of the phrase. 

The misconception referred to above arises from many causes, chiefly from the fact that certain anomalies of the law of evidence, logical in their result, but unsupported by mere legal reasoning, at an early date had established the admissibility of certain evidence. Examples of these were the complaint of the victim after a rape had been committed," statements made by a person before and after he actually had moved in a change of domicile," and statements and acts of bankrupts which tended to show that they had "kept house," or had absconded. These anomalies unfortunately came to be considered as based on the principles of res gestae. They logically should never have been

The doctrine of res gestae when it was established as including these acts readily attracted to it other acts not performed at the time of the main act. The doctrine then showed tendencies to override all principles which excluded hearsay. This danger was observed in time to save the law of evidence from an unwarranted infringement on the hearsay rule. The court at least in the last half of the last century began to recede from its former position and to carve out from the mass of matters which were tending to be considered as within this rule, certain principles now well established. Examples of these arise in the doctrine set out in the chapters on "State of Body and Mind,” ⁹ "Dying Declarations," 10 "Pedigree, 11 Declarations against 

Interest," 12 "Admissions and Confessions," 18 and "Matters of 

General and Public Interest." 14 As shown in the preceding chapters, the fact that certain evidence, admissible under the principles set forth in those chapters "accompanies an act" is referred to as material; thus the doctrine still savors of a basic principle of res gestae. 

Perhaps an analogy to the development of a science similar to the law is not out of place. At the beginning of the study of philosophy as a recognized science, in the days of Thales and the "physicians," that study included all professions and all branches of arts and sciences. 15 As each profession and science became more clearly defined, it was recognized as a separate branch of knowledge and so termed. Until then those intangible subjects, as yet undefinable, remained within the definition of philosophy.16 So of res gestae. Under this doctrine and in its name, evidence which clearly violates the fundamental rules of exclusion of evidence, and lies within no defined exception to those rules, will be from time to time admitted, until a clearer

II. An exception to the rules of exclusion. Evidence ad mitted under the so-called rule of res gestae frequently violates the rule against hearsay and against self serving evidence.17

Frequently it has been said that words uttered as part of the "res gestae" are not hearsay, but "acts." So in some cases they are. It is not intimated that all evidence of words admitted under this rule are in violation of the hearsay principle. When "A" and "B" make by an oral agreement or contract,18 what they say as showing the contract, is the contract,—the words are the acts; but when "A" tells a physician of his pain,19 or when a third person remarks on the condition of a tree,20 or when the victim of a murder says: "Dan Hackett has stabbed me,' repetition of these statements is hearsay which to be admitted must be supported by some exception to the rules of exclusion. >> 21 III. Definitions. Res gestae means the things done; as formerly used, in the singular, it meant the thing done. Logically the doctrine should admit every act and word not excluded by some rule of substantive law or evidence relevant to the main act on trial performed or uttered at the immediate time of the main act and directly connected with it, as a part. If the doctrine is thus confined, the evidence, even if hearsay, should be admitted without further restrictions and the jury should give it such weight and draw such conclusions as it sees fit. The numerous definitions of various courts confuse, rather than assist.22 Massachusetts thus has defined the doctrine: "When the act of a party may be given in evidence, his declarations made at the time, and calculated to elucidate and explain the character and quality of the act, and so connected with it as to constitute one transaction, and so as to derive credit from

the act itself, are admissible in evidence. The credit which the act or fact gives to the accompanying declarations as a part of the transaction, and the tendency of the contemporary declarations as a part of the transaction to explain the particular fact, distinguish this class of declarations from the mere hearsay"; and further: "Such a declaration derives credit and importance as forming a part of the transaction itself, and is included in the surrounding circumstances which may always be given in evidence to the jury with the principal fact. 

There must be a main or principal fact or transaction; and only such declarations are admissible as grow out of the principal transaction, illustrate its character, are contemporary with it, and derive some degree of credit from it." 28 

IV. Similar matters admitted without reference to res gestae. 

Certain evidence which would fall within the broadest definition of res gestae has been admitted without mention of that doctrine. 

Thus in prosecution for maintaining a disorderly house, evidence of solicitation of intercourse by female inmates of the house, their statements and conversations, though uttered in the absence of the defendant,24 have been admitted; 25 so in a suit which involved annoying sounds emitted by talking machines, evidence of exclamations and remarks by person who heard the sound, to establish its annoying qualities and loudness have been received; 26 likewise in prosecution for rape, without expressly mentioning res gestae, the court has admitted evidence of the victim's complaint made two hours after the attack.27 In a suit based on an allegation of false and injurious statements which led to the plaintiff's difficulties with his employer, letters from his employer to the plaintiff stating that if the defendant continued to annoy the employer by his letters, the plaintiff's resignation would be desired, are admissible.28 Similarly, statements made by agents of a surety company in refusing to issue a surety bond to the plaintiff, in effect that the reason was certain charges

A case which requires more than passing consideration pertains to the possession and sale of liquor." When police were about to search the defendant's premises, a person claiming to be the husband of a woman who had procured liquor on the premises, appeared and accused the defendant of selling liquor to his wife. His remarks, on account of the defendant's clear denial of the charge,32 were not admissible as admissions. The court, however, admitted the evidence possibly "as bearing on the intent of the defendant” and chiefly on the ground that "the excitement and resentment of the husband, expressed vocally, in the immediate presence of facts vitally affecting his domestic happiness was a part of the competent incident or at least an accessory of it." Such evidence was not to be considered proof of the truth of the facts stated."

V. Matters admitted as res gestae, admissible on other grounds-A. Introductory. The doctrine of res gestae has been given as the ground of several decisions which could have rested on other grounds. These decisions have not aided in crystallizing a rule which will define this principle. Some of those are now reviewed.

B. Statements of agents. An attempt has been made to admit as part of the res gestae declarations of agents. This has received little encouragement in Massachusetts. If an agent says at the time of making a contract that he represents a certain principal this statement is admissible not to prove the agency, but to show simply that the agent acted for another and not for himself.45 The agency to act for the alleged principal must be shown otherwise. Such a statement fairly is within the implied authority of the agent, and should be admitted on that ground for the limited purpose of showing that he acts as an agent.

Massachusetts has distinguished clearly the rule of agency from the rules of res gestae. The rules of res gestae have little or no bearing in a case which hinges solely on agency. "The rule which says that a man shall be chargeable with the acts and declarations of his agent or fellow-conspirator is not a rule of evidence; and when in stating and applying this rule it is said that the agent's declaration must have been made in and about his principal's business, while actually engaged in it, and as a part of the res gestae,—or again, when it is said of a conspirator's declaration, offered against his fellow-conspirator, that it must have been made while he was actually engaged in the common enterprise, about the affairs of it, and as a part of the res gestae, -the Latin phrase adds nothing; it is used as a compact expression for 'the business,' as regards which' the law for certain purposes identifies the two conspirators or the principal and agent. In such cases, evidently, the declaration may be about a past fact as well as a present one, so long as it comes up to the above-named requirements." 46

C. In rape. In prosecutions for rape, certain accusation and complaint made by the victim shortly after the act are admissible. This is said to be part of the res gestae. Such classification tends to confuse. The accusation and complaint occur after, sometimes long after, the attack.49 In this respect their admission in evidence violates the fundamental principle of res gestae that the statement must accompany the act.50 This peculiarity of the law of rape though now considered within the doctrine of res gestae, originally rested on grounds other than res gestae. 

That principle is clearly stated by Mr. Justice Holmes in the following quotation: "The rule that in trials for rape the government may or must prove that the woman concerned made complaint soon after the commission of the offence is a perverted survival of the ancient requirement that she should make hue and cry as a preliminary to bringing her appeal. Glanville, XIV, 6; Bract. fol. 147 a; Fleta, I. c. 25, sec. 14; St. 4 Edw. I St. 2. Appeals became obsolete and left rape to be dealt with by indictment before the development of the modern law of evidence. 

Lord Hale, after stating the old law as to appeals, quoting Bracton, went on to deal with the evidence upon an indictment for rape. Having stated that the party ravished might give evidence upon oath, the value of which would be affected by corroborative facts, he recurred to the matter of fresh complaint, and said that if she 'presently discovered the offence, made pursuit after the offender, etc., 'these and the like are concurring evidences to give greater probability to her testimony.' 1 Hale P. C. 632, 633.

Obviously this was suggested by and merely echoed the requirement in appeals, but it gave that requirement a more or less new turn. If it means what it has been taken to mean, that the government can prove fresh complaint as part of its original case, it are res gestae, if relevant to the matter in issue."' Wright v. Doe D. Tatham (1837), 7 A. & E. 355.

D. "Keeping house:" "Departing the realm:" Bankruptcy.

Ancient statutes made "keeping house" 58 or "departing the realm," 54 an act of bankruptcy,-one who remained in his dwelling or left the county to avoid service of process, might be adjudicated a bankrupt.55 To prove such act of bankruptcy evidence of remote statements by the bankrupt frequently were admitted.56 Unfortunately these admissions were based on the rules of res gestae.57 Though authority lies to the contrary," usually such statements seem admissible as admissions, 59 or at least as evidence of a state of mind. Because they were so frequently remote from the act of secreting or departure, and by no means accompanied it, they confused when spoken of as part of the res gestae.1 The decisions in which the evidence has been admitted as part of the res gestae have done much to make a definition difficult.

words which constitute the default are admissible." Two matters need consideration. If the principal admits in his statement that he at a previous time defaulted, is this admissible against the surety? If the statement was made after the principal's discharge from service, or after the obligation of the bond had terminated, if the surety is sued alone, it is not admissible.72 

If the surety and principal are sued jointly, as against the principal at least, and perhaps against the surety, it is admissible.78 

If the statement were part of the res gestae, joinder or nonjoinder of parties would make no difference. Perhaps the better reason for the admission of the evidence is that the principal during the life of the contract of suretyship impliedly is authorized to bind the surety by his admissions of default. While the bond is in force, the implied authority might well exist; on its termination it should end. Principles of agency, then, and not of res gestae, should govern this situation."7 

Frequently the offered statement of a principal is an admission of his default." This is offered to prove that he at a time before the statement defaulted, and is frequently admitted in evidence. This cannot be on the ground of res gestae." The res gestae of a default would be an act in violation of the condition of the surety bond. Usually when a principal admits his default he is not violating the obligation of his bond by disclosing his default, but is doing a faithful act,-disclosing his misappropriation or other wrongful act; thus disclosing is not a default. Matters within the doctrine of res gestae in such case must be matters which constitute a default. This evidence of admissions is better supported by an implied agency of the principal to speak to bind his surety.78

The effect of a joint bond, as distinguished from a several or joint and several bond, and the result of joint and separate suits against the surety and principal have been considered heretofore.79

Many statements which affect title have been referred to as admissible under the rules of res gesae; so statements derogatory of title of land or against inerest,81 or of one in absconding as to the ownership of wool,82 or of a person making a fraudulent conveyance as to his intent,88 or as to the intent to make a gift, have been admitted on these grounds. H. Statements in course of duty: Accounts: Train sheets. 

Evidence that is admissible under the rules which admit certain statements and entries in the course of duty has been referred co occasionally as admissible as part of the res gestae.85 So when accounts are to be proved under the rules at common law, evidence of the oral report of sales or charges, submitted by a clerk co a bookkeeper, supplemented by the oath of the clerk, have been admitted as part of the res gestae.86 Likewise train sheets, in which entries have been made of the course of trains as reported from station to station by telegraph, have been admitted under this doctrine.87 Both seem to be admissible more suitably as entries in the course of duty, or records of public and quasi public agents. They, and matters which should be distinguished from them, have been considered heretofore. 88

J. Accusation of murder at time of act: Commonwealth v.

Hackett. The court has established by the leading case of Commonwealth v. Hackett, a contribution to the rule of res gestae. 

That case has been reviewed as follows: 98 "In Commonwealth v. Hackett, 2 Allen 136, upon a trial for murder, a witness testified that, at the moment the fatal stabs were given, he heard the victim cry out, 'I am stabbed,' and he at once went to him and reached him within twenty seconds after that, and then heard him say, 'I am stabbed-I am gone-Dan Hackett has stabbed me.' This evidence was held competent as part of the res gestae. 

Bigelow, C. J., speaking of this evidence, said: 'If it was a narrative statement wholly unconnected with any transaction or principal fact, it would be clearly inadmissible. But such was not its character. It was uttered immediately after the alleged homicidal act, in the hearing of a person who was present when the mortal stroke was given, who heard the first words uttered by the deceased, and who went to him after so brief an interval of time that the declarations or exclamations of the deceased may fairly be deemed a part of the same sentence as that which followed instantly, after the stab with the knife was inflicted.

It was not, therefore, an abstract or narrative statement of a past occurrence, depending for its force and effect solely on the credit of the deceased, unsupported by any principal fact, and receiving no credit or significance from the accompanying circumstances. But it was an exclamation or statement contemporary with the same transaction, forming a natural and material part of it, and competent as being original evidence in the nature of res gestae.' The learned judge also said that the rule which renders res gestae competent has been often loosely administered by courts of justice so as to admit evidence of a dangerous and doubtful character; and that the tendency of recent decisions has been to restrict within the most narrow limits this

The offered evidence may be a resent inarticulate outcry of pain, or a statement of present ain or condition, or a statement of past pain or condition, or narration of past events which caused the injury; it may be ade to a layman, a nurse, or a doctor. The rule has been stated thus: "While a witness, not an expert, can testify only to such exclamations and complaints as indicate present existing pain and suffering, a physician may testify to a statement or narrative given by his patient in reation to his condition, symptoms, sensations, and feelings, both past and present. In both cases these statements are admitted from necessity, because in this way only can the bodily condition of the party, who is subject to injury, and who seeks to obtain lamages, be ascertained. But the necessity does not extend to declarations by the party as to the cause of the injury, which is the principal subject matter of inquiry, and which may be proved by other evidence.'' 116

A declaration made to a nurse does not fall within the rule which admits declarations made to physicians; a nurse in this respect stands as a layman.117

This kind of evidence constitutes an exception which is, and should be recognized as such. It should be admitted, not as res gestae but as evidence of the state of mind and body. Under his heading it has been considered above.118 To admit the evidence with full probative value to establish the facts related, is reasonable, would save time, clarify the issues, and avoid the repetition of details in the trial. If a witness has made statements to a physician who is attending him or is about to testify, ne doubtless will repeat his statements if required to do so on the stand, and will substantiate any statement made to the physician. It would seem proper to allow the physician, who generally can set forth the evidence more logically and quickly han the patient, to testify to these statements. The adversary may, if he desires, cross examine the party who made the statenents and thus attack their truth. This and similar matters have been considered in the other chapters of Part III.

C. B. In this case two points are submitted to our consideration. The first is whether Baron Martin ought not to have received evidence of remarks which passed between a gentleman, a passenger in the car with the female plaintiff, and the conductor of the car, immediately after the occurrence of the accident in question. The learned judge refused to allow Mr. Moir's proposed question, and so the jury did not hear what the remarks proposed to be given were, but we have them now before us. It appears that the plaintiff's wife, as soon as she got out of the car, and while standing on the spot where she had alighted, heard the gentleman say, 'By Jove, this fellow's conduct ought to be reported;' and the conductor of the car replied, 'He has already been reported, for he has been off the line five or six times to-day; he is a new driver.' Now, if these remarks can be considered part of the res gestae, I think they ought to have been admitted. But I am of opinion that they are not part of the res gestae. It is just this species of evidence which a judge ought to reject. The conductor's remark had no relation to the accident in question, but referred to the conduct of the driver at another time or times. His remark was well calculated to prejudice the jury against the driver, and might have induced them to believe in his culpability in the case before them, when in truth it referred to his conduct under perfectly distinct circumstances. If it had been admitted, a number of questions quite foreign to the issue would have arisen; for instance, whether the driver had been reported, whether he had been off the line, whether he was a new driver? The remark had no relation to the question before the jury, and was quite properly rejected. Now, as to the second point, i. e., that there was evidence for the jury of negligence; we have that the car toppled over;' that some one called to the lady to get out; that the window of a vehicle in close proximity was broken. No doubt there was a shock and an accident, but in all this I cannot find a scintilla of evidence of negligence to make the defendants liable. It lies on the plaintiff in this, as in all other actions, to make out facts from which a defendant's liability may be inferred. This he has failed to do, and on both grounds I am of opinion that there ought to be no rule. (Bramwell, B. and Channell, B., concurred. Their opinions are omitted.)" Agassiz v. London Tramway

VII. Acts and statements compared. Though questions of evidence under the doctrine of res gestae usually concern statements, the same general rules apply to acts. The res gestae are all the facts and circumstances which surround an occurrence. All attendant circumstances and acts that are part of the offense, tort, or transaction are admissible.188 So on a charge for operating an automobile while under the influence of liquor, evidence that the defendant just before the fatal collision which resulted, had been at a certain club; that one occupant of his car was killed at the collision,189 that the clothes of the deceased at the time of autopsy on his body smelled of liquor, that a bottle of liquor was found in his pocket, and that an occupant of the car on leaving the car staggered and smelled of liquor is admissible against the driver of the car.140 Evidence which tends to show what is customarily done in a house is admissible to show the house a disorderly house.141 Statements and acts at the time of making an alleged will, even if the same be now lost, to establish the testator's intent and to prove its contents likewise are admissible.142

VIII. Rule: Possible future rule-A. Stated. An accurate rule is not possible.148 The last word from the court confirms an earlier rule which covers many cases. "When the acts of a party may be given in evidence, his declarations made at the time, and calculated to elucidate and explain the character and quality of the act, and so connected with it as to constitute one transaction, and so as to derive credit from the act itself are admissible in evidence." 144 This quotation, however, contains but a part of the desired universal rule. Perhaps the rule as it will develop may be stated as follows. First, all acts and words part of the circumstances which constitute events of the main issue and are necessary to elucidate it-such as the words and acts

The prisoner was charged with manslaughter, in killing John Ferrall, by driving a cabriolet over him. On the part of the prosecution, a wagoner was called. He stated, that he was driving his wagon, and that he saw the cabriolet drive by at a very rapid rate, but did not see the accident; and he further stated, that immediately after, on hearing the deceased groan, he went up to him and asked him what was the matter." 

C. Phillips, for the prisoner. I submit, that what the deceased said in the absence of the prisoner, as to what had caused the accident, is not receivable in evidence. Gurney, B. 

What the deceased said at the instant, as to the cause of the accident, is clearly admissible. Clark, J. I am of opinion, that his evidence ought to be received. It is the best possible testimony that, under the circumstances, can be adduced to show what it was that had knocked the deceased down. 

The case of Aveson v. Lord Kinnaird, in which I was counsel many years ago, bears strongly on this point. Patteson, J., concurred. The evidence was received. Verdict-Guilty.' "" Rex v.

1. Formation and terms of contract: Making of wills. If an oral contract is in issue evidence of what was said and done at the time when it was made, if it tends to show that a contract was made and what the contract was, is admissible. If the alleged contract is written, evidence of acts and words to show that the writing was executed and delivered as a binding contract or the contrary is admissible.160 So in the making of a will evidence of what was said and done to show the testator's intent to make a will, is admissible.161 

2. Actions of mobs. The outcrys and actions of a mob at the time that it performs a material act,162 to indicate that it is riotous and to show its intent and general conduct is admissible as part of the res gestae.168 

3. Assault and battery. In actions, civil or criminal, acts and exclamations, statements and outcrys at the time of the acts of assault are admissible to show the general surrounding circumstances of the offense. 164 

4. Knowledge and notice. When knowledge of a defect is material, statements of bystanders who observed the dangerous condition, on the issue of knowledge or negligence in failure to have knowledge, are admitted. The court thus sums up an important case: "Tort for personal injuries occasioned to the plaintiff by the fall of a shade tree standing in Worthen Street in Lowell." "The defendant excepted to the admission of evidence of what was said by persons looking at the tree and its exposed roots while the street was being paved. This was not admitted to prove the truth of anything stated, but only upon the question whether the city had notice of the defect, or might have had notice of it by the exercise of reasonable care and diligence.

In the case at bar, it appeared that the earth had been dug away from the tree, and the roots had been exposed a day or more while the street was being paved. The street was

a thoroughfare near the centre of the city, and in that part of the street where the tree stood were two churches, a school-house, and private residences. The decayed roots were visible to persons on the sidewalk opposite, and the evidence tended to show that large numbers saw them. All this was competent evidence of the notoriety of the defect, and was not objected to. The acts of persons in looking at the roots were an important part of the evidence. From this it might be inferred that they noticed the decayed condition of the roots, and so that knowledge of the defect became general. But that evidence might properly be strengthened by introducing as a part of the res gestae the declarations which accompanied the acts, and which characterized them as acts that communicated intelligence of the condition of the tree to those who looked. The remarks made at the time rendered it certain that the view of the roots gave notice of the defect to those who then saw them. If the fact that these persons looked at the decayed roots was competent as tending to show the notoriety of the defect, then clearly the accompanying declarations which tended to show the nature of the act of looking were also competent." 185 

5. Torts: Carriers: Where a high degree of care required:

Statements by agents. In actions of tort by plaintiffs who are owed by the defendants a high duty of care, the rule admits unauthorized statements by agents, and others for whose acts the defendants are liable, to prove that they did not employ the degree of care in the matter on trial required by law. This applies to employees of common carriers. Statements to or by such agents, or persons, made at the time of the wrongful act tending to show negligence are admissible against the defendant.166 

These cases are to be contrasted with others where no special degree of care is required. As yet such evidence has not been admitted in those cases.167 However, the surrounding circumstances apart from statements, in all cases are admitted.168
